Leaving Plaid for the SMB tax bet

Alex Rampell

Hello, everyone. I’m Alex Rampell, a partner at Andreessen Horowitz, and I’m here with Jean-Denis Greze, CEO and founder of Town.

Jean-Denis Greze

Thank you for inviting me.

Alex Rampell

I think it’s cool that we worked together when you were CTO at Plaid and I led our investment in Plaid.

Jean-Denis Greze

Yes.

Alex Rampell

I heard you were leaving to start a company. Then I remember you told me you were working on a small-business tax tool.

Jean-Denis Greze

Yes, we had coffee.

Alex Rampell

We had coffee here, in Menlo Park or Palo Alto. I was a little upset. I was excited, and then I heard “small-business tax tool,” and thought, “Oh, this is difficult.”

Jean-Denis Greze

Well, now you know. The cards are on the table, right?

Alex Rampell

You didn’t tell me about it then.

Jean-Denis Greze

I know, I know, but I always have to keep a happy face.

Alex Rampell

You never know. That’s what I find so funny about this—I think you know the whole story. Ben Horowitz writes to me, “I found this incredible tool. It’s called Town. It changed my life.” And I’m like, “Okay, right? This is an app, so it falls under my fund. Wait, this is Jean-Denis’s company, but he does taxes for small and medium-sized businesses. This makes no sense at all. I’m so confused.” That’s what I wrote to you.

A week later, before I knew it, we’d become partners, which I’m extremely happy about. But maybe tell us what Town is about. I think everyone will be extremely interested to know how you got to this point since leaving Plaid. You left Plaid and started doing taxes for small and medium-sized businesses. Tell us about the founder’s journey from then to today.

Jean-Denis Greze

I left Plaid and took a few months off to be with my family because I knew that if I became a founder, I wouldn’t have any free time anymore. Then I started researching, in a B2B style, what markets would be interesting and where AI could really change the product experience. For many reasons, the tax space turned out to be very logical. Taxes contain a lot of text, and large language models work very well with text. You’re dealing with a lot of structured input formats, like financial statements and leases, so this seemed like an environment where we could take the process of generating a business tax return—which is very different from a personal one—and automate it.

I did what engineers do: we did a technical check to prove to ourselves that it was possible. We felt that, within the next 2 years, the process for small and medium-sized businesses—from financial reports and piles of paperwork to a finished tax return—could be automated using AI. We spent a year building it. I think it made sense, and it worked from a product perspective, but not from a go-to-market perspective. I have no doubt that tax preparation will be automated, but how do we effectively reach millions of companies and sell them this product? That raised many more questions than we expected.

A year later, we had what I would describe as a good business before the AI era. If I showed you the revenue numbers and growth in our first year—just under a million—and what we thought we could do in the second year, which was $2.5 million to $3 million in revenue, I think that, before the AI era, you would say, “That makes perfect sense.” But after the advent of AI, it became clear that this wouldn’t be a venture-scale company.

More importantly, we realized that incumbents would be able to use this technology to automate tax return preparation for their clients faster than we could gain market share. That’s a key point to think about if you’re a founder. Your advantage as a new player is that you move faster, can create a different product, and can use different go-to-market strategies. But the clock is ticking: how quickly can you get real word-of-mouth and market penetration before the incumbents, who have other advantages, do? They have distribution advantages, right? For example, before they can catch up with you and copy what you do effectively enough.

In the case of taxes, it seemed we wouldn’t be able to reach hundreds of millions in revenue before our incumbent competitors, because taxes can only be sold once a year.

Alex Rampell

Yeah. And it’s not just that they sell it once a year; the interaction itself fundamentally can’t be a tool for everyday use.

Jean-Denis Greze

That’s true. It doesn’t have much of a word-of-mouth effect, because few people brag about their experience preparing tax returns. Even when they do, they can only do it once a year, after they’ve filed their return. When you’re bragging about how good your experience was, that’s usually not the time when people are purchasing these services or looking for a new tax advisor or accountant. They’ll forget everything by next year.

Alex Rampell

That’s true. These gaps make hyperscaling extremely difficult. That’s why it wasn’t a great business idea. It’s funny: one of my best friends built a successful EdTech company, and one of the things he always complained about in EdTech is the same thing. You can only sell this technology twice a year. You can sell in the summer for the fall, and then there’s a short window at the end of the fall and winter season, right before the New Year. Those are the only 2 periods when you can realistically sell software to schools and school districts. He said it really limited his ability to hyperscale.

Jean-Denis Greze

I decided to forget about it when we were dealing with taxes. So, yes, we created Tax. A year later, after the first tax season, my co-founder and I went out a lot, drank a lot of coffee for a week, and really thought about the meaning of life, entrepreneurship, and capitalism. We decided we should do something else. We needed to find a better, more fertile market if we wanted to impact millions of people. There are better ways to achieve that goal.

Walking away from a working business

It was quite a bold act. Most people probably wouldn’t do that, especially since it’s not as if it wouldn’t work. At that moment, it felt like a failure, like we were failing. But I think one of the main motivations for building a business is this, right? As a founder, you have these moments—more often than you’d like—when you really ask yourself, “Why am I doing this?” For us, influencing the world was very important. We really wanted to create something important and help people. We stopped believing that we could have the kind of impact on the world that we should have, because we didn’t feel like we could scale the business fast enough.

The second reason we build a company is the real pleasure of working with our team. But everyone on our team has opportunity costs. They could work at Town or at many other great companies in the Valley. If you stop believing that you can achieve great results, it’s really hard to come into the office every day and look people in the eye when they say, “Hey, I’m having a hard time with this.” Or when you’re trying to convince a candidate to join your company and you know they have an offer from somewhere else that’s liquid, you think, “Who am I as a person? I have to believe in myself.”

Alex Rampell

I feel your pain. I’ve been there.

Jean-Denis Greze

There are a few things we looked at and said, “We have to make this decision.” The other side of the coin is that maybe we would have found a way out. You never know for sure, right? We’re very inventive people, so you can always try something different, but we just didn’t feel like we had the idea to make this a truly breakthrough business.

The hardest part is admitting to other people that you’ve failed, and to some of your employees. For example, our tax team wouldn’t have a future if we weren’t going to do taxes in the company. You come to this and think, “First of all, who cares what other people think of you? My friends will still be my friends, whether I succeed or fail. As for the workers, we’ll help them find their next job. We can treat them well in terms of severance pay and other things, and do everything right.” Then you realize it’s not as difficult a decision as you might have initially reacted to emotionally, and it’s the right decision. You start to feel that confidence, and then you just do it.

Alex Rampell

One last point: since tax filing is an annual affair, I think making a decision at that point in time was the only period when you could have done it.

Jean-Denis Greze

You can’t change course on April 16, after promising a bunch of people that you would do their tax returns. You can’t change course in January, after signing contracts with half of your partners. We had a window around October 15, about a month, where we could live in 2 worlds: a world where we continued to do taxes, and a world where we didn’t. After that, the doors were closing, so I think that time pressure helped us make decisions more efficiently than otherwise.

If you’re not in a cyclical business, you can always say to yourself, “Well, let’s try the next idea for a month. Let’s try the following thing for the next 3 weeks. Maybe this will work.” We had a short window when we could potentially change direction, and as soon as the window closed, we realized, “Hey, we have to decide right now. Otherwise, we’ll be here in a year, and after a year we’ll no longer have the capital to change anything.”

Alex Rampell

So from there, of course, the name didn’t change. It’s still Town. This is a good domain. Town.com is a very nice domain. But how did you get from that point to where you are now?

Jean-Denis Greze

We considered all 4 ideas quite seriously. No need to list all 4. Before Town became a thing, we were led by the question: Why hasn’t anyone created a great AI that works with email and calendar yet? We started asking this because when we were building a tax product, a lot of customers would say, “Hey, it’s great that you automate taxes, but I also spend a lot of time scheduling appointments with clients. When I go to meetings, I forget what the meeting was about. Clients keep asking me the same tax questions. Wouldn’t it be great if you could prepare the answers for me in advance?”

We understood from these needs that these aren’t very complex things, but no one had created high-quality AI for common work processes like meetings, preparing for them, following up on their results, responding to fairly simple emails that come in constantly, and preparing people for the workday. We started exploring this idea right around the time Opus 4.5 came out and agents, at least in programming, started doing more and more autonomous work. I’d say that this simple epiphany, plus the fact that the models suddenly became more autonomous, allowed us to achieve product-market fit very quickly.

Product-market fit is a magical thing. When you have it, you want to grab it with a death grip and pull on that string forever. So we didn’t sit back and ask ourselves, “What could the market size be? Will everyone want to do this? What does it mean to win?” We just thought, “Hey, we’re getting a huge response from users. Let’s dedicate a few months of hard work to this, study the market, and see what opportunities open up before us.”

In the process, we started to realize that most businesses operate through email and calendar, especially any role in business that focuses on external communications, like sales, business development, or recruiting. Companies collaborate mostly through email. So we thought, “The TAM must be big.” And this isn’t just in the U.S.; it’s all over the world.

When our customers started telling us what they liked about the product, we realized there was depth in the requests they made of us. It’s not as simple as connecting an LLM to your email. It takes a lot more effort to make the experience better every time. I’m not saying we’ve seen the “moat” yet, but there was enough complexity for us to understand that we could dive deep into this and create a great product.

We did this from December of last year until April and just kept going every day. Literally every day, the product grew by 1% or 1.5%. Our customers kept asking for more, the development plan was very clear, and we felt it was time to end the closed beta. We were ready to release the product to the world.

Alex Rampell

One of the things I thought was very brave about what you did is that you have product-market fit, but we also talked a lot about the PLG model. Do you choose big companies that say, “Hey, give us your product. I want it”? You understand that if the customer isn’t the user, the customer writes the check, and the user has to work with the product. If the customer isn’t the user, you can create a bad product because you’re satisfying the CISO and not the real needs of the user.

Jean-Denis Greze

My co-founder and I worked at Dropbox, and I think one of the important lessons for us is that you can take a world-class product and adapt it for the enterprise segment. Let me rephrase: It’s a difficult path, but it’s possible. It’s almost impossible to start with an enterprise’s compliance requirements and IT infrastructure and then try to make the product incredible from that starting point.

Until recently, maybe a few months ago, we believed that the greatest value was in improving the product, and that’s what we should focus on. Growth occurred naturally. We reasoned like this: if we got the product working and created a solid foundation from an enterprise, data security, and privacy perspective, we could later adapt the administrative part of the product to meet business needs. I think it was the right decision for us, especially given that consumer expectations regarding AI capabilities are growing. That will be the level of consumer services.

Our thesis is that CIOs and CEOs will say to themselves, “Hey, this amazing personal assistant I have in my private life—I want to have the same one for my company.” So whoever offers a corporate tool that feels like a consumer one will have every chance of winning. We decided, “This is where we want to be as a business,” and I think we’ve mostly succeeded in achieving that.

Now the question is, “Okay, we already have big companies using the product. How do we go from one corporate deal to effectively doing dozens of such deals? How do we meet data privacy and security requirements not just for a few clients, but for any large company?” That task seems much clearer now, and we can fully devote ourselves to it because the core functionality of the product is already at its best.

The iPhone moment for AI at work

Alex Rampell

Yes. You know, I agree, and I know you and I have talked about this a little bit. I remember when I had a BlackBerry.

Jean-Denis Greze

Yes.

Alex Rampell

Let’s say it’s 2007. The iPhone comes out, and Steve Ballmer says, “Nobody’s going to buy an $800 phone. It will be a failure. This is just ridiculous.” Microsoft eventually buys Nokia. But BlackBerry “died” pretty quickly because, at least in my theory, every CEO that year got an iPhone or something for Christmas, took pictures of their kids, and thought, “Wow, that’s really cool. This thing—not so much. Hey, I’m the boss here. Figure out how to make this thing work for us.”

Jean-Denis Greze

Yes, true.

Alex Rampell

I talk to a lot of company leaders, and it’s interesting that those who have seen the future say, “I need this.” Some people say, “Oh, no, AI doesn’t work that well. I use Watson,” or something like that. There are still many skeptics, but it seems that the iPhone has become a kind of watershed: people have learned the wonders of AI in their personal lives, but not in their work lives. Why is that? This is an open question. Part of it is about permissions, but I’d like to hear your thoughts on whether you agree with this vision and what AI for work will look like in the next few years.

Jean-Denis Greze

First, I agree with this vision. As a small digression, there was a company—I think it was called Good.

Alex Rampell

Yes, Good Technology.

Jean-Denis Greze

Yes, it was a corporate email client for the iPhone. It was an app. It was the ugliest app in the history of the world.

Alex Rampell

Yes, I used it.

Jean-Denis Greze

I think this isn’t just a BlackBerry story. I don’t want to be like Good. Good ultimately wasn’t a good business because people would say, “Yes, of course, you offer a corporate service for the iPhone, but in terms of quality you don’t reach the level of other applications.” I believe that’s our risk. We risk not only becoming like BlackBerry, but also becoming like Good, instead of people just using the Gmail app on their iPhone, because it combines convenience and corporate features that are truly important for business.

I often think about how everything happens at human speed. First of all, assistants as a category are only used by a few million people around the world today. We’re still at the very beginning of the adoption curve. I don’t think all CEOs have reached this point yet. Just like with the iPhone, it will probably take 6, 12, or 18 months for most people to experience this magic in their own lives. When that happens, the question will be how to implement it in the company.

I think it’s more difficult than the iPhone because agents work more effectively when they have access to the data and APIs that your business relies on. If they have access to these things in a secure, confidential way, they can do a lot for you. They’re only as smart as the data they have access to.

I think we see this path as follows: first, you need to come into a company and bring in a few people by simply connecting their email and calendar—not yet the systems of record—so they feel enough magic to say, “Oh, this will be very useful in my work.” As I said, for external roles, calendar and email are a real source of insights on how to automate some of the work. Then you can show up with an assistant and say, “I can help prepare for these meetings.”

I can adjust the presentations for the meeting to better reflect the corporate identity and update the latest figures from the PDF you were sent. From this, people will begin to feel the magic. Then you ask yourself, “Have I earned the right to ask you to connect your CRM? Have I earned the right to have you go to your IT department and ask to connect all the other tools?” I think this path will happen more at the speed of people.

You need the other side of the coin. You should have audit logs and settings that allow you not to share sensitive information with the agent. You need cost control for the CFO, so they understand that if the entire team is using AI, they can see what the money is being spent on and whether the tokens are being used effectively. This is the part that will take people more time to adapt to, because you’re still selling to a Fortune 100 company that has to be managed with a certain level of accountability.

As you move into smaller market segments, into small and medium-sized businesses, I think you have fewer of those requirements, and implementation will be much faster. So our current bet is to focus on product experience and self-service for the SMB market, and on security, compliance, and financial controls for the enterprise sector. We think we can cover this entire space.

Alex Rampell

Yes, I think there’s a Jevons paradox in the market for assistants, too. I have an executive assistant here. I trust her. I like her. I don’t want her to read all my emails.

In fact, this just happened. I was in London and thought I should go to dinner. I could have sworn I’d gotten an email about it. I wrote to Snap[?], my colleague, asking, “Don’t I have dinner tonight?” And he replied, “Yes, you do.” It wasn’t on my calendar. It was my fault, not my assistant’s. I hadn’t replied to the email, so they didn’t add it to the calendar. It’s not their fault; it’s mine.

How Town was born

But now it’s caught on, and it automatically scans everything for me. It reads my emails all the time. This is a situation where my firm is kind enough to provide me with an executive assistant. There are many people who don’t have one. You might say the market for executive assistants is pretty small because most people don’t have them. But if you can build one with silicon, the market becomes quite large. Then you find people saying, “I’m going to let someone read my email all the time,” something I would never do for privacy reasons. It’s a double Jevons paradox—a Jevons paradox of privacy.

For those who don’t know, the Jevons paradox is that when the steam engine became more efficient—when James Watt made a more efficient steam engine—the assumption was that demand for coal would drop. What used to take a pound of coal would now take an ounce. But demand actually increased a thousandfold, because now you had something that could do the job very efficiently. It seems like this probably applies to the assistant market as well.

But I’m curious: how do you define your market? Is it some kind of assistant? That seems like too narrow a definition.

Town as a token-allocation machine

Jean-Denis Greze

I think of this market as an attempt to create a product that works with people to find more and more opportunities to use AI to do their jobs better. In some cases, I think of our product as a token distribution machine. We try to give people options for where they can apply the tokens, and then they can choose whether they want the outcome.

As tokens get cheaper, there are more and more places where you could apply them that you wouldn’t use them for with today’s expensive tokens, and certainly wouldn’t use people for. The simplest example is writing preparatory notes for every meeting you go to. Even if you have a personal assistant, they won’t take the time to write perfect preparation notes for every 30-minute meeting. That’s an irrational use of time. But an LLM can do it for pennies.

Suddenly, it’s possible for everyone to have prep notes for every meeting, including research on who else is in the meeting and whether they’ve said anything on X in the last week that might be relevant. All this niche research now makes sense because it’s much cheaper. Our job is to find more and more of these things and ask you, as the user, “Hey, do you want us to do this for you?”

I’ll give you another example I’ve been really into lately. If you’re a small business owner running a restaurant in America, your wholesalers—the people you buy ingredients and other things from—probably email you an Excel spreadsheet or PDF with prices for their entire range once a month, or maybe once a quarter. These are thousands, if not tens of thousands, of products, and prices are constantly changing. If you own a restaurant and have a part-time finance person, that person should check once a quarter how prices have changed, to see if you can order something from other wholesalers or if you’re being overcharged because the price of something has gone up 20% or 30%.

Mostly, you don’t do that. It’s a rare occurrence, and while it could save you money, it’s a hassle, it’s not part of your operating activities, and you don’t have a full-time employee to do it. With AI, you can set up a process to run once a month and perform an analysis. You can literally create a tool like this for yourself in five minutes with a prompt. If it doesn’t find anything worthwhile for 11 out of 12 months, it’ll cost you about $1 a month. But the interesting thing is that in the one month a year when it finds something, it’ll save you hundreds, if not thousands, of dollars.

Now what may or may not have been worth the effort is worth doing at least once a month. You should do this every time there’s a change. It might be worth doing every day if your wholesaler changed prices every day, but that’s not the case. Our job is to show this opportunity to the restaurant owner. It’s not that they’re not smart or don’t understand their business well; they do. They just won’t find this valuable unless we show them. So we’re saying, “Hey, listen. Do you want me to make sure your wholesalers don’t change prices in a way that hurts your business?” The answer is, “Of course, do it.”

You don’t really care how often it runs. You care that every now and then you get an email saying, “Hey, you should probably move these things to another wholesaler. They’re offering a discount, or this place is really raising prices on these items, and it’s getting a little too expensive. Maybe you should take those items off the menu.” It’s not high math. But you need a product that tells you this is possible and does it for you.

Horizontal vs vertical

Jean-Denis Greze

I think most AI products today will have very similar capabilities. Most of the tools in the work context will be able to do the same things. So the differentiator—the thing that has been the main thing in Silicon Valley for a long time, having product features that are ahead of the market—is going to be harder and harder to sustain as an advantage.

We can put that aside and have an interesting conversation about the fact that I think the unit of value in software has shifted from the app to the computer. But what that really means is that it’s going from the app to everything a human can do, and a human can do almost everything with a computer. So we’re completely abstracting away from the app level, and I think the value at the app level is going to go down.

If the capabilities are the same, how do you build a successful company? Our view is that, as AI gets better, it will be able to tailor the product to each user’s needs much more specifically. If you’re an electrician who signs up at Town, the things we recommend you automate during onboarding will be very specific to electricians. If you’re a venture capitalist, they’ll be very specific to venture capitalists. If you’re an executive assistant, they’ll be specific to EAs in that industry, and so on.

How do you do that? The models aren’t sophisticated enough yet that, if you just ask a model, “Hey, recommend things Alex, who’s a venture capitalist, could automate with Town,” you’ll get more than pretty good surface-level suggestions. You won’t get anything really deep. And we don’t look at user data, because part of being ready to work with enterprise customers is that you can’t look at user data. So we look at the overall metrics for who our most active users are on the platform, and then we go talk to them. When we talk to them, they tell us what they’ve automated.

We can talk to 10 power users who run restaurants. In those conversations, we might notice that there are 5 things they all do in common. Then we sit down as a team and prototype automations, which we call “routines,” for restaurant owners—things we think are really useful, like one that deals with wholesale suppliers. We use those as a foundation. When someone comes on board, we look at their email and inbox and say, “It looks like you’re a restaurant owner.” Then we offer them templates of problems and potential solutions for restaurant owners that we think are really good, based on what we’ve extracted from those interviews.

You sign up and start using the product. Then the AI gets better, and we talk to more restaurant owners. Now we don’t have 5 things we can do for restaurant owners; we have 15. It’s still a little manual, but it can be sped up. You can automatically schedule interviews, offer restaurant owners a free Amazon gift card, and interview them with AI to see what they’re doing with your software. So you’re not working at human speed anymore; you’re working at AI speed. That library gets better, and the models get better. The recommendations then rely less on the library, and we think that over time, with this approach, we’ll be able to offer 80/20, highly personalized software for people.

People in the future won’t just have one role. You might be a restaurant owner, but you also manage your restaurant’s finances because you don’t have a separate person for that. You might also have a vacation rental property. You want your Townie to be good at all 3 things. And you have 2 kids in school, and it can help you plan their summer classes. This is completely custom software, and we believe you can use AI to build it.

Another strategy you’re seeing in the market, and what I think the labs are doing, is the FDE approach. That’s a completely different thing. With FDE, a person comes into your business, learns how it works, and then builds custom software using AI from the labs to serve you better. If you’re a company willing to spend about $5 million a year paying OpenAI for FDE, that looks pretty good right now. But I think that over time, as the models get better, the FDE approach will actually get a lot worse, while our approach—using automation and AI to build custom software—will scale a lot better.

We’re betting on starting with PLG: small and medium-sized businesses that are very tech-savvy, because our approach scales really well there. We’re going to let others compete in the enterprise sector with this more hands-on software. Our bet is that the knowledge we gain from the flywheel of development will make us more successful in the long run than these more individual approaches.

The second reason, which is very important, is our position that, as a business, you truly own the data, memories, and contacts that are created in Town. In the old world, before computers, businesses had different assets: physical assets, and maybe human assets. Now, increasingly, people might call it context, but there’s a set of assets—everything AI knows about your business to help you run it effectively. I believe you should own that entire set. You should own it to the point where, if there were ever a better solution than Town, switching to another solution would take a day. That’s what I’m selling: the idea that you want to own this asset.

If you look at people who hire developers to build software for them, they’re actually trying to make it harder for you to switch to someone else. So that’s the second reason. First, you want neutral intelligence, but you also want an application layer above the intelligence that allows you to switch easily. When you build a startup, you always have to think about what the future will look like. I believe that in the future, human participation will be minimal compared with what we see today. Those who have more money than time won’t use CamelCamelCamel, and those who have more time than money will take advantage of it. But wait a minute: What if you could give everyone who has more money than time all these tools, so an agent could do it for them? Of course they would use it.

Jean-Denis Greze

This is an IQ test.

Alex Rampell

These things are definitely going to become much more common. Sometimes you don’t even have to imagine what could happen. Just look at coupons.

Jean-Denis Greze

Yes.

Alex Rampell

You shouldn’t use a coupon if you’re rich, because it takes too much time. You’ll spend about 2 hours searching for the right coupon. But this is another arrangement that’s falling apart, because it was a very convenient way to divide the world.

Jean-Denis Greze

Yes. I mean, the Amex premium membership is the same thing. Now it just optimizes all your advantages.

Alex Rampell

Yes, all your advantages. The unused benefits model is dead.

Jean-Denis Greze

Yes, and so we’ll all be abusing all our Chase and Amex benefits, and they’ll have to change that. This is unprofitable for both, because then it will become a hostile confrontation. It’s a kind of confrontation between hostility and synergy.

Alex Rampell

But the bottom line is that I think supply aggregation has become much less valuable than it used to be. It used to be very important because human attention was limited, and now supply aggregation is much less valuable because human attention can be automated.

Jean-Denis Greze

Yes.

Alex Rampell

It was a great conversation. Thank you again for coming today.

Jean-Denis Greze

Yes, thank you very much, Alex. It’s always nice to chat. Thank you.

注：BidClub 仅提供原文全文文稿；中文版为标题、要点与摘要的译文。

来源：YouTube

item.title: 50亿美元收购案5年后：Apollo的雅虎打法
item.description: Lanzone称，Apollo基本收回48亿美元收购成本，资金来自早期回款及出售AOL等资产。重组关停年耗数亿美元的亏损广告技术业务，让雅虎库存接入竞争性需求，同时保留DSP。Scout让雅虎重掌搜索；Lanzone未承诺IPO，也不愿称用户分发是护城河。
item.content:encoded:
Sourcery · Jim Lanzone、Molly O'Shea · 2026-10-19 · 56 min · 原语言 EN

Lanzone称，Apollo基本收回48亿美元收购成本，资金来自早期回款及出售AOL等资产。重组关停年耗数亿美元的亏损广告技术业务，让雅虎库存接入竞争性需求，同时保留DSP。Scout让雅虎重掌搜索；Lanzone未承诺IPO，也不愿称用户分发是护城河。

要点 TL;DR

  • Lanzone称，Apollo基本已经收回收购雅虎的成本，同时仍保有押注增长反弹的机会。这笔48亿美元的交易让Verizon保留了10%股权；早期现金回流，以及出售AOL等资产，帮助它成为“Apollo史上回报最快的交易之一”。按他的说法，雅虎现在相当于“拿着赢来的钱继续玩”。
  • 广告技术业务重组通过削减成本、改善雅虎广告库存的变现，提升了经济效益。接手的业务持续亏损，每年运营成本高达数亿美元，还限制雅虎获取竞争对手广告需求。管理层于2023年2月裁掉2,000多人，关闭SSP，将原生广告业务以25%股权卖给Taboola，并把DSP作为“皇冠上的明珠”保留下来。
  • 雅虎与用户的直接关系及登录用户群，是其广告和AI布局的基础。在总计7亿用户的组合中，体育和财经业务的月活用户都超过1亿；约75%的用户直接访问雅虎，每天约75%的用户处于登录状态。Lanzone称，第一方数据帮助DSP在正面对比测试中赢下10场中的9场，但他仍不太愿意把分发称作“护城河”。
  • 新产品和年轻用户为雅虎的复苏提供了可量化的增长依据。大学梦幻橄榄球的用户中，40%是雅虎新用户；今年Yahoo Fantasy创下NFL相关业务史上最好的3个单日表现。超过一半的受众是Z世代或千禧一代；Lanzone称，营销让Z世代的“品牌喜爱度”提升了约31个百分点，但产品修复仍要先于推广。
  • Scout通过轻量级模型处理雅虎自有数据，让雅虎重新掌控搜索。在外包搜索17年、主要交给Microsoft之后，雅虎会先整理搜索历史、出版商信息、知识图谱及可用的用户数据，再交由模型处理；Scout上线时使用Anthropic的Haiku。Lanzone强调，Scout能提供有差异化的实时答案，并称重新拥有搜索资产“改变了一切”。
  • 雅虎面向消费者的使命为AI布局划定边界，也让Mail拥有现成的切入点。作为“互联网可信赖的向导”，雅虎要通过信息聚合和有用分析，帮助用户实现个人目标。面对智能体请求访问邮件和日历，Lanzone表示，已有用户依赖雅虎的产品处理这些事务，雅虎有责任提供帮助；他也承认，雅虎之所以受到较好的对待，部分原因是“我们没有在开发大型语言模型”。
  • Lanzone称，私募股权投资者期待最终退出，但他没有承诺IPO，也没有判断市场时点。他纠正了O’Shea关于雅虎将上市的预设，并称有些搜索初创公司的估值是雅虎的6倍，尽管雅虎已有用户、收入和盈利能力。被问及市场周期何时见顶时，他回答：“我要是知道就好了”；他真正有把握的是雅虎的韧性。

摘要 Digest

1. Apollo收购雅虎；此前Verizon已将其与AOL合并

  • Lanzone称，Apollo以48亿美元收购雅虎，Verizon保留了10%。此前Verizon先后收购AOL和雅虎，并将两者合并；Lanzone说，这些资产当初的收购价约为Apollo出价的两倍。在Verizon手中，合并后业务的使命转为支持5G。交易于2021年9月完成，雅虎因此成为“一家运营着30年老品牌的5年新公司”：一家有空间重设优先事项的新运营公司。
  • O’Shea认为，这笔交易不同于常见的剥离资产式扭转。Lanzone称，Apollo看到了“非对称的上行空间”，并招募了一支增长团队；如果任务只是防守，这些人不会加入。“我做扭转，只为走到有意思的那一段”——为既有用户群投资、建设。他将私募股权的目标描述为实现某种退出，比如IPO或出售。
  • 他上任的前6个月主要用来评估团队、了解哪些内部数据与外界认知不符。“我不会第一天就大刀阔斧地动手。”他此前操盘扭转的经历提供了参照：Ask Jeeves股价在出售给IAC前上涨了50倍；CBS Interactive的受众则从7,000万增至2.2亿。雅虎已经拥有最难买到的资产：流量。

2. 去中心化管理、重申使命，推动雅虎收窄业务组合

  • 雅虎在各个市场分别与对手竞争——财经业务对标Bloomberg和CNBC，体育对标ESPN，Mail对标Gmail——但接手时，却由一位产品负责人、一位技术负责人和一位内容负责人横跨所有品牌。Lanzone在CBS Interactive也犯过类似错误：“我试过让所有人都向我汇报。”他对产品的热情，反而成了运营瓶颈。
  • 2022年的重组任命了更具创业精神的总经理，为他们配备独立的产品、技术和内容负责人，并分配商业支持资源。部分管理者来自内部，另一些则是从外部聘请的专业人士。CEO的职责转为制定计划、督促管理者承担责任并协助执行，同时让各业务独立运作。
  • 搜索是一个历史教训。Lanzone认为，雅虎的“原罪”最终是在2000年6月把搜索交给Google；此前雅虎已将服务外包给Inktomi等公司。当时搜索还没有商业模式，看起来像个成本中心，尽管他认为92%的互联网访问都从搜索开始。为一个被视为非核心的业务省钱，最终让雅虎交出了核心能力。
  • 回归1995年的使命——成为“互联网可信赖的向导”——意味着帮助消费者实现个人目标，从去泰姬陵旅行，到在梦幻体育中击败UCLA的朋友。Lanzone排除了转型为企业或B2B公司的可能。信息聚合和“提供背景信息的内容”，包括梦幻体育和市场分析，都符合方向；白宫记者团队和TechCrunch则不符合。私有化让雅虎有空间做出这些调整。

3. 广告技术重组止住亏损，并释放广告库存收益

  • 首个剥离的是与Akamai竞争的内容分发网络EdgeCast：雅虎在这一领域没有“经营的正当性”。TechCrunch也被出售；规模最大的剥离则是AOL，于前一年10月售出。
  • 雅虎和AOL各自都收购了30多家广告技术公司，最终形成由SSP、DSP和原生广告组成的“三条腿凳子”。这套业务持续亏损，每年运营成本高达数亿美元。更糟的是，雅虎自己的广告库存只能接受这套业务投放的广告，限制了它引入竞争性需求、优化收益的能力。因此，重组既要解决直接亏损，也要释放受内部优先安排限制的收入。
  • 2023年2月，雅虎裁掉了2,000多人。尽管有买家感兴趣，公司仍关闭SSP，以避免在雅虎页面上给予任何一方优待。原生广告业务以Taboola 25%的股权为对价出售。DSP则被保留下来：管理层认定它是值得继续投资的“皇冠上的明珠”。

4. 先修复产品，才有资格推出新赌注

  • “电子游戏的关卡不能跳着打。”Lanzone这样告诉团队。有些产品近10年来几乎没有得到改进；当务之急是引进优秀的产品人才，修复用户体验。每位总经理至少创办过一次公司。新产品发布和品牌投入，则是运营基础扎实之后的回报。
  • 产品判断要从数据出发，但不能陷入无止境的实验。他在UCLA读书时朋友们对梦幻体育产品的抱怨，是有用的输入，却未必代表普遍问题。雅虎可以大规模开展A/B测试，也可以借助AI加快实验；但团队仍需要判断力。他认为，团队想要“同时做200个测试”时，可能就变得过于谨慎。
  • College Fantasy Football带来了明确的拉新成效：40%的用户是雅虎新用户。另一个结果是，Yahoo Fantasy今年创下NFL相关业务史上最好的3个单日表现。这些成绩体现了他对业务扭转的期望：利用现有分发渠道打造新产品，扩大用户群。
  • 雅虎的品牌受众比外界印象更年轻：超过50%的受众是Z世代或千禧一代，75%的Z世代使用雅虎或其某款产品。Lanzone称，包括Cardi B营销活动在内的推广，让Z世代的“品牌喜爱度”提升了约31个百分点。他认为，雅虎有大量尚未被唤起的“品牌喜爱度”。

5. 与用户的直接联系，让受众价值不止于规模

  • Yahoo Sports和Yahoo Finance的月活用户都超过1亿；三分之一的美国人拥有Yahoo Mail账户。雅虎全业务组合每月触达7亿用户，在美国排名前5，通常在全球也位居前5。新闻业务仍是前三大聚合平台之一，战略重心已重新放在分发出版商的报道上。
  • 约75%的用户直接访问雅虎——这是全网最高的比例之一；每天约75%的用户处于登录状态。Lanzone将这种用户黏性和第一方数据与广告表现联系起来：他说，DSP在正面对比测试中赢下10场中的9场。尽管如此，他仍不太愿意把分发称作“护城河”，因为如果产品不再值得用户选择，这项优势就可能消失。
  • 谈到信任时，他承认雅虎受到较好的对待，部分原因是“我们没有在开发大型语言模型”。他也承认此前发生过数据问题，并称信任“失去了就无法挽回”。Mail是“你人生的保险库”；智能体请求访问邮件和日历，说明其中存在机会，但帮助用户本来就是雅虎的责任。他将雅虎长期以来的表达风格形容为不拘一格、积极、带点调侃；营销应该让人发笑，或做得与众不同，而不是试图让人落泪。

6. Scout将自有数据转化为由雅虎掌控的战略性搜索产品

  • Scout于今年早些时候上线，整合了30年的搜索历史、与出版商的合作关系、知识图谱，以及可用时的用户数据。Lanzone称，雅虎仍是美国排名第三的搜索引擎。雅虎先整理这些输入，再交给轻量级模型处理——上线时使用Anthropic的Haiku，如今也使用其他模型——最后由雅虎自行呈现模型返回的答案。他的主张是，雅虎的数据能带来独特结果。
  • 按他的说法，实时信息是最明显的差异化优势。雅虎受常青内容被语言模型吸收的影响较小，但他也称，雅虎自己的内容同样曾在未经许可的情况下被拿走。与出版商的合作关系旨在强化流量回流：“把流量送给他们是我们的职责，也是我们的传统。”他希望雅虎与出版商合作，而不是与他们竞争。
  • 雅虎将搜索外包了17年，主要依赖Microsoft，使一个重要的产品和收入来源受制于外部供应商。Microsoft仍是雅虎重视的合作伙伴，但重新拥有这项资产“改变了一切”。Lanzone在搜索领域工作的前10年里，结构化答案一直是他关注的产品方向；如今，搜索不再只是“10条蓝色链接”，也让他重拾这份长期兴趣。

7. 现金已基本收回，退出选择仍然开放

  • O’Shea称，Apollo几乎已经收回收购价；Lanzone确认，这笔交易是“Apollo史上回报最快的交易之一”。他将其归因于交易本身带来的早期现金回流，以及包括AOL在内的资产出售，而非快速偿还投资的压力。“现在我们基本是在用赢来的钱继续玩”（playing with house money）——这就是他对剩余上行空间的描述。
  • 他纠正了O’Shea关于雅虎目标必然是IPO的预设：雅虎更像一家“处于IPO前后期阶段的硅谷公司”，投资者期待最终实现某种退出。IPO或出售都有可能；他没有给出IPO时间，也没有确认一定会上市。他称收入和盈利能力“都非常好”，但没有披露具体数字，并暗示增长可能会让人意外。
  • 收购纪律取决于初创公司的定价。有些估值高于雅虎的公司，用户数不到雅虎的0.1%；Lanzone称，有些搜索初创公司的估值是雅虎的6倍。他说，雅虎无法与一家用户规模达数十亿的公司合并，却由雅虎贡献全部价值。雅虎收购过一些规模较小的初创公司：它们的产品有用，团队也表现出色；这不只是为了收人而进行的收购。
  • 被问及市场泡沫何时破裂时，他的回答是：“我要是知道就好了。”他认为，从2010年代中期起，人们一再预言市场崩盘，助长了可能代价高昂的保守倾向。雅虎经历过多轮低迷，他预计公司能挺过下一轮。他愿意迎来持续50年的黄金时代，但也说：“即便没有，我们也会没事。”

8. 经验有帮助，前提是领导者不断改进产品

  • 最顽固的反对往往来自老用户：“他们不想让你动他们习惯的东西。”即便新界面提供的功能相近，UI改动也可能导致用户离开。但如果永远保留旧界面，就会失去未来的用户。Lanzone认为，这种矛盾无法回避，尤其是在梦幻体育领域。
  • 业务规模越大，越容易“开车时打瞌睡”：保守的管理者会丢掉产品焦点，初创公司则不断向前。关键失误可能外界根本看不到——没有收购的公司、没有推出的功能，或被卖掉的资产。他偏好的运营姿态是“只有偏执者才能生存”（only the paranoid survive），由以产品为导向的领导者持续为用户冒险。
  • IAC的经历揭示了集中管理的风险。IAC旗下有60个品牌，却没有通用基础设施；Barry Diller曾试图建立共享运营架构，Lanzone称Diller后来对此感到后悔。2008年与John Malone的争执引发了拆分，也改变了IAC持有Ask的理由；搜索业务随后被关闭并外包给Google。Lanzone钦佩Diller的大胆和原创性，也亲身经历了这一结构调整的后果。
  • Tinder的经历再次说明，外界认知可能具有误导性。Lanzone保留了Tinder原有管理团队，他们的使命是“帮助人们找到自己的另一半”，尽管外界给Tinder贴上了约炮应用的标签。他说，若不是为了雅虎，自己不会离开Tinder：他早在2010年的一条推文里就称雅虎是“终极扭转案例”。在获得执掌雅虎的机会之前，他就相信雅虎值得拥有优秀的产品。

全文文稿（原文）

Speaker 0 Apollo has been one of the most prolific deal makers of 2021.

Speaker 1 Private equity powerhouse.

Speaker 0 Apollo would be acquiring Yahoo from Verizon for $5 billion.

Speaker 2 Yahoo is one of the most iconic brands in internet history.

Speaker 1 This is a legacy brand.

Speaker 2 The original sin of Yahoo was giving search away to Google in June 2000. There’s this myth on the internet that they were defeated by Google because they took their eye off the ball or whatever. It was worse than that. They outsourced it. Yahoo hadn’t had its own search engine in 17 years.

Speaker 3 So where does most of the audience come from?

Jim Lanzone Yahoo Sports has over 100 million users a month. Yahoo Finance has over 100 million users a month. Yahoo Mail—one-third of all Americans have a Yahoo Mail account. All those things fit together and add up to 700 million users a month. There are companies valued more than us that have less than 0.1% of our user base.

I really believe that the best days of Yahoo can be ahead of it. I think now we’re in a comeback phase.

Molly O'Shea Jim Lanzone, welcome to Sorcery.

Jim Lanzone Awesome to be here, Molly.

Molly O'Shea Well, I know you’re traveling all around the world.

Jim Lanzone Totally.

Molly O'Shea So, thanks—

Jim Lanzone Yeah.

Molly O'Shea —for making the stopover here in L.A.

Jim Lanzone I know. We made it work.

Molly O'Shea So you’re here for the Snap board meeting?

Jim Lanzone Yep, that was why I was in town for this. I came straight from Aspen at the Forbes CMO conference, and I’m on my way to Amsterdam next week for HumanX. This is just that time of year.

Molly O'Shea Oh my gosh.

Jim Lanzone Back out of the summer, right into it.

Molly O'Shea I understand.

Jim Lanzone Yeah.

Molly O'Shea It’s like back to school.

Jim Lanzone Yep, 100%.

Molly O'Shea Well, I’m so excited to talk today about everything Yahoo and the legend behind Jim Lanzone.

Jim Lanzone Oh, jeez.

Molly O'Shea Because there’s a lot. There’s a lot going on there.

Jim Lanzone Oh, okay.

Molly O'Shea But I think it would be great to start off with Yahoo, because Yahoo’s on a tear. So, back in 2021—

Jim Lanzone Yep.

Molly O'Shea —that’s when Apollo bought Yahoo from Verizon, and Verizon sold off a couple of assets. It was AOL and Yahoo. So that was around $4.5—

Jim Lanzone Yeah.

Molly O'Shea —about $5 billion.

Jim Lanzone A little more—$4.8 billion.

Molly O'Shea Okay.

Jim Lanzone Yeah.

Molly O'Shea So, nearly $5 billion. You bought the assets. Could you walk me through that? What was that process like?

Jim Lanzone At the time, I was somebody they called during the process of deciding to buy the company. I wasn’t part of Apollo then. I left another job to come do this, which we can talk about—why I did that.

The history was that Verizon, under different leadership, had bought AOL and then, a few years later, Yahoo. They merged them into one company, first called Oath. They then changed that name to Verizon Media, but it was all those assets under one roof. The new Verizon management team decided they didn’t want to be in that business anymore. I think it took them a few years to find the right buyer at the right price, but Reed Raymond from Apollo, one of the leaders of their private equity group, got in there and figured out how to construct a deal that would work.

Molly O'Shea So what was the construction of the deal?

Jim Lanzone It was about getting the right framework for Verizon, because they wanted to maintain some ownership, which they did. They still own 10% of us. Then there was having a vision for what this thing could be going forward.

I think combined, they were bought for about twice what we bought it for. During that time, they’d had a different mission than I think either company had ever had before. It was really to help Verizon grow 5G and be a part of that. A lot of the decisions were based on that, and not really on the real mission of what Yahoo itself was about.

The company that was set up was a brand-new company. We’re a 5-year-old company managing a 30-year-old brand at this point. It was a completely new company, stood up from scratch to house these brands under one roof. They bought it in May 2021, and it closed in September 2021. I started around the end of September 2021, so it’s been almost exactly 5 years for me.

Molly O'Shea Well, congrats.

Jim Lanzone Yeah. We made it.

Molly O'Shea So this isn’t your first turnaround. When you came in, where did you come from? What were your first couple of steps for the next 6 months or so?

Jim Lanzone It was the middle of COVID. September 2021, if anybody remembers, was when I think the Delta variant was starting. We still didn’t meet people in the office for a while after that, and the decisions were, “If you come in, do you have to be vaccinated?” That’s what that time frame was like, so it was kind of a weird time to pick up a company.

I had just done it a year earlier with Tinder. I had worked for the IAC family before they bought our company in 2005. That’s how far back I go. Those same people brought me back for that job, again in the middle of COVID. That was July 2020, so it was an even more difficult time to pick up a company because we really never met anybody for that year. Here, we were back to work pretty quickly after that.

For me, this was actually the third time I was going in to lead a turnaround. The first was Ask Jeeves, which is kind of the poster child for the Web 1.0 crash. However difficult this one would be, nothing would be harder than turning that brand and those products around at that time. I think I was announced on 9/11. I think that was actually my first day on the job.

They had bought the ’90s startup I was part of, where I was one of the founders. I joined there as one of the heads of product and, over time, worked my way up to CEO. We 50x’d that stock and sold it to IAC and Barry Diller. I stayed for another 3 years as CEO, then left to do another startup. That was bought by CBS, the television company.

I joined as the CEO of their internet group, which had bought multiple public companies over time that just weren’t performing at their best. That was turnaround number 2. I think that’s still the sixth-largest internet company by unique users. I think we went from 70 to 220 million users with those properties.

I’d been through big internet turnarounds before. Yahoo was one that I knew had great bones for a great turnaround. It had the thing that was hardest to get, which is traffic. It had a lot of traffic, but the products had seen better days. Coming out of years at Verizon, the company structure and composition were not optimal. But those are things you can work with.

The first 6 months were from the playbook I’d run before: evaluate the team. I don’t come in guns blazing on day one. I get in there and get to know everybody. There are always great people wherever you go, and there are always things you don’t understand from the outside. Until you’re inside running a company, it’s never exactly what you’d think. The data will tell you differently how the products work, who the audience is, all those kinds of things. Those first 6 months are really about getting to know it, and then that leads into all the different steps of a turnaround that come after.

Molly O'Shea I think this is interesting because there are so many different angles to this. I just had a conversation with Bending Spoons, which is the opposite of a PE playbook, but this also isn’t really a traditional PE turnaround because you’re leading the way. It’s not like a private equity company is coming in and just stripping out as much as they can, but you’re really ushering this. So talk about how that’s different for you and maybe the traditional Apollo PE playbook.

Jim Lanzone It’s interesting because I still have people ask me, “What’s it like working for private equity?” The reputation isn’t always great for how they’re going to manage these things, but I’ve had the opposite experience. Reed and I still talk almost every day in some form, 5 years later. He was wearing a “Make Yahoo! Great Again” purple hat around.

PE is in it for a reason. They want an outcome, whether that’s an IPO or a sale. They’re not here to hold it forever, to be Stripe and just never have—

Molly O'Shea Yeah.

Jim Lanzone —an outcome of some kind. At the same time, there aren’t that many companies they view as having asymmetric upside relative to others, where you just run the PE playbook. They hired a team, starting with me, who wouldn’t be here if they did that. I’m a growth person. I only do the turnarounds to get to the fun part, which is when you get to start putting irons in the fire for growth, reap the benefits of the turnaround, and start investing and building new things for the huge audience you inherited.

Jim Lanzone Um, that really is how Apollo was treated the whole time. I’ve had to work for many different kinds of people, including venture capitalists. At my first startup, I’d never had a real job before; at my second, Bill Gurley and Jeff Yang were my 2 main investors. I’ve also worked for Barry Diller and Les Moonves. Everybody has to serve somebody, and I haven’t found private equity—at least with my Apollo team—to be a particularly difficult force to reckon with compared with other people I’ve had to work for.

Molly O'Shea So what are the main questions you start asking once you get into the company?

Jim Lanzone There are a couple of things. One is that Yahoo, in particular, is a conglomerate. It’s not one brand. If you look at other companies around our size in the industry—Pinterest, Snap, Reddit, Roku—they’re mostly one-product companies. Yahoo is a conglomerate of many different brands that compete independently in their spaces.

Yahoo Finance competes with Bloomberg, CNBC, and maybe The Wall Street Journal. We have a new product that competes with TradingView and others in that space. Yahoo Sports competes with ESPN and others like that. Yahoo Mail competes with Gmail. They all have very different competitors, and that creates this ecosystem of brands.

That’s not the first time I’ve seen that. IAC had 60-plus brands, and with Ask, we joined that family. CBS Interactive had 30-plus brands, many of which had nothing to do with CBS. CNET was the leading technology site. SportsLine was one of the OGs in sports and fantasy sports. Last.fm was in music. You go down the list: GameSpot in video games. We had all kinds of different brands, and we had to figure out the right structure for them.

I did it wrong at CBS Interactive the first time. I tried to have everything report to me. My background is all product, and I was a pig in slop with these brands, many of which I was a user of. It turned out I was just going to slow things down; we needed to move much faster. I had to hire general managers who could be entrepreneurial and independent. My job was to work with them on their plans, hold them accountable, help where I could, and let them run.

It was interesting when we got here. Whatever had happened through the years at Verizon, the company had evolved into one with a single head of product, one head of technology, and one head of content across all the brands. There were people and engineering teams who specialized, but they were spread across them. So the first thing we did was reorganize the company into more of a conglomerate structure, with GMs in all these groups.

That means each group gets its own head of product, technology, and content. Even for central functions, they’ll usually have their own head of sales, marketing, PR, and business development. Those people will be assigned to those divisions. We had to put that structure in place, and then I had to hire for it. Some of those people were great internal candidates who were going to be part of it. For some roles, I had to go get true experts who were badasses in their fields.

That’s what we did. We started putting that team together, and that was really the 2022 timeframe. The next step, once you have that team and understand what you’re doing, is to ask: Are we doing all the right things? Do we need to reduce our focus? Are there things we should spin off? Where are we off the mission of the company?

The mission also had to be reinstituted. If you go way back, the original sin of Yahoo was giving search away to Google in June of 2000. There’s this myth on the internet that Yahoo was defeated by Google because it took its eye off the ball or whatever. It was worse than that: Yahoo outsourced search—

Molly O'Shea

What?

Jim Lanzone

—first to a company called Inktomi, and there were actually others before that. Then the market crash happened, and to get a better deal and save money on something viewed as a cost center, Yahoo gave it away. Search was viewed as a utility that wasn’t core, even though 92% of all sessions on the internet at that point, I think, started with search. One reason was that there was no business model yet. What became Overture, and then AdWords and AdSense for Google, didn’t exist.

All the search engines—and there were 10-plus of them that were public companies, including Ask—had banner ads everywhere on their search results pages. Just imagine how bad that was. It came from the right place; it just wound up being something really hard to recover from.

Generations of Yahoo started to figure out other ways forward. In the 2000s, while they did some very interesting things in search and other places, they made forays into Hollywood. They had Yahoo Music and TV, and all kinds of other things. They hired a lot of people from Hollywood. There were then a series of different CEOs. In the 2010s, they went back at Google and tried to go that way, and then eventually sold to Verizon.

The mission of the company was to help Verizon with its mission. It turned out that underneath all that, the reason Yahoo continued to be successful all those years, with its huge audience, was the places where it was still fulfilling the original mission Jerry Yang and David Filo had in 1995: being the trusted guide to the internet, helping people through the Wild West the internet had become and helping them get things done.

In Yahoo Finance, Sports, News, Mail, and different parts of Search and Weather, and in all these places where we still had leading brands, that’s what the company was doing. So we had the benefit in 2022 and 2023 of focusing on the things Yahoo was doing well. We didn’t have the burden, first of all, of being a struggling public company. It’s very difficult to make those changes in public. And second, we could focus on the things we did really well, where we were already successful. That’s where our focus went during that timeframe, which meant we spun a lot of things out or shut—

Molly O'Shea

Nice.

Jim Lanzone

—or shut them down.

Molly O'Shea

That’s really fascinating. It’s also really funny to think back that Verizon bought Yahoo. What an interesting—

Jim Lanzone

Well, it was first AOL.

Molly O'Shea

Yeah.

Jim Lanzone

—and AOL had tilted more toward media during that timeframe.

Molly O'Shea

Mm-hmm.

Jim Lanzone

Tim Armstrong, who’s a great CEO and a good friend, had gone that way. Verizon had a vision that, if you remember, AT&T also had because it bought Time Warner.

Molly O'Shea

Mm-hmm.

Jim Lanzone

At that time, those 2 companies thought that was the way forward. AT&T made a much bigger bet with Time Warner that wound up obviously spinning back out. At Verizon, it was AOL, and that team was the one that convinced them to buy Yahoo and merge the 2 things together into this huge internet conglomerate with an immense audience and immense amounts of data that could then be used to target in really interesting and good ways. It was a really good vision, but it was inside the wrong company.

Molly O'Shea

So where does most of the audience come from now and then?

Jim Lanzone

It’s back to the conglomerate structure, piece by piece. Yahoo Sports has over 100 million users a month. Yahoo Finance has over 100 million users a month. One-third of all Americans have a Yahoo Mail account. That’s hundreds of millions of accounts.

Then there’s News, where we’re one of the top 3 properties as an aggregator. We talked about that as another strategic move we made: going back to focus on aggregation instead of enterprise news and competing with the Associated Press and others. That shouldn’t have been our job. It had gone that way over the years.

All those things together add up to 700 million users a month. Every month, we’re in the top 5 in the U.S., usually top 5 globally, and number 1, 2, or 3 in all these different categories.

Molly O'Shea

You did mention that you guys divested a couple of things. You divested some pretty notable assets, whether it was AOL, TechCrunch, or a handful of others.

Jim Lanzone

Yeah.

Molly O'Shea

So what were the ones that you divested, and what were the decisions behind that?

Jim Lanzone

AOL was the biggest. We could talk about that. The first one was Edgecast, a content delivery network competing with companies like Akamai, which we felt we didn’t have a right to operate.

The second, and probably the biggest transformation job we had to do up until now—now we’re having to transform the whole company around AI—was the ad tech business. AOL and Yahoo had each purchased 30-plus ad tech companies over the years. What we inherited was a three-legged stool of an SSP, a DSP, and a native platform, with a couple of issues. One was that it lost a lot of money.

Molly O'Shea

Mm.

Jim Lanzone

Operating those things was massive, and it was hundreds of millions of dollars a year out the door that we had to fix. The second issue was that it was the primary source of revenue for Yahoo. Instead of being able to play the field with our supply-side platform, pull yield levers, take all comers, and optimize for the highest yield, we were only taking ads from the ad tech business.

Offloading that did 2 things. We shut down or sold money-losing businesses, and we were able to truly optimize revenue on Yahoo proper. So it was 2 things. As part of that, in February 2023, we had to let go of over 2,000 people.

Part of that was because we didn't want to sell the SSP. A lot of people wanted us to, but we didn't want to give anyone preferential treatment on our pages the way we had been doing. We wanted to be able to optimize yield, so we had to shut that down. We sold the native business to Taboola and took 25% of their company. Those were the 2 things.

We offloaded more things, like TechCrunch, which you mentioned. We just did AOL in October of last year, while focusing on the DSP. So it wasn't just offloading things; there was also the decision that there was a crown jewel in there, and we could invest in it. A lot goes into all that.

Molly O'Shea

Mm-hmm.

Molly O'Shea
