In the conversation with Bending Spoons, the biggest misconception about the AOL transaction was that it was actually a really healthy asset that you got to a really healthy point. So let's talk about the transformation within the company. You joined during the height of this AI hysteria and invention time.

Jim Lanzone

No, it wasn't even on the map yet. That was November 2022. In September 2021, we had no idea.

Molly O'Shea

I don't know how you manage it. Now we're in this crazy world of AI, whether it's transforming your company or your business model, or competing with you and challenging everything around you. How did you think about rebuilding the company over that time period and incorporating more technology?

Jim Lanzone

The first thing is, in a transformation job, I always tell the team: You can't skip levels of the video game. You have to go level by level and win each one to earn the right to the next. It always comes down to product. We're a consumer internet company. That's what we do for a living: build great products. If you're not doing that, it's like The Shawshank Redemption: You're either getting busy living or getting busy dying. That's how it is with this. Some of these products hadn't been worked on in 10 years.

Molly O'Shea

Really?

Jim Lanzone

Some of these things hadn't really been improved. It was time to get back to work. We hired great product people, and we have an amazing team now that I would put up against any other big consumer internet company. We brought in great people who share our passion for putting this brand back on the map, all of whom have entrepreneurial backgrounds. Every general manager, from me on down, has been an entrepreneur at least once and started companies.

Improving the products is definitely game one. If you can do that and start getting growth going again, then you can get to building brand-new things like Yahoo Scout, our search engine that we launched earlier this year. Yahoo hadn't had its own search engine in 17 years.

Molly O'Shea

That's so crazy.

Jim Lanzone

Or College Fantasy Football—

Molly O'Shea

Yeah.

Jim Lanzone

—which we kind of broke the internet with when we announced it this summer, and it's been amazing. Forty percent of the people coming to the platform are brand-new to Yahoo. Yahoo Fantasy is huge. We had our 3 biggest days ever this year for NFL, but 40% of the users for College Fantasy Football are new to Yahoo.

Molly O'Shea

Wow.

Jim Lanzone

Doing these brand-new things is the reward you get for doing the hard work and the turnaround work in the first place. The next step is the brand, which has been one of the most surprising things about this. Having been through the wringer with some other brands through the years, it's been incredible to see that Yahoo has a lot of latent brand love, especially with younger audiences.

We've talked about this, but over 50% of our audience is Gen Z and millennial. Seventy-five percent of Gen Z is using Yahoo or one of our products. When we market, we've done a lot of really interesting things. We have a great social media team and a really creative brand advertising team. We've seen a 31% absolute-point lift in brand love with Gen Z, which is one of the things you track. That's from our Cardi B campaign—

Molly O'Shea

Yeah.

Jim Lanzone

—our Kyle Cooke Weather Boy campaign from Summer House, and all the social media things we've done. It really is met with great reception.

Molly O'Shea

Mm.

Jim Lanzone

That gives me hope that the more we turn that dial, the more there is to do. Again, if you don't have great products, you have no business even trying.

Molly O'Shea

This is going to be a theme throughout the conversation because you're a product expert. To get into that further, what makes a great product? What are the hardest lessons you've learned in that process?

Jim Lanzone

That's art and science. It starts with data and understanding your user base, which you never really understand from the outside. I have a bunch of college friends from UCLA, and to help me get to know this college product, I got a bunch of them on it. They beat me up all day long for things they're finding in the product. When I then go talk to the actual product team on the sports team about what's driving things behind the scenes, whether something's really wrong or it's just one person's opinion, it's different.

Take search, where what happens on the other side of that search box is so complicated, especially now with AI, but even going back to the old days of 10 blue links. You enter that query, but what we have to do on the other side to capture that and understand what to do with it is incredibly complicated. How to do that for hundreds of millions of people and move the needle forward is different from what it might be for one user. Data is going to lead you forward.

After that, it's creativity and people who have a sensibility for users. One benefit of having a huge audience is that you can A/B test your way to things. You can have a hunch, and especially now with AI, we can experiment even more. I do think product teams can get a little too addicted to that or become too cautious and want to do 200 tests at one time. You can't do that. You have to have some passion for what you think the product should be and lead with that.

Yahoo had something I experienced at prior companies: this huge audience. That's so hard to get. If you look at the top internet companies in Comscore or Similarweb, it's incredible how many are from the '90s. It's amazing how many are from the early 2000s: YouTube and Facebook. We're all about 30 years old. Google is almost 28 years old. YouTube is 21 years old, and Facebook is 22. We're all kind of in the same age range at this point. New brands only get added to that once every 3 to 5 years, right?

Molly O'Shea

Mm.

Jim Lanzone

ChatGPT was the latest. Before that, it was probably TikTok, Snap, and Instagram. It just doesn’t happen very often. I hesitate to call it a moat, because you can lose it so easily if you don’t treat it right, but this level of distribution allows you to improve the products and have them work, right? That’s different from trying to light the wet log from scratch, which is what entrepreneurs have to do.

That’s why so many of the biggest consumer internet companies happened by accident. They really weren’t the thing they intended to be a lot of the time. We have a great platform to build great products on. We’re lucky to have that.

Molly O'Shea

Of the other companies you mentioned, it’s interesting because you have great brand perception and brand love around Yahoo, but these other ones in the AI world have horrible brand recognition and are seen as evil. Why do you think you’ve built up so much trust and excitement around the brand instead of being cast into the doomerism side of the internet?

Jim Lanzone

To be honest about that one—

Molly O'Shea

Yeah.

Jim Lanzone

—it’s because we’re not building a large language model. We’re not at the frontier. We’ve built our search engine, our AI answer engine, in an entirely different way that I think is bespoke, cool, and interesting, and provides really unique results compared to all of them, which were all created in a similar way. I think they start to blend together in certain ways when it comes to search.

It’s probably that. Yahoo did have a data issue in a different regime 14 years ago, but other than that, it’s been a really trusted brand over time and has continued to reward that trust. If you’re going to have your email be the vault of your life, the operating system of your life, that’s why every one of these new agent products first asks, “Can we have access to your email and calendar?” I think that gives us a place to play in that space.

Molly O'Shea

Absolutely.

Jim Lanzone

Yeah.

Molly O'Shea

It’s the trend we see right now.

Jim Lanzone

But it’s our obligation—

Molly O'Shea

Yeah.

Jim Lanzone

—to do that for people anyway. We have to build those products to do our job as best we can for our users, no matter what. But we also have trust. We already have people using us for those things.

I think that’s happened over 30 years. It’s always been an irreverent, positive brand, with a little tongue-in-cheek kitschiness to it. Even when it first started, that was always part of the Yahoo brand. We’re really leaning into that. Our social team has a lot of fun with it, and a lot of the brand work we’ve done will continue in that direction.

We’re never going to have a Super Bowl ad that tries to make you cry. It’s always going to try to make you laugh or be different. But trust is ours to lose, and new brands will always have to figure that out.

Molly O'Shea

It’s interesting to go into that world and talk about your new products, especially Scout. Where does Scout fit in terms of AI search, compared with ChatGPT, Perplexity, Anthropic, and even Google?

Jim Lanzone

From the start, it was more like Perplexity.

Molly O'Shea

Okay.

Jim Lanzone

Perplexity isn’t its own large language model. They were doing metasearch on the others, which has happened before. There was a product called Dogpile in the early days of search that was a metasearch engine on other people’s search engines. Yahoo Scout is totally different. The others are all large language models: Gemini, ChatGPT, and Claude.

Ours is a product based on our own data. There was so much interesting data, which is another asset. I’ll put “moat” in quotes because I’m always paranoid about it—you can’t rest easy with this. But it’s an asset: hundreds of millions of users a month over 30 years, and we’re still the third-ranked search engine in the U.S. We have 30 years of search history. Even though we’re much smaller, that’s still a ton of search history.

Our publisher relationships are another way we’ve taken the company back. Instead of competing with our publishers, we’re trying to make sure we partner with them. It’s our job and our legacy to send them traffic.

Molly O'Shea

Yeah.

Jim Lanzone

We firmly believe in that. It’s part of our job in the ecosystem. Having been a partner of Yahoo’s at other companies, I can attest to how much traffic they could send us.

So we have publisher data, search data, our knowledge graph, and our user data, if we know something about you. The way Yahoo Scout, our AI answer engine, works is that we take all that data, ground it, and send it to a lightweight model. At launch, it was Haiku from Anthropic. We use others today. They process that and send it back to us, and then we do the rendering, the formatting, the UI. What that creates is an entirely unique result that can only happen because of Yahoo data.

We’re also a top-20 publisher whose content has been taken by large language models without permission. You’ll see the Yahoo brand show up all the time in citations. For the most part, our content is real-time. We excel in categories that are real-time, so we weren’t as susceptible to the evergreen content that large language models photocopied and took with them. Especially in certain categories that are more real-time, our results are awesome and totally unique.

The other reason we had to do that is that for 17 years, we were outsourcing search largely to Microsoft, with whom we’re still great partners. But that left us in a really vulnerable position for one of our most important products and revenue streams. The ability to fend for ourselves and own that asset again was life-changing for us.

Besides that, I spent my first 10 years in search, and our old team innovated a lot of the most interesting things, especially in structured data search. Things that went beyond 10 blue links were already an area of search I was personally passionate about. We have our own unique entry there, and it was also a very strategic asset to own.

Molly O'Shea I think about this when I talk to all of the high-growth tech companies and see all the pivots. We were joking about this earlier, but with Allbirds and its AI play, for example. When you’re taking the reins and rebuilding and transforming the company, how do you stay focused and avoid getting into these money-grab areas, like AI coding, AI assistance, becoming a neocloud all of a sudden, or using your data centers for other stuff, and instead stay focused on one product at a time?

Jim Lanzone Yeah.

For us, it went back to the thing that can feel like the cheesier side of this job: the mission. It really mattered here, and I took my time with it. I rolled out a brand-new mission for the company with a 45-minute-to-an-hour-long presentation. It was actually much longer for the management team at my team offsite. We did a condensed version for the whole team. I spent almost a year working on it with the team, and it came into focus over 6 months of really doing the work. Everyone in our company understands it now, can recite it back, and knows what we’re doing and why, in real detail.

As I said earlier, we’re the trusted guide to the internet, helping our users accomplish their goals, no matter how big or small. We’re not judging. A trip to see the Taj Mahal, beating the snot out of your friends from UCLA in fantasy—it doesn’t matter. Our job is to help you make a dollar in Yahoo Finance, make a million dollars, or whatever it is. That’s a mission that’s 30 years old. It’s also a mission we can carry out for another 30 years as things change.

The internet is changing more right now than it ever has. That’s both an opportunity and a threat to how we deliver on being the trusted guide. As part of that, we were very specific in saying, “We’re not going to be an enterprise or B2B company. We’re going to handle your personal life.”

Yahoo Mail is where that’s most important, because Gmail sits in the Google Cloud group now and is really an enterprise-level product. Outlook is an enterprise-level product. There are things you would do differently if you were focusing on someone’s personal life with mail, as opposed to their work life. That’s an example of where we would do that.

What are the assets around that? Superior aggregation, proprietary data sets that you can leverage, and what we call content that provides context.

That’s why we got out of competing for breaking news. Some of these people, like Shams and Woj in the early days at ESPN, started at Yahoo!. When I got here, we had White House correspondents and all these different things. TechCrunch is another example: one of the most important brands in tech journalism, but it wasn’t right for us. Instead, we have the best fantasy analysts. We have amazing business analysts for analyzing the stock market. We just signed Deidre Bosa from CNBC—

Molly O'Shea

Yeah, I saw that.

Jim Lanzone

—who’s coming over to join Brian Sozzi and people we already had. That’s where we wanted to do content: to help our users make better decisions and accomplish their goals. That’s all cheesy, but it actually provides a really important filter for what we would and wouldn’t do. That still guides us today. We’ll look to add other brands, too. They don’t have to be Yahoo!-branded, but they do have to be places where we can provide those services for our users.

Molly O'Shea

What’s been the biggest pushback you’ve gotten?

Jim Lanzone

Probably just—do you mean from our own team, or from—

Molly O'Shea

From your team, from investors, from the decisions you’re making: products to launch, products you’re not launching. What’s the biggest friction, or the thing people want most that you’re getting pushback on?

Jim Lanzone

I’d say the easiest version of that is that when you’ve been around a long time—even though our user base is now skewing younger, and our fastest-growing areas, including Mail, are from Gen Z—people who’ve been around a long time don’t want you to move their cheese.

Molly O'Shea

Mm-hmm.

Jim Lanzone

Evolving those products in ways that you know are better for future users is hard. People who’ve been around a long time just don’t want to see those things change, especially the pure UI. They want things to stay the same, and the problem is that you’ll lose tomorrow’s users if you do that. I’ve experienced this at other companies, especially in places like fantasy sports, where if you change something, you lose certain users. They’re like, “I’m out of here,” even if the place they’re going has a lot of the UI or features we just launched. They’ll leave simply because you changed things. I’d say that’s probably always the hardest part.

Internally, I think we have a lot less of this now. The team we have is united around what we’re trying to accomplish. They’re people who have the right chip on their shoulders to be at a company like ours, which was going from turnaround to—now I think we’re in the comeback phase. I think we’ve graduated to—

Molly O'Shea

Yeah.

Jim Lanzone

—now it’s a comeback. They want to be here for that. They love the assets. They love to build. But in the early days, you’re telling some people there’s no Santa Claus, and there’s not, you know—

Molly O'Shea

What?

Jim Lanzone

Oh, shit. Sorry. We accomplished that here today. But, yeah, it’s just hard sometimes. You’ve been indoctrinated with certain things over the years, and I show up to start heading in a different direction. Some people just aren’t going to want to go along with that.

Molly O'Shea

Mm-hmm. So you already paid back pretty much the price of the—

Jim Lanzone

Yeah.

Molly O'Shea

—yeah, Apollo acquisition.

Jim Lanzone

Yeah, we’ve said that publicly.

Molly O'Shea

Okay.

Jim Lanzone

Yeah, it’s one of the fastest-returning deals in Apollo’s history, and there were certain things that went into that. The AOL sale was another part of it. But, yeah, we’re playing with house money now, in terms of what the upside could be here.

Molly O'Shea

Did you feel pressure to pay that back quickly? What was the—

Jim Lanzone

No, because Reed and the Apollo team constructed a really interesting deal.

Molly O'Shea

Okay.

Jim Lanzone

At first, some of the things they put in place were to return cash really quickly. I also worked with them for a few months leading up to this, and I knew I was pretty aligned with them on which assets probably weren’t going to make it. That was something we were pretty unified on.

Molly O'Shea

And the goal is to go public. What do you think is going to surprise people most when you go public?

Jim Lanzone

Well, I’d actually put the goal a little differently. It’s weird to think about Yahoo! this way, because it’s the OG, but we’re the same as any later-stage, pre-IPO Silicon Valley company. If we’ve created a lot of value—and I think we’re still one of the most undervalued assets out there—we have an audience this big. Something I didn’t mention is that we’re also not one of these companies whose traffic comes from SEO. We get SEO traffic, but 75% of our users come directly to Yahoo!. That’s one of the highest percentages on the internet. On any given day, about 75% of our users are logged in.

This is a very loyal, dedicated audience. The other benefit is that we’re incredibly effective for advertisers. We’re not a place to just throw random money at. We provide outcomes and performance at levels that other people don’t. Our DSP, which is an entrepreneurial venture here, wins nine out of 10 head-to-head tests, and that’s because of our data.

Molly O'Shea

Yeah.

Jim Lanzone

That’s because of our first-party data with our audience. We have these incredible assets that I just don’t think grow on trees, and I think that’s very valuable to a lot of other companies. If you’re venture-backed or private equity-backed, I think your investors expect an outcome, not for you to just be a standalone private company forever. That’s how I’d think about it.

What would be most surprising? I don’t know. Weirdly, I don’t know how surprising it’ll be. We’ve been pretty open.

Molly O'Shea

Yeah.

Jim Lanzone

I think our audience and assets are pretty well understood. When people hear our revenue and profitability, they’re both really good, and I think they’ll probably be in a range that’s relatively expected. Maybe what will surprise people is just how healthy we are and how much we’re growing—the rate at which we’re growing, which is really healthy growth, especially for a 30-year-old brand.

Molly O'Shea

What do you think are the biggest mistakes companies make at scale?

Jim Lanzone

Probably falling asleep at the wheel and becoming really conservative. People who’ve succeeded by climbing the company ladder—some of whom are probably great—tend to lead to a certain kind of management, based on what those people have been rewarded for over time. If they’re not product-driven leaders, honestly, in our space, it tends not to work.

In our space, you tend to lose sight really fast of what matters. Sometimes it’s the things an executive team misses: the chances they didn’t take, the company they didn’t buy, maybe the thing they sold, or a deal they did that they might not have done if a different set of leaders had been in place. Those wind up being the things that make a huge difference. The problem is that you’d never know from the outside, because you weren’t a part of it. You don’t know what was on the table and what wasn’t.

But you’ll start to see things catch up to them, especially on product. They’ll get beaten by a startup with something they didn’t launch, or something they didn’t get out ahead of. I just think product-driven companies, where you follow “Only the Paranoid Survive” and you’re going 100 miles an hour, seven days a week, trying to crush it for your users, are the only way to make this work.

Molly O'Shea

Are you worried at all about any startups? Are you pinching yourself or kicking yourself over any acquisitions you didn’t make?

Jim Lanzone

Here’s what I’ll say: no, because startups right now are so highly valued.

Molly O'Shea

Yeah.

Jim Lanzone

There are companies valued more than us that have less than one-tenth of 1% of our user base. I was seeing that early on. Search companies that launched were being valued at six times what we were, even though we already had a lot of searches and search users, as well as our overall user base, revenue, and profitability.

It is funny. We’ve been at a moment in time when those things have been really expensive. I’ve benefited, and I was one of these a long time ago. My ’90s startup, which I was one of the founders of, didn’t work out. We were writing our S-1, and the market crashed, and we crashed. We went on fumes until Ask Jeeves bought us.

But a bunch of us went over in the acquisition, and we were really important to that turnaround.

Molly O'Shea

Mm-hmm.

Jim Lanzone

We’ve actually bought a few startups where they weren’t pure acqui-hires. We used the product, but the people we brought in were incredible and have been leading the charge on some of the most important things we’ve been building. We’ve been able to be active that way, but are we going to do a merger with somebody who has a base in the billions when we bring all the value? We can’t do it.

I don’t know that we’ve really had the opportunity to buy anything we would’ve missed, but there are a lot of things out there that I think are really interesting in search, agents, fantasy, and finance. Our Slack channels are very active every day with things we’re all looking at and playing with.

Molly O'Shea

I would imagine. It’s super exciting.

Jim Lanzone

Yeah, yeah. We compete in so many areas that—

Molly O'Shea

Mm.

Jim Lanzone

—it’s almost hard to keep up with it. But that’s why we have great leaders across the business.

Molly O'Shea

Because you’ve seen so many market cycles, when do you think this one pops?

Jim Lanzone

Damn, if I only knew. It’s funny, though. If you go back to the mid-teens, that’s how many times people have called it, and people have gotten really conservative, thinking the market was about to crash, but it has continued to go up. If you tried to take your chips off the table at any point, it would’ve been a huge mistake.

I’ve been through how many crashes? The first one was the global financial crisis, then COVID, then there was a mini-crash in 2022. On the other side of COVID, pretty much right after I started here, we went right into that one. Even now, with the war and certain things, and tariffs last year, there have always been curveballs thrown at you.

This is another place where Yahoo excels: we’re a very resilient company. I always say that if we were able to survive before we had a team like this building the things we’re building and growing the way we’re growing, we’re going to be okay now. We’re in a great spot to survive if something like that happens. I’m in no way rooting for it. I’d love it if we were in some golden age that lasted 50 years, but we’ll be okay if we’re not.

Molly O'Shea

How good is AI at real professional work? Mercour's AI Productivity Index, or APEX, tracks it with every major frontier model release. Built with partners like Harvey and Cognition, see where the frontier actually stands at mercour.com/apex. Just tell your agent. Automate your investing at public.com.

Speaker 1

Founders scale faster on Deel. Set up payroll for any country in minutes. Hire anyone anywhere, get visas handled fast, and get back to building. Visit deel.com/sorcery. That's D-E-E-L.com/sorcery

Molly O'Shea

I know we started this and I said, “I want to know about the Jim Lanzone lore.” You mentioned so many people you’ve worked with and worked for. Maybe we can go back to Barry Diller and what it was like working with him. What is it like working with Barry Diller? When we talked a couple of months ago, right after the Dara interview, you also mentioned Dara. It’d be great to get into that a little bit and know what you’ve learned.

Jim Lanzone

John Foley, who founded Peloton, was one of the people at IAC. He called me a journeyman at a conference we were at together, and he meant it as a compliment. He said, “You’ve been in so many different places and seen so many things.” It’s true. I’ve been around a long time and have been part of all these different regimes and companies.

If you’re not naturally good at this stuff, experience probably doesn’t help. But if you have experience, it can help a lot, and the people you’ve worked for are a big part of that. It was a really interesting time at IAC. Dara left right when I joined.

Molly O'Shea

Mm-hmm.

Jim Lanzone

He left to do Expedia when it spun out, pretty much right as I joined. I had a great first couple of years with Barry. He was extremely intense. Again, this was 20 years ago.

Molly O'Shea

Yeah.

Jim Lanzone

It was very different from the IAC that Joey took over and ran later. We had 60 brands at that point, and they went through something Barry later said he regretted: trying to turn into an operating company.

Molly O'Shea

Mm.

Jim Lanzone

Jack Welch was one of his main advisers at the time. Somehow, the decision was made to take these 60 brands that had nothing to do with each other and no common infrastructure, reverse that out, and give them a common central structure. That just wasn’t easy at IAC, given the way it was put together.

Then Barry and John Malone got into it in 2008, and that led to the breakup of a lot of the IAC brands. It really changed the rationale for why they bought Ask. We shut down search, outsourced it to Google, and that was how I wound up leaving. But Barry’s such an original thinker. I still don’t think there’s anybody who’s a better interview. When you see him on stage or on CNBC, his language is so unique to him. He’s so smart and so bold in the things he does.

I loved working with him. Steve Berkowitz, who was probably the biggest mentor I’ve ever had in this space, was the CEO of Ask Jeeves when we were bought by IAC. That turnaround was so respected that Steve was poached by Microsoft to run all of its internet business. Satya reported to him.

Molly O'Shea

Wow.

Jim Lanzone

I remember, as Steve was leaving, Barry and I had tussled over something, and Steve said, “You guys are just so much alike.” I thought, “Huh.” I wouldn’t have thought that. I was the Silicon Valley internet guy, but he’s very entrepreneurial, and I’m still inspired by him. I loved his book last year and told him that. It was an amazing experience.

The CBS years were great, too. The stock had gotten down to $3 a share a couple of years before I joined, and it went back up to almost $80. I was the Silicon Valley guy going to a place where they had to wear suits. I was told that because I was the internet guy, I didn’t have to wear a tie. They were number one 13 years in a row, and the stock was a juggernaut and always delivered.

If we’re lucky enough to be a public company again, I learned so much from being part of those public companies: how they were managed, how those teams were run, what made them special, and what made them work. I can take that with me.

Molly O'Shea

So what was Tinder like?

Jim Lanzone

Short, and during COVID. Those COVID times were difficult. I loved the team. I didn’t change one person on that team. I loved the management team I inherited, and I loved the fact that Tinder was viewed one way from the outside, but on the inside, you’d never met a team of people more passionate about the mission of helping people find their person. It was always perceived by others as a hookup app or whatever, but that’s not how the team internally viewed it.

Molly O'Shea

Mm-hmm.

Jim Lanzone

They were also very proud of being a source of diverse relationships. I think 40% of all marriages started online, and Tinder was 25% of those. That means almost 10% of all marriages in the United States were started on Tinder. The people there are very passionate about that.

I never would’ve left. It’s the only time I’ve ever left a job. Everywhere else, I stayed for a long time.

Molly O'Shea

Mm-hmm.

Jim Lanzone

Someone found a tweet I posted in 2010 where I said this was the ultimate turnaround, and these were the best assets for it. There was something about it I always wanted a crack at. I was always very passionate that Yahoo deserved to be treated right, to have great products again, and to put that brand back on the map the right way.

Maybe it was just part of me being part of startups and then turnarounds. I just always wanted to take a crack at that, you know? So here we are five years later. Yeah.

Molly O'Shea

Is there anything we haven't covered yet that you'd want to go over?

Jim Lanzone

I know we'll see it in the comments.

Molly O'Shea

Okay.

Jim Lanzone

And I'll go, I'll call and answer.

Molly O'Shea

Okay.

Jim Lanzone

Yeah, I think a lot of it is still things that we can't even talk about. We have a lot of awesome stuff we're cooking up in the labs.

Molly O'Shea

What's the biggest secret you can tell us?

Jim Lanzone

Yeah, no. I don't have an IPO date, or whether it's happening or not. I always am trying to keep the things that we're building a secret until we launch them.

Molly O'Shea

Mm-hmm.

Jim Lanzone

We have some really interesting things that we're working on. I really believe that this is one of those times when the best days of Yahoo can really be ahead of it.

Molly O'Shea

Mm-hmm.

Jim Lanzone

It took a lot to get it to this spot, but we are jamming now. I think people really have an open mind to us as a brand again, which has just been really gratifying. We don't take that for granted. We want to deliver on it, so onwards.

Molly O'Shea

Amazing. I mean, I was gonna close out and ask: what are you most looking forward to in the next 12 months?

Jim Lanzone

Yeah, I can't tell you.

Molly O'Shea

Can't tell you. It's a secret.

Jim Lanzone

Yeah. But there's some really great stuff, and it's just our team. I love our team. It's one of those jobs where I get up every day ready to go.

Molly O'Shea

Mm-hmm.

Jim Lanzone

There's just not one day where I'm dreading it. It's just, let's go.

Molly O'Shea

Awesome. Well, Jim, thank you so much—

Jim Lanzone

All right. Thanks for having me.

Molly O'Shea

—for taking the time. This was so much fun.

Jim Lanzone

Okay, good.

Molly O'Shea

Awesome. Thank you.

Jim Lanzone

Thanks, Molly.

Molly O'Shea

Hey, it's Molly. If you enjoy our interviews, check out our newsletter, Sorcery.vc, where we deliver a once a week top deals and tech headlines email, and also go deeper on our podcast interviews. Subscribe to Sorcery today. And don't forget to subscribe to the podcast on YouTube, Spotify, Apple, or wherever you listen. Link in description to sign up.

item.title: 哪些企业能在 AI 时代存活？| Michael Dempsey
item.description: 推理市场若年增10倍，增长6倍的供应商仍可能丢失份额；技术栈趋同还可能让估值约300亿美元的资产在9个月内面临替代风险。Compound约23家公司的投资组合中有16家生物科技、仅3家AI投资，体现Dempsey偏好能掌握商业化路径的科学型企业。
item.content:encoded:
Empire · Michael Dempsey · 2026-10-19 · 71 min · 原语言 EN

推理市场若年增10倍，增长6倍的供应商仍可能丢失份额；技术栈趋同还可能让估值约300亿美元的资产在9个月内面临替代风险。Compound约23家公司的投资组合中有16家生物科技、仅3家AI投资，体现Dempsey偏好能掌握商业化路径的科学型企业。

要点 TL;DR

  • Compound 评估 AI 企业能否穿越技术周期、长期存活。Dempsey 最新一支基金的投资组合约有23家公司，其中16家是生物科技公司，只有3笔 AI 投资。基金于2021年结束募集后，Compound 等了约16个月才开始投资；他承认，2023年出手还不够积极。“真正的痛苦是亏钱。”
  • AI 营收快速增长，可能掩盖竞争地位正在下滑。以一个年增10倍的推理市场为例，一家公司增长6倍，尽管数字亮眼，实际仍在丢失份额。供应商彼此侵入对方的技术栈，可能在9个月内威胁到价值300亿美元的企业；关键在于它们能否“胜过替代者”。
  • Dempsey 持有 Figma 多头，但围绕 AI 增强创意工作、按使用量付费的看多逻辑，是主持人而非 Dempsey 提出的。Dempsey 认为 Figma 的产品晚了18个月才推出，股价仍不便宜，也不在他的4大仓位之列。他说公司从 Figma 转向 Claude Design，随后又表示 Figma MCP 改变了设计体验。他认为 Salesforce 的业务惯性比空头预期更强；对 HubSpot 则略偏看空。
  • 即使技术持续进步，AI 在政治上的接受度也可能带来波动。Dempsey 预计，政府将扮演“比人们想象中更激进的角色”，因为反对 AI 会成为一种受欢迎的政治立场。他认为，怨气背后是贫富差距、变化加速，以及人们害怕被时代甩下；他不认为仅仅资助癌症相关企业就能修复科技行业的声誉。
  • Dempsey 不愿把金融过度化变成自己的投资生意。他18岁起便通过体育博彩和期权交易赚钱，但仍表示“我讨厌预测市场”，也拒绝投资 Robinhood 或 Pump.fun 代币。他认为，过度赌博着眼短期，损害创造与成就感。他提出，可将赌博年龄门槛提高到约25或26岁，或征收简单的财富转移税。
  • Dempsey 看好能把科学发现转化为产品、并掌握商业化主动权的企业。Orbital Materials 将 AI 设计的吸热材料嵌入模块化数据中心，专门优化 GPU 散热。吸引他的地方在于“更能掌控自己的命运”，降低企业依赖他人把技术突破转化为收入的程度。
  • Dempsey 看好生物科技带来的成果，但质疑 AI 实验室能否从中获益。他认为，约20年后，今天主要致命疾病中有50%将不再致人死亡，并持有 Eli Lilly 多头。加快安全性验证、推动监管变化和拓展分销，与药物发现同样重要；生物科技的“隐性知识”仍是 AI 实验室面临的限制。
  • 相比新投加密风投，Dempsey 认为流动性较好的加密资产更有吸引力。他认为，加密风投“差不多死了两年”；而已充分分发、开始积累价值的代币，可以从基本面和叙事角度评估。主持人认为他预测未来24个月将有超过20家加密公司 IPO 过于乐观，Dempsey 随后同意这一数字应为10家。他还花了约18个月尝试买入 Chainalysis 的股份。

摘要 Digest

1. 基金周期长，耐心不可少，踩错时点代价高

  • Compound 的研究从机器学习、机器人、生物科技和密码学等领域的科学或工程风险入手。材料科学、能源和太空也在覆盖范围内，但通常只有在存在显著科学或工程风险时才会考虑。Dempsey 认为，相比从5家相似初创公司里排出名次，团队更擅长识别“独一份”的机会。某个无关领域突然走红时，通常选择不跟风。投资的关键，是找出团队具备优势的具体领域，再逐步建立相应能力。
  • Compound 在2021年募资后，于2023年3月开始投资，距离基金结束募集约16个月。Dempsey 区分了 LP 施加的烦人压力和真正亏钱的痛苦，但承认团队当时过于谨慎。一些有意思的2023年公司就此错过，因为下游投资者尚未给出足够有说服力的融资信号。“这是风险投资最糟糕的部分——你得依赖别人”接着投资。
  • 主持人提出的质疑是：要保持相关性，参与泡沫或许比保持克制更重要。Dempsey 认为这部分成立，并指出 LP 也可能不愿承认自己投错了。他提到，一些基金办公室的投资人承诺跨多个基金和募资年份持续投资，因此改变方向在职业上并不容易。Compound 每4至5年募一次资，而其他机构的周期约为24个月，2021年则在9个月内完成投资部署。等到下一轮募资时，表现不佳的公司已有时间失败：“我们必须有能力维持自己建立起来的投资组合。”

2. AI 增长可能掩盖护城河薄弱和竞争逼近

  • Dempsey 认为，AI 实验室对其他企业的替代“总体上更可能是真的”，但承认自己低估了一些公司的短期营收增速。算力、数据和性能持续扩展，应会淘汰中间层；能够长期留住用户的产品入口仍可能积累价值。真正缺少的工作，是定义中长期护城河。“建公司时唯一免费的事，就是思考。”
  • Fireworks、Together 和 Modal 等推理服务商，体现了衡量增长的难题。假设市场同比增长10倍，某家服务商增长6倍，那么亮眼的增长数据掩盖了相对表现的恶化。市场动能趋稳后，真正“胜过替代者”的公司会与靠补贴和异常强劲需求托举的公司拉开差距。一项看似成功的资产，可能已经跑输市场。
  • 技术栈正在趋同：推理服务商购买 GPU，Neocloud 则开发优化推理的软件。Dempsey 的警告带有条件，但措辞直接：如果竞争对手决定收购某家公司所掌握的特定技术栈环节，一项估值约300亿美元的资产可能在9个月内面临被替代的风险。毛利率受压或 GPU 获取受限，也可能造成同样严重的冲击。理解整条价值链，比接受每家公司对自身“独特细分市场”的说法更重要。
  • 二级市场出售股份，提供的保护不如种子轮投资者所说的那么多。一笔成功的早期投资可能变成数亿美元的仓位，而有意义的流动性往往集中在极少数资产上。因此，Compound 假设自己可能“永远持有这些资产”。团队的公开市场研究也帮助其理解大型科技公司，包括哪些 Neocloud 值得买入、做空或回避。

3. Figma 检验应用层能否在模型之外保住价值

  • 假设 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 的估值都在2万亿美元左右，Dempsey 可能会考虑持有10年；但看24个月，他更愿意不碰这两家公司。他对 Salesforce 不多也不少，认为投资者低估了其业务惯性；对 HubSpot 则更偏看空。他不赞成一概做空 SaaS。
  • 他通过 GitHub 仓库和星标，跟踪约100家上市 SaaS 公司的可信开源克隆项目。大约6个月前，相关活动明显上升；Claude Opus 拆解软件的能力又加重了这一担忧。需要说明的是，企业不会随手购买来路不明的开源分支。尽管如此，复制成本下降仍会对许多老牌企业形成结构性压力。
  • 主持人提出 Figma 的看多逻辑：创造和设计需要扎根于产品环境，AI 能改善使用体验，而按使用量付费的支出可能达到预期的10倍。Dempsey 确认自己持有 Figma 多头，称 Figma 的产品晚了约18个月才推出；股价自 IPO 以来已大幅下跌，但仍然昂贵，也不在他的4大仓位之列。
  • Dempsey 说，公司从100%使用 Figma 转向 Claude Design，并表示：“我会说，Figma 已经死了。”主持人认为，批评 Figma 的人可能落后了，因为他们没用过 Figma MCP。Dempsey 随后表示，有了 MCP，他们设计出来的东西已经让他的“垃圾感应器”失灵了。他反对创始人一遇到与模型实验室业务重叠，就立刻认定自己注定会输。

4. 社会对技术的反弹，可能演变成政治风险

  • Dempsey 将 AI 面临的舆论反弹，与科技圈的封闭感、创始人主导的沟通方式，以及一边承诺带来富足、一边威胁人们生计联系起来。他认为，社会更像钟摆，而不是一列“失控的货运列车”，因此当下的文化方向可以逆转。主持人谈到自己在 Cleveland 的观察，进一步说明这一点：线下民众对 AI 和数据中心的愤怒，远比以 Twitter 为中心的视角所显示的更强烈。
  • Dempsey 预计，短期内政府将扮演“比人们想象中更激进的角色”，因为反对 AI 和科技会成为政治人物争取支持的热门立场。他不确定这对长期趋势有多大影响，但预计会带来波动。他更悲观的预测是，未来5至7年，针对科技行业领军人物的暴力企图“很可能”会增加。
  • 主持人问，资助更多有价值的企业，例如癌症治疗公司，能否重建公众信任。Dempsey 不这么认为；他将反弹归因于贫富差距、变化加速，以及害怕被时代甩下。他说，人们很会适应，但很难在变化发生时及时消化。主持人补充说，生活质量可能改善，但相对处境仍会让人不满；Dempsey 的意思是，科技往往被当作头等大事，而人则成了附带牺牲品。

5. 金融虚无主义与创造和公民责任相冲突

  • Dempsey 反对过度赌博，但也承认其中存在矛盾：量化体育博彩曾帮助他支付大学生活费，他从18岁起就交易期权。尽管如此，他仍表示：“我讨厌预测市场。”他理解为何受益者反对这类活动，可能会被看作是在“抽走梯子”；但他认为，如今的规模及其对年轻人的影响具有破坏性。
  • 主持人的反问值得保留：投资人做的也是资本配置，并非创造产品，两者的界线在哪里？Dempsey 认为，创造也关乎人的满足感。写作、摄影和绘画能让“脑海和心里的东西走进现实”。他担心的是，人们失去把人生看作一门长期手艺、不断精进的想法，而不只是担心人们不去创办公司。
  • 他提出的干预措施包括将参与赌博的年龄门槛设在25或26岁左右，以及对大额遗产征收简单且力度足够的财富转移税，不留规避空间。他也拒绝投资 Robinhood 和 Pump.fun。Robinhood 过往的游戏化设计和推送通知令他担忧，因为这些机制会吸引用户，并诱发相应行为。
  • 主持人提出，与其竞相在18个月内把 ARR 从零做到1亿美元，不如多创办一些更有意思、更有趣的公司。Dempsey 部分认同，但提醒不要把这完全包装成欧洲式的浪漫主义：他形容镀金时代有一种建立在公民责任之上的技术官僚式浪漫主义。浪漫主义也需要管理层立场一致；他对比了 Figma 以设计为中心的说法和 CFO 强调工程团队增长的表态。他认为，当代一些科技领袖缺乏这种公民责任感。

6. 材料只有嵌入产品，才能从发明变成生意

  • Compound 最新的风险投资组合约有23家公司，其中16家是生物科技企业，3家是 AI 投资。3家分别是 Prime Intellect（从分布式算力转向开源后训练）、General Intelligence Company（一家面向个体经营者或原生代理业务的代理平台）和 Orbital Materials。这样的配置反映出团队寻找持久企业形态的意图，而非最大限度押注当前 AI 热潮。
  • Orbital 的基础模型可以帮助创造新型材料，使其在精确设定的温度下吸收热量。将材料嵌入模块化数据中心后，它可以在 GPU 运行的温度下高效散热，也适用于预计很快推出的某一类 GPU。实体实验室很重要：当其他人想把所有工作都放在计算机模拟中完成时，Compound 坚持生成物理实验数据。商业上真正有意思的产出是散热产品，而不是孤立的科学发现。
  • 这种模式带来“更能掌控自己的命运”。Dempsey 将其与机器人公司作对比：后者依赖系统集成商或客户，才能从试点走向大规模部署。一家公司技术上取得成功，商业结果仍可能由另一方决定。他希望科学能力能与企业自身可以影响的市场路径相结合。
  • 研究合作关系可能需要几年才能成熟。Dempsey 在 Alex Kendall 创办自动驾驶公司前2年半，就读过他的 Cambridge 博士论文；听说他创业后，又重新联系了他。较长的基金周期让这种耐心成为可能。但失败的风险也很明确：Compound 可能变成“一家拿着过高报酬的研究机构”，产出出色的点子，却无法把它们转化成好的投资。

7. 生物科技的上行空间未必属于 AI 实验室

  • Dempsey 明确预测：“我认为，今天主要致人死亡的疾病中，有50%在大约20年后将不再致人死亡。”他认为自己和主持人都能活过120岁。他最近一笔投资涉及 AI 精神科医疗服务；他认为，如果美国的心理健康服务供给能增加100倍，显然会带来好处。这些成果支撑着他的乐观态度，但他并不确定最终由哪些机构实现。
  • 把生物科技纳入 AI 实验室，尤其在 IPO 前后，从叙事上说得通，因为其潜在市场可能超过软件。但运营层面的归属是另一回事。Dempsey 认为，目前在 Anthropic 从事生物科技工作的人员，“很可能”5年后都已不在那里。生物科技包含大量“隐性知识”，无法像人们对其他 AI 能力所设想的那样，通过递归改进轻易提升。
  • 他持有 Eli Lilly 多头，并特别看好公司转向直接面向消费者销售。更多生物科技公司可能创造有价值的资产，但必须在依赖现有公司的临床试验基础设施、监管经验和规模，与独立建设之间作出选择。他提醒，不要简单线性外推；他指出，Novo Nordisk 的股价低于其开始投资 GLP-1 时的水平。他认为，现金充裕且能力出众的公司，营收可以同比增长50%，最终达到数千亿美元。

8. 更快获得安全性证据，可能改变生物科技的融资结构

  • 主持人描述了生物科技独特的公开市场结构：规模很小的团队早早上市，之后一项 Phase 2b 结果就可能决定公司是否有价值，还是实质上只剩空壳。Dempsey 预计，AI 能更快判断药物对人体是否安全。这可能降低成本、支持减少监管并加快商业化。他的论点不止于发现候选药物，还包括改变药物研发的整套机制。
  • 他举例提到 Montana 的《尝试权法案》，这是让患者更早获得临床试验后期药物的一项尝试。他也支持人体挑战试验：让志愿者感染病毒，给一组受试者使用候选药物，另一组作为盲法对照，并让所有人留在中心观察2周。目前这类试验主要用于呼吸道病毒；他认为，这种做法可以拓展到其他领域。
  • 如果干预会影响大脑，仅仅得到一个答案还不够；Dempsey 希望看到支撑结论的完整过程。他也预计，未来10年会有很多人因生物学自我实验而遭遇负面影响。他的投资立场介于“极度天真、非常乐观的人”和“极度冷漠、非常聪明且有才华的人”之间。懂得何时不理会这两种观点，是他所称投资优势的一部分。

9. 加密资产的流动性机会，比加密风投更清晰

  • 对 Dempsey 而言，加密仍是“上行不对称性最高的领域之一”。通过组织资本、编写更高效的系统来创造价值，有望经受住社会钟摆的变化；罕见病研究就是一种可能的应用。他是 Bitcoin 的拥趸。已披露的持仓包括 Hyperliquid、HairDAO 和 Kinetic，另有约13种加密资产；Helium 则是过去持有过的仓位。
  • 他认为，加密风投“差不多死了两年”。监管确定性正在改善，但原本可能去其他领域创业的人才，已被 AI 吸走。代币化也会损害他看重的长期激励机制。流动性市场更有意思，因为已充分分发的代币开始积累价值，可以从基本面和叙事角度加以评估。除了新兴的永续合约 DEX，他很少看到有创新性的风投尝试。
  • 有现金流的企业开始选择发行代币，扩大了可投资范围；潜在的股权上市则提供了另一条路径。Dempsey 起初预计，未来24个月加密行业会有超过20家企业 IPO。主持人认为过于乐观，并提出10家，Dempsey 同意。他举出的公开市场加密资产包括 Coinbase、BitGo、Circle 和 Securitize。Fireblocks 和 Ledger 未来也可能上市，但不少这类企业还没准备好。
  • Chainalysis 是他尝试买入股份约1年半的私营公司。他说自己“总是受到某位投资人的压力”，但没有解释具体含义。吸引力首先来自上一轮融资的“非常、非常大的折价”。如果加密行业变得更重要，网络犯罪又持续快速增长，他认为 Chainalysis 是3家有合理胜算的公司之一。他提到，公司在加密安全领域已有可验证的成绩，也在努力争取难以拿下的客户。

Speaker 1 This is a very rigorous approach. Does everything start with research?

Michael Dempsey Yes.

Speaker 1 So how do you invest if there’s something like, damn, you know, I think these markets are driven by the fear of missing out, right? Michael Dempsey Usually, you just skip it. We have a pretty narrow field for high-tech companies: machine learning, robotics, healthcare, biotech, and cryptography. I think what we’ve learned over the last 10 years is that we’re pretty good at analyzing companies as an n-of-1 and saying, “This could be very interesting and very big.” We don’t think we’re good at analyzing five early-stage companies and saying, “This is the best one. Speaker 1 Yeah, it’s like AI for lawyers, AI for accounting, all these different types of businesses. We just think, “That’s not our style, and that’s not where we’re getting the highest growth. We just shouldn’t be doing that.”

Ads (Fidelity Crypto)

I think investing is about figuring out the specific areas where you have alpha, if someone wants to use that word, and then continually developing those. Are all the founders of your portfolio companies scientists and engineers?

Michael Dempsey Many of them, yes, but not all. Some are more creative or imaginative technologists. Some are doctors, who I think are considered scientists. Sometimes they’re just operators who have novel insights.

Speaker 1 Have you been doing all these deep-tech things since 2016? In 2021, I would largely have called it SaaS plus cryptocurrencies. Was it a bubble?

Michael Dempsey Yeah, we started in 2016, so we’ve been doing this for a while. My life has been talking to LPs and managing funds. In 2016, we were doing a lot of things related to artificial intelligence, and then we started doing cryptocurrencies as well.

Then we changed our LPA and said, “Hey, we want to buy crypto tokens,” and our LPs were like, “Why are you buying things that people were buying drugs with online?” In 2018, our cryptocurrency portfolio decreased by about 95%, and they were asking, “Why, why, why, why did you do cryptocurrency? We told you not to.”

In 2020, our cryptocurrency portfolio grew significantly, and they asked, “Why aren’t you doing more crypto?” In 2021, they asked, “Why aren’t you making more crypto? What are these AI robotics companies? Why don’t you have any fintechs, consumer unicorns, or SaaS? What are you doing?”

We raised a new fund in 2021. We hadn’t invested for about 16 months, and they were like, “Why aren’t you investing? Everyone is investing now. Now is the time. Don’t have good deal flow? What’s going on?” In 2023, they were saying, “Thank God you didn’t invest in 2021.”

Our lives are like sitting in front of the 2 biggest tech waves—or bubbles, if you want to call them that—of the last decade and trying to figure out how to consistently play our game despite all this excessive hype around us.

Speaker 1 Do you feel like you’ve been rewarded for sitting idle? You raised money in 2021 and then didn’t invest for another 16 months, which is very difficult, I would say. Do you think you’ve been rewarded? I’m sure in ’23 people said, “Oh my God, thank you. You didn’t cost us money.” But were you rewarded based on the amount of pain you had to endure?

Michael Dempsey That’s a good way to put it. I don’t think it was that much pain. The pain was more like an irritation, not real pain. Real pain would be an LP saying, “Hey, buddy, come on.”

Speaker 1 Yes. Yes.

Michael Dempsey But real pain is losing money. That sucks. I think we didn’t handle it as well as we could have. I will say we made a mistake. I think we weren’t aggressive enough coming out of it. If you look at the 2023 class of companies—and we’ll see, who knows how much of this AI stuff will matter—there are some really interesting things that we didn’t get into as quickly because we weren’t able to get any signal from downstream capital that they were able to make meaningful investments.

That’s the worst part of venture capital: you rely on other people to make money to invest after you.

Speaker 1 So, in 2021, there’s this thing from Charles Hudson. I think Turner Novak posted it on Twitter, and I even have the quote on my computer. That’s my lesson from 2021: it’s not like people who were sober and restrained in 2021 received a lot of credit from their long-term investors for not participating in the circus.

Can AI Transform Biotech?

I think to myself, is this really what modern venture capital looks like? If there’s a speculative frenzy, the rational solution, if your goal is to remain a venture capitalist, may be to simply participate, even if you’re deeply skeptical about the ultimate outcome. The reason is that you have to stay relevant, stay in the industry, and be able to raise capital. To do that, your company has to be relevant and feel like it gets the message.

If that’s true, it takes you in a completely different direction from thinking, “Hey, people who go crazy and lose a lot of money on bad things are going to be punished, and the punishment is that you won’t raise another fund.”

Michael Dempsey Unfortunately, I really don’t think it works that way. I think this is partly true. In venture capital, there are institutions that are too big to fail, or institutions where you reach a point of no return. The reason you get to that point of no return is because your LP investors don’t want to look foolish either.

When someone from the fund office who runs the books comes in and says, “Listen, this new fund is the best,” they often come in and say, “We’ll invest $20 million in three funds over the next three vintages, and it’ll take, let’s say, a year.” To do that for a year and then say, “Actually, I messed up a bit, and this person is no good,” is also detrimental to their career.

Instead, they might say, “Hey, everyone else did it, so they’re just like everyone else who participated in the bubble.” I just don’t operate under the principle that if everyone else is doing it, we should too. It doesn’t make sense, and I think it works both ways.

We raise funds every 4 to 5 years. Most venture capital funds effectively operate on 24-month cycles, sometimes faster. In 2021, some funds invested their entire funds within 9 months. You could say all these companies are great, people will fund the next fund, and you can collect fees and make a ton of money. But we can’t say that.

We have 5 years, so companies that are like shooting stars, or companies that are great in 2021, will eventually fail in the third or fourth year. And that’s when we start raising funds. So we can’t play a pyramid scheme where we say the next company is the best. We must be able to maintain the portfolio we build.

Will AI Labs Eat Every Startup?

Speaker 2 Yes. Can we elaborate on this further? What do you think about it? I told you before we started recording: I was at a founders’ dinner last week, let’s say, and there were a lot of founders there, let’s call them Series B and Series C. The big question in that room is, “Are the labs going to eat us all?” So I’m curious what you think about it.

Michael Dempsey All companies, especially high-tech or applied-research organizations, have short-term, medium-term, and long-term moats. I think the problem is that no one can clearly define these moats in the medium and long term. I think the biggest problem with technology today is that people throw up their hands and say, “Everything is changing so quickly. How can you imagine where the world is heading?”

We often say internally that the only free thing in building a company is thinking. What you should focus on is understanding how to continually iterate your way toward the ultimate future you believe in. For us, I would say that I’m a moderate believer in the Bitter Lesson: these labs are going to continue scaling compute, data, and performance, and a lot of things are going to break down in the intermediate phase. Then you have to think about which layers will start accumulating value.

This could be a product layer. A group of people will go to specific places to get a set of products, which will evolve as models improve. But I think there are a lot of companies that are basically canonical GPT wrappers or something like that, and they don’t deserve to exist. There are also many areas of the market where so much is hidden.

A simple example is that everyone is fascinated by inference companies these days. You can look at a lot of these companies, whether it’s Fireworks, Together, Modal, or Foul, and there are a lot of them. They’re all growing very quickly, and they all have slightly different approaches and slightly different parts of the stack. But today, inference is growing, say, 10-fold year over year.

If you look at these companies, you’ll think, “Wow, they’re growing so fast. These are amazing companies.” But if the market is growing 10× and one of those companies is growing 6× year over year, you might start to wonder, “Is this company any good if it’s not even above replacement level?” If a company isn’t good above replacement level, eventually, when things calm down, the companies that are great above replacement level will start to win. That means companies that looked amazing on the way up will start to look really bad as the momentum stabilizes.

I think you’ll see underperforming assets that don’t look underperforming at all, because the numbers and the growth are so large and so heavily subsidized. Secondly, people are starting to think about where they want to own parts of the value chain. All these companies revolve around the idea that there’s unlimited demand for intelligence. Everyone agrees on that. Everyone says it, and everyone has these general numbers. They say Anthropic will spend a trillion dollars on compute, OpenAI will spend a trillion and a half dollars, and NVIDIA—

There’s a famous scene in The Big Short, or rather a quote from the book, where he did something no one else wanted to do: he went and read all the mortgages. I think there’s a perception that if you look at all these moving parts, you start to say, “Okay, obviously consolidation has to happen. Obviously people are going to start understanding more and more of the stack they want to own, because owning more different parts of the stack has its advantages.”

You’re going to have software optimization, you’re going to have compute, and what you’re seeing is that all these companies have gone from telling the story that they’re all playing in very specific slots in the ecosystem to, for example, some inference vendors starting to buy GPUs, and some neoclouds starting to work on software that optimizes their inference stack. That’s when you start to enter a completely different game. As an investor, you’re playing a game where you have assets valued at about $30 billion that could be displaced by competition in 9 months if someone decides to acquire a specific part of the stack they own. Or there could be drastic margin erosion, or you could just get squeezed out because you’re working with a limited number of GPUs.

We think a lot about all these steps and the long term. I’ll stop there, but the next order of business is: “Okay, in terms of understanding these steps, what are you doing?” You have to understand the entire value chain. You have to understand your very early-stage companies and which ones you can invest in. Then I have to understand what the biggest companies in the world are doing, because the technology market has a very interesting structure where the most innovative companies are actually the biggest. With pharmaceutical companies, it’s the opposite: the biggest companies don’t spend anything on R&D.

That’s why we look at the public markets: they allow us to learn a little more about how these companies work, what they do, and which of these 12 neoclouds are the most interesting to own and which ones to short or not hold.
