  • Jerry回忆，对方问他这次会面想得到什么时，他其实没想过——“作为喜剧演员，能见上这次面就算成功了。”

5. 1988年11月的Larry David：41岁的无名之辈

  • David对“Larry David是谁”这个问题直截了当：“他什么也不是。”41岁、单身、没钱，住在补贴艺术家住房里；他是“喜剧演员的喜剧演员”，笑点只对同行有效，对观众不奏效，已经被这个行业“嚼碎后吐了出来”。David说，Larry在《宋飞正传》之前的人生故事，“你们都知道，就是George Costanza的故事”。
  • 最典型的一段是：他在《Fridays》写剧本——那是ABC全面照搬《SNL》的节目，他在那儿认识了古怪的年轻喜剧演员Michael Richards——后来又在《SNL》待了1年，只有1个小品播出。他当场愤而辞职，随后开始担心交不起房租。邻居、真实的Kenny Kramer劝他：“你干吗不明天照常回去，假装什么都没发生？”这招奏效，后来也成了一集George的故事。
  • 还有两个关键细节：Larry在《SNL》认识了另一位没被充分使用的演员Julia Louis-Dreyfus；而NBC“讨厌这个人”——在他仅有的名声里，他是个失败者，无法在任何企业环境里正常做事。“结果他是个天才。”

6. 一家韩国杂货店、一家餐馆，以及真正的故事前提

  • NBC会面3天后，Jerry在Catch a Rising Star演出结束后找到Larry。两人在Lee's Market逛货架时闲聊，Jerry看到无花果条说：“这看起来像有人在地下室里做的。”Larry打断他：“就是这个。这才是这部剧该有的样子……两个男人就这么聊天。”
  • 第二天午夜，两人去了Westway Diner。Jerry提起喜剧演员最常被问的头号问题：你的素材从哪来？Larry说：“对了，这就是我们设置这部剧的方法。”真正的前提是：单口喜剧演员如何获得创作素材。Ben纠正流传已久的说法：“David从头到尾都没说过‘一部关于无聊的剧’。”这句话来自第4季的一条故事线：Jerry和George向虚构的NBC推销节目；后来它才被当成剧集起源的传说。
  • 这个前提决定Jerry在剧里演自己——他的感受方式、他的观察式幽默。Ben带着几分亲昵地说：“大家都知道Jerry不会演戏。”

7. FIN-SYN：塑造股权结构的监管意外

  • 回顾这段制度史：电视网和制片厂原本是不同公司。电视网承担60%至80%的制作成本，换取有限播映权，这种模式称为“赤字融资”；制片厂则拥有IP及后端收入，包括辛迪加发行、海外发行、周边和家庭录像。1960年代电视网越界，要求分走辛迪加收益，FCC于是于1970年出台“金融利益与辛迪加规则”，禁止电视网持有自己播出节目的经济权益，尤其是未来辛迪加发行权。
  • David认为，由此形成的生态“很像硅谷创业公司：资本主义式的创业激励”。独立制片公司拥有真正的权益，Ben补充说，这也带来了真实的幂律回报：“大多数剧集会失败，但成功的剧集会大获成功”，利润流向股权表上的个人，而不是大型集团。
  • Ben解释各方的激励：制片厂按设计每集都亏钱，5年或更久后的辛迪加发行才开始回本；电视网则经营“非常短期的生意”，租用法律上不能拥有的内容，赌广告收入高过租金。电视网到1993年已赢得废除规则的决定；访谈后面提到，废除于1995年生效。《宋飞正传》是“这套制度下最后一批作品之一”。

8. Castle Rock：可口可乐出资，Sony负责发行

  • 时间线是：可口可乐于1982年以7.5亿美元收购Columbia Pictures；Castle Rock于1987年由包括Rob Reiner在内的5位合伙人创立，理念是“由艺术家创办、为艺术家服务的制片厂”。可口可乐在公司成立时投资3000万美元，持股40%。Ben补充：“出资并制作《宋飞正传》的制片厂，本身的钱就来自可口可乐。”David打趣道：“你们觉得Jerry为什么在《宋飞正传》里喝Diet Coke？”
  • 关键条款是：Columbia获得Castle Rock所有作品的发行权。Sony于1989年11月收购Columbia后，这些发行权连同Castle Rock少数、非控股股权一起转到Sony手上；真正的IP仍留在独立公司Castle Rock。David提醒：“这一点之后会变得非常、非常重要。”

9. 电视史上最值钱的交易

  • David强调，这笔交易颠倒了常见流程：通常是制片公司先做试播集，再求电视网播出；这次却是NBC先向两个人承诺制作。用硅谷打比方，“就像你在投一轮A，而有人已经保证会在后面的C轮把它估值抬高10倍”。Jerry和Larry可以自己决定跟哪家制片厂合作、写下什么条件；他们选了Castle Rock，因为“他们看起来还不错”。
  • 据报道，收入分账大致为：Jerry和Larry各约15%，West和Shapiro约5%，Castle Rock及其继承方约50%，Sony作为发行商先行抽取约15%。确切条款从未公开，只有当事人知道。
  • Ben谈到这两人被问及收入时的应对：他们从来不完全否认。有人开口说6亿美元，他们回答：“荒谬。这数字太离谱了。”但“你也没说它完全不沾边”。

10. 《Stand-Up Diary》变成《The Seinfeld Chronicles》：批准节目的是不对口的部门

  • Larry觉得要做出90分钟单口喜剧“实在太难让人笑满90分钟”，于是提出把特别节目改成标准的30分钟情景喜剧试播集，实际内容22分钟，并将《Seinfeld's Stand-Up Diary》改名为《The Seinfeld Chronicles》。Jerry说：“一路上我们都在等着有人进来，说‘你们不能在电视网上这么做。’但没人来。”
  • David强调，这次意外在结构上很关键：NBC的深夜节目和特别节目部门批准了情景喜剧试播集——“这种事以前从没发生过”——完全绕开喜剧部门的剧本审查、意见、清单和委员会。NBC之所以点头，部分也是因为30分钟比90分钟更容易安排播出时段。

11. 选角：托尼奖得主、倒立，以及最好笑的姓氏

  • Rob Reiner建议让百老汇演员Jason Alexander饰演George；他当时即将拿下托尼奖，角色也需要一位演技成熟的演员与Jerry搭戏。Alexander最初把角色理解成Woody Allen，试镜时模仿Woody，后来才意识到George是以Larry为基础的松散写照。
  • Kramer最初叫“Kessler”，部分是为了避免可能涉及真实的Kenny Kramer的版权问题或付款；直到Larry和Jerry盯着剧本承认：“我们能想到的所有名字里，Kramer确实是最好笑的名字。好笑最重要，其他都排在后面。”Michael Richards试镜时倒立做瑜伽，边倒立边念台词。Tartikoff说：“你们要好笑的话……”

12. 试播集测试惨败，评估备忘录被贴在厕所墙上

  • NBC高管看完后的结论是：太纽约、太犹太。David反驳说：“美国喜剧的起源基本上就是纽约和犹太人。”从杂耍表演一路传下来的传统只是换了名字；到了1980年代末，“人人都知道Woody Allen是犹太人。他是喜剧界最大的名字”。
  • 测试流程是研究人员打冷电话，招募400户家庭去看一个闲置有线频道。原话反馈包括：“没人会因为要去洗衣房就兴奋起来”；George“不是个有冲击力的角色”；“他们为什么要用这些蠢故事打断单口表演？”David最喜欢研究报告里的这句：“没有任何一类观众急着再看这部剧，试播集整体表现被评为较弱。”Jerry和Larry后来把备忘录挂在制作办公室的厕所里。
  • NBC于1989年7月5日在一个冷门时段播掉试播集，秋季档没有订购，转而选了《The Nut House》和《Sister Kate》。Ben反复强调的一点是：“没人知道任何事。”

13. 一档被取消的Bob Hope特别节目，换来电视史上最短的季订购

  • Littlefield和Ludwin放不下这部剧——“要是它不好笑，我还真不信”——于是取消了一档2小时的Bob Hope特别节目，用它的预算订购4集。Littlefield回忆当时的电话：“Jerry最后问我，‘电视史上有没有哪部剧只拍4集就成功？’我不知道，所以我就照实告诉他。”Larry的反应是：“啊，没关系。我觉得我最多也就能拍4集。”后来他担任首席编剧，写了135集。
  • 另一条没走的路是：他们以为NBC已经放弃，于是把剧拿出去卖；Fox保证订购24集。Jerry拒绝了，因为创业初期的Fox“还不算大联盟，而我想进大联盟”。
  • Ben以创业公司的视角解读试播集的狂热小众反响：“你不是要让所有人都觉得还行，你要让一小群人觉得这东西有9.9分”，然后由他们主动向别人推荐。

14. “你们需要一个女人”——定义这部剧的颠覆

  • David说，NBC历史上唯一有用的创作意见是：试播集中女性观众评分最低，所以要加一个女主角。但这条意见的潜台词是给Jerry安排恋爱对象，像Sam和Diane、Ross和Rachel。George Shapiro说：“这是电视网的常规想法。幸好我们有两位创作者，根本不在乎……他们已经准备好因为这件事退出。”
  • 解决办法是让Elaine成为Jerry的前任：两人的关系早已失败，观众不必再看他们发展恋情。唯一深入讲这段关系的《The Deal》更加颠覆：他们重新试着交往，然后“再也不提这回事。没有结果……就当没发生过”。

15. 不给拥抱，不让成长：把单口喜剧嫁接到情景喜剧上

  • David对《宋飞正传》的定义是：单口喜剧与情景喜剧的结合。它像情景喜剧，有持续发展的角色和场景；又像单口喜剧，几乎不写角色成长——“Jerry永远是Jerry，George永远是George……他们什么都学不到。”Larry那句著名的规则“不给拥抱，不让成长”，据Ben说并非正式提出，而是大家共同遵循的创作理念。
  • David引用Jerry的说法：“Larry和我带给情景喜剧形式的，是单口喜剧演员的结构感。我们没时间交代角色到底是什么样的人，因为我们得把笑点写出来。”Ben转述编剧Jeff Schaffer的检验标准：“剧情本身必须在复述时也好笑。”因此剧集常在问题未解决、画面定格时结束，角色也没有后果。
  • Ben认为这部剧和观众之间的约定是相互尊重：“你跟我们一起懂这个笑点。”角色则是观众的愿望投射：“George是我们最糟糕一面的化身。我们都想从垃圾桶顶上拿走那个泡芙，但我们忍住了。”David补充说，其他情景喜剧里的拥抱和成长“全是假的”，观众最终看穿了这一点，这也是《宋飞正传》至今仍好看的原因。

16. 1990年夏：定制Nielsen数据帮了剧集一把，随后NBC勉强续订

  • 4集剧集从1990年5月31日起接在《Cheers》重播后播出。《The Seinfeld Chronicles》被缩短成《Seinfeld》，以免和ABC的《The Marshall Chronicles》混淆——“去掉The，干净利落。”同月Tartikoff离职，支持这部剧的Warren Littlefield出任娱乐部门总裁。
  • Littlefield按都会区定制Nielsen报告，检验“这剧只有纽约人看”的说法。结果显示，在纽约、芝加哥、休斯敦、西雅图和旧金山，观众从《Cheers》留存到《宋飞正传》的比例都相近，而且都很高。“这部剧有普世性。”
  • 后续续订则显得勉强：只订了13集，作为季中替补剧。NBC知道创作团队不会采纳意见，便让高管Perry Simon扮演砍稿人。Littlefield回忆录里记录Simon的话：“我试着临场发挥，给一些典型电视网意见……他们转身就走，我知道他们心里大概在说‘去你的’。现在回想起来，我真得感谢上帝。幸好他们没听。”

17. 《中国餐馆》引发冲突，以及“天才”的前提

  • NBC一度考虑因一集从头到尾都在餐馆大堂的剧集而停掉制作。Rick Ludwin带Larry在片场走了一圈，Larry当场爆发：“这就是这部剧。这是我的愿景。你们不喜欢，我就辞职。好，剧集就此结束。”David说：“没人这么做过。”
  • Ben强调，不能把这件事理解成“当个自大狂”的教训：“坚持自己肯定正确，从来不听意见，然后成功。大多数人、在大多数情况下，这样做会失败。”David转述Littlefield对于“为什么之后没人再这样做剧”的回答：“如果你要让天才做天才，就得先确认你合作的真是天才。”就像创始人一样，“大多数人不是天才”。
  • 第2季大结局《The Busboy》引入多条故事线交织的结构：4条并行剧情最后汇合，形成“一场暴烈、意外的爆发，同时毁掉所有人的生活”。David解释他们为什么摸索出这套方法：“每个真正伟大的单口喜剧段子都是这么收尾的”——到最后才发现，一切都在铺垫同一个回扣。

18. 看不见的制作创新

  • Ben梳理出的结构数据是：普通两幕情景喜剧22分钟通常有7场戏；《宋飞正传》有14至25场戏，而且完全抛弃幕结构。Larry想采用电影式的单机位拍法，NBC拒绝了；但剧组加入电影感灯光，并大量增加外景拍摄。
  • 剧组坚持纯粹：不用人工笑声。外景戏会拿到片场给现场观众播放，录下真实笑声；这也成了实时反馈机制，没效果的笑点可以及时重写，“因为这些人都是从单口喜剧来的”。
  • Ben的一个顿悟是：剧集不是用现场切换镜头拍摄，而是在后期剪辑，因此能切得更紧，也能实现现场切换做不到的笑点。例如《The Contest》的蒙太奇在角色彻夜未眠与“睡得像婴儿”之间切换。他们“发明了一套新制作流程，把两种拍法的优点都拿到手”。

19. 《The Contest》：秘密写作，靠MTV的广告商救场

  • 第4季第11集，也就是“掌控自己身体”那集，和许多《宋飞正传》的故事一样，取材自Larry的生活。创作团队担心内容“太过火”，所以秘密写剧本，不把内容写在办公室白板上，直到开拍前6天围读时才公布——“这是Larry和Jerry能把剧本拖到最后、又不致无法开拍的极限”。
  • 播出标准部门负责人Dr. Roz Weinman气得不行，最终还是松口：“也许这部剧和观众之间已经有默契，我们可以把这事做过去。”Ben解释，剧里从来没有说出那个明确的词，真正的问题是观众会爱它还是讨厌它；而《宋飞正传》已经培养出一群观众，对他们来说，“这么做完全没问题，尤其是处理得这么巧”。
  • 广告商撤出后，Littlefield转向MTV的赞助商名单，包括酒类品牌和Nike，补上广告位。留下来的赞助商得到皮面装订、全体演员签名的剧本。2009年，《TV Guide》把这集评为史上最佳电视剧集；它也让《宋飞正传》成为“茶水间热议的话题”。

20. 周四黄金档：Larry和Jerry的分歧，以及价值超过其他所有晚间档的时段

  • NBC把节目挪到周四，安排在《Cheers》之后播出。Larry愤怒而固执地说：“如果他们周三不看我们，我也不想让他们周四看我们。”Jerry的回应，以及这段合作为何行得通：“非常感谢。我们接受新时段。”Ben解读Larry时说，George身上那种可悲的劲儿被拧到了11档，但同一类矛盾也存在于Larry身上：“觉得自己是地球上最了不起的人……同时又极度自我意识、自我厌恶、自我怀疑。”
  • Ben说自己以前一直没弄明白周四为什么重要：这是广告商在周末电影上映和购物前，最后一次触达观众的机会。David给出的数据是，NBC周四的节目排期“比其他所有晚间档加起来还赚钱”。
  • 结果是，1993年2月收视率上升57%；一周之内，节目从当时播出电视剧中最受欢迎的第45位跃至第5位。更让电视网意外的是，《宋飞正传》的观众不但没有在《Cheers》播出后流失，反而增加。NBC随后为周四节目推出“Must See TV”口号。那时每集平均观众约3000万，Larry对《LA Times》说：“这大概意味着灾难就要来了。”
  • 时机也帮了节目一把：流行语（“yada yada yada”“shrinkage”和Festivus）走红时，互联网刚刚兴起。David转述Steve Case的故事：AOL的连接人数只有在《宋飞正传》播出时下降；“节目一结束，大家又都上线，在AOL上聊《宋飞正传》。”

21. 高强度运转：7天流水线，以及最后一刻的现场改写

  • 据编剧Alec Berg、David Mandel和Jason Alexander回忆，剧组周三开工，下一周周二拍摄，于是周末也变成额外改稿时间；这没什么问题，因为“他们几乎没有个人生活”。Alexander描述围读后的惯例：“他们会提意见，然后Larry就辞职。接着意见被扔掉。然后Larry答应留下来。”剧本没有舞台指示，只有对白，因为大家都是喜剧演员；演员即使没有自己的戏，也会留在现场，大家一起排戏。
  • 人才来源方面，Jerry和Larry不再生活在普通人的世界里，于是每年从新编剧那里挖掘新鲜素材，包括一批哈佛讽刺剧团的编剧：“把大家生活里最好的素材都拿走，然后换下一个人。”Festivus和小费罐的点子都来自编剧的真实生活。
  • 《The Marine Biologist》里George走进海里的镜头没有引发预期笑声，剧组当场围在一起讨论。Larry现场写出整整一页独白；托尼奖得主Jason Alexander说：“教练，让我上。”随后冷读“海那天很愤怒，我的朋友们”，没彩排、第一次读，就把前面Kramer的高尔夫球故事接了回来。“这是一颗Titleist吗？”

22. 第一轮辛迪加发行：5亿美元，以及Castle Rock卖在了错误时点

  • 剧集达到约100集时，Sony于1995年以超过5亿美元的价格，将《宋飞正传》卖给创纪录的224家地方电视台。这笔钱只对应首个5年窗口，仅含地方电视台，还不包括有线电视。播出重播的电视台开始在各自时段里超过直播节目，包括地方新闻。它被称为“有史以来最适合辛迪加发行的剧集”：没有连续剧情，任何一集都能按任意顺序看。
  • Castle Rock于1993年12月卖给Turner，收取1亿美元现金并承担约3亿美元债务，总价约4亿美元。Ben先透露结局：Castle Rock按分账最终本可以获得“20亿至25亿美元”，但这笔钱被Turner、后来又被Warner Bros.拿走。Ben修正自己的判断：“Castle Rock绝对不该卖，但没人能预料《宋飞正传》会经历6轮辛迪加发行。”
  • 有条传闻需要谨慎看待：David提到Steve Bannon曾是Turner交易的投资银行家，可能以《宋飞正传》股权形式拿了佣金；Ben说细节不清楚，但他看到过报道，称Bannon至今还在收辛迪加版税。

23. Larry的锁定期结束，演员争取唯一一次涨薪机会

  • Larry于1996年离开，既精疲力竭，也已结婚。用David的创业比喻来说，“公司上市，锁定期结束了”：1995年的辛迪加发行收入让他从此有钱，不论后面还有没有新集数。剧集的损失是：Larry是让每集剧本变好的“CPU”；他离开后，所有编剧都开始周末工作。Alec Berg曾发现自己连续56天每天都去办公室。
  • 到1997年，《宋飞正传》当年为NBC带来2亿美元利润，约占全网约10亿美元利润的20%。这还低估了它的价值，因为要买3000万美元的《宋飞正传》广告位，广告商得承诺在NBC黄金时段总共投放2亿美元。“这就叫捆绑销售，宝贝。”
  • 演员是没有后端收入的雇员；据引述，Alexander估算他们一生累计从工会拿到的剩余收益约为每人25万美元。第8季之后，演员集体争取加薪。Jerry站在他们这边，表示3人都签约他才拍第9季。最终他们拿到每集60万美元，即当季每人1440万美元；Jerry的片酬则达到每集100万美元，在当时创下电视演员片酬纪录——这还不包括他的所有权收益。

24. Jack Welch的1.1亿美元邀约，以及Ben认为拒绝是最佳商业决策的理由

  • 1997年底，Welch在Bob Wright位于Trump Tower公寓的早午餐会上播放幻灯片，论证剧集还没到巅峰，最后以这句话收尾：“所有来找我说话的人，只想知道一件事：Jerry Seinfeld还会不会回来拍下一季？”随后他把Jerry叫到一边，在纸上写下：每集500万美元，22集，总计1.1亿美元——这是第10季的确定片酬，是Jerry此前纪录片酬的5倍，相当于NBC年利润的11%；而开价的人正是以六西格玛成本纪律闻名的Welch。
  • 在Central Park的一张长椅上——21岁的Jerry曾在同一张长椅上告诉父亲自己要做单口喜剧演员——Howard West说他愿意再拍一季，George Shapiro则说，巅峰离场会很漂亮。1997年12月26日，《New York Times》把这条消息放在头版左上角。Jerry解释自己的想法：“你站在台上已经很久了，观众还在尖叫；如果你这时离场，他们会喊得更响。他们永远不会忘记你。”
  • Ben认为，拒绝邀约是“Jerry Seinfeld做过的最佳商业决策”，因为这保护了文化影响力，也支撑了之后几十年的辛迪加发行。David称这是假设得挺有意思，也看得出其中的逻辑。两人提到的估算是：剧集完结后看过《宋飞正传》的人数，是播出期间的3至5倍——“《宋飞正传》的观众大多数是在那个圣诞决定之后才来的。”Ben认为，关键在于人们心里“留下的那种味道”。
  • 两位主持人十年来反复引用Jerry在2017年HBR访谈中的回答。有人问他，为什么不找更有效率的方式拍剧，McKinsey会怎么建议？Jerry回答：“McKinsey是谁？……他们好笑吗？那我不需要他们……如果你做事很有效率，那你就做错了。正确的路，是那条难走的路。”David将其概括为：在创意或创业领域，“如果你想要离群的成绩，就得走难走的路”。Ben把这和Bezos的“发明与漫游”联系起来。

25. 没人喜欢的大结局（但这不重要），以及第二轮发行的11亿美元

  • 1998年5月14日播出的结局由Larry回归执笔：剧中几人因违反见义勇为法受审，一众客串明星出庭证明他们都是坏人。结局吸引7630万观众，占当晚所有电视观众的58%。NBC的30秒广告位最高卖到200万美元，比1998年超级碗的130万美元贵54%；Apple还特别投放了一次《Think Different》广告，把Jerry加入广告阵容。David认为，结局是在“向客串明星致谢”；它不受欢迎“也许反而添了传奇色彩——没人学到任何东西，所以我们连一个令人满意的大结局都不给你”。
  • Ben指出，《M*A*S*H》、《Cheers》和《The Fugitive》的大结局观众都更多，“但现在没人花钱买它们的流媒体版权。它们没有跨代传播。”
  • 1998年的辛迪加发行加入有线电视。拥有Castle Rock的TBS为每集出价100万美元，合计近2亿美元——这实际上是从自己拥有的公司买版权，因为Sony持有发行权，版权必须放到市场上竞价。这轮发行据报总收入达11亿美元；剧集还没完结，辛迪加发行累计收入就达到16亿美元。25年后的喜剧尾声是：2024年《Curb》大结局让Larry入狱，直到Jerry出现说：“你不会想要这个的。相信我，没人想要这个。”

26. 30年的经营：品牌代言人、DVD，以及一次险些引发的灾难

  • 完结后的总账包括：创纪录的6轮以上广播电视辛迪加发行；截至2010年，辛迪加收入27亿美元，到2013年升至31亿美元；DVD按每次1至2季陆续发行，后来推出全集套装，估计又带来5亿美元收入。演员们为DVD后端收益再次集体争取，据报道每人拿到了数千万美元的低位数金额。
  • David这样概括Jerry和Larry的第二职业：“他们之后主要的经济工作，就是永久为《宋飞正传》做巡回宣传。”《Curb》、《Comedians in Cars》和特别节目都沿着迪士尼飞轮的思路，围绕核心IP继续创造内容，却不打乱核心。Larry David做《Curb》25年的收入，只是他做《宋飞正传》7年收入的一小部分。
  • 2006年Michael Richards的种族主义爆发事件，从商业角度看，“会让商业模式面临风险”。Ben分析其中的沟通尺度：谴责要足够明确，让人看出Jerry没有装作没事；但又不能说得太过，让观众转而觉得“我也不喜欢Kramer了”。David说，这项资产的价值“和当下的文化相关性绑得太紧”，因此哪怕只是让人潜意识里觉得不舒服，也很危险。

27. 流媒体：最后一个自由球员，以及70亿美元的总账

  • 版权交易的顺序是：Hulu于2015年以1.5亿美元买下5年版权；到了2019年，Netflix失去《Friends》和《The Office》——Warner Bros.以报价4.25亿美元收回《Friends》，NBC则以5亿美元收回《The Office》。Warner Bros.掌握《Friends》的发行权，NBC拥有《The Office》。Sony没有自己的流媒体平台，是《宋飞正传》的独立发行商，Netflix据报为全球独家版权的5年合约支付超过5亿美元。Ben说，3部剧里只有《宋飞正传》是“确实有一家公司在给另一家公司付钱”。
  • 据报道，Netflix在2026年续约的金额略低于首份合约，但版权范围仅限美国和加拿大。Sony押注可将海外流媒体版权单独变现，并很快开始这么做。David预计，每10年还能再叠加“超过10亿美元的流媒体版权收入”。
  • 全生命周期账本是：通过辛迪加发行、流媒体和DVD，沿《宋飞正传》的股权表累计约50亿美元；NBC首播广告利润再贡献约20亿美元，合计70亿美元以上，对比约2.5亿美元的总制作成本。“成本回报达到30倍。”Jerry个人从后端收入中估计拿到7.5亿美元；Castle Rock则按设计在首播制作阶段亏钱，“就像早期创投组合的前9年”。

28. 流媒体为何付钱、类似《宋飞正传》的剧为何可能变少，以及它真正拥有的力量

  • Ben用拉新与留存来解释：新剧帮助平台吸引订户，所以他猜测如今一季通常只有8集——第14集的1000万美元，可能更适合拿去拍另一部剧的第6集；而《宋飞正传》是“完美的留存工具”，像舒适区里的食物，能从两个层面降低退订率：用户浏览时可能被吸引看下去；知道平台上有这部剧，也就不想取消订阅。Ben认为喜剧的国际传播范围，可能让它很难适配追求规模经济的业务；David补充，喜剧需要慢慢发酵，未必适合拉新。Ben抛出一个让人头大的观点，David有保留地认同：NBC在1990年代的广告模式会鼓励吸引受教育程度高的观众；而在流媒体里，“你只是用户每月12.99美元的载体”。
  • 这样的作品还能再出现吗？两人都认为，如今不受委员会干预、由创作者主导的作品，大多只能出现在体系之外（YouTube、播客），因为体系内“赌注太大”；在今天的电视行业，创作者很难拥有足以让自己亲自赚到5亿美元的剧集股权。Ben猜测，现代发行商是受过科技公司训练的企业，习惯前期投入并掌握运营杠杆。David原以为NBC高管会后悔没有拿到《宋飞正传》的后端收益，但他发现他们对这笔交易很满意：“一年就能收回投资，而且投资回报倍数很高。”两人也都认为，废除FIN-SYN规则“可能是这个行业遭遇过的最糟糕的事情之一”，它让内容来源趋于集中。
  • 把《宋飞正传》的股权结构套进Seven Powers框架，能看到几种力量：错位竞争——Friends和《The Office》“受所有权结构束缚”，无法以同样方式在公开市场上竞争；网络效应，而非规模经济——“你知道《宋飞正传》的所有梗，对我来说非常有价值”；独占资源——“可能就只有这一点”；制作期间还有流程优势。David说，Larry没法在《Curb》重现《宋飞正传》的制作流程，因为《Curb》靠即兴创作，制作方式也完全不同。
  • 对于剧集的精髓，两位主持人强调了不同部分。David认为，巅峰收官帮助《宋飞正传》维持了“史上最佳剧集”的地位；Ben的说法是“观众带来观众”：1995年和1998年的成功发行让剧集无处不在，渗进日常生活，再代代相传。Nielsen数据显示，2021年的观众中有41%在剧集完结时还是幼儿，或尚未出生。Ben举的例子是他3岁的孩子指着屏幕问：“那是Jerry Seinfeld吗？”

29. 值得留下的冷知识：乐高式配乐和痴迷数据的观众

  • 作曲家Jonathan Wolff把Jerry的独白声线当成“歌词”，找到Jerry单口表演约110 bpm的节奏。他没有写一首固定主题曲，而是设计出一套系统，为每集音乐创作不同变体。他说：“我需要把它设计成模块化，能像乐高音乐一样移动、变化。”电视网高管当然很讨厌这套做法；David认为，这恰恰是质量的信号。
  • 其他趣闻包括：Julia Louis-Dreyfus出身于法国Louis-Dreyfus大宗商品交易家族；她的祖父曾驾驶私人拥有的Ferrari 166参加勒芒赛事。David选的剧集是《The Marine Biologist》，以及《The Jacket》和《The Dinner Party》。Ben找到的网站seinfeld.visualizingdata.com，则是Andy Kirk制作的121页数据可视化：逐场、逐个笑点全部手工标注，“他坐在沙发上，打开电子表格……那时还没有AI”。

全文文稿（原文）

Ben Gilbert So, David, I bought a DVD player for research for this episode.

David Rosenthal No way. Did you buy the box set?

Ben Gilbert There’s some stuff, like facts about the pilot, that’s only available in the DVD commentary—

David Rosenthal Yes.

Ben Gilbert —and doesn’t exist anywhere online. So I had to go on eBay, buy a copy of the Seinfeld DVDs, and buy a brand-new DVD player here in 2026 to view it.

David Rosenthal Do they even sell those on Amazon anymore?

Ben Gilbert They do. Sony makes them.

David Rosenthal Wow.

Ben Gilbert They’re, I don’t know, $100 or something.

David Rosenthal Sony. There you go. Appropriately, distributors of Seinfeld.

Ben Gilbert That’s right. All right, shall we do it?

David Rosenthal Let’s do it.

Ben Gilbert Today, listeners, we’re taking a giant left turn. David and I were staring at each other, poring over our usual topic list, and we decided we only wanted one criterion for selecting this episode: What would we have the absolute most fun making, and can we do something different and fresh for Acquired? We found something we’re very pumped about: the business of Seinfeld, the show.

We had both just read this astonishing stat: In the first 6 months of 2026, Seinfeld was watched by 60 million Americans, about 20% of the entire U.S. population.

David Rosenthal This show went off the air almost 30 years ago.

Ben Gilbert I reached out to Nielsen to verify this. Not only is it true, they said that if you update it through the end of August, that number is up from 60 million to 72 million Americans.

David Rosenthal Oh, wow. That’s almost the same audience size as the Seinfeld finale when it aired.

Ben Gilbert This is a show that finished making new episodes nearly 3 decades ago, and yet we’re all still watching it. Netflix’s 2019 deal for Seinfeld, which was reported at well over $500 million over 5 years, was the largest sum a streamer had ever paid an outside studio to license a series that was no longer in production. That’s more than $100 million a year, decades after they were done making new episodes.

The economics, the way it’s owned and structured, are essentially a complete accident of history. Seinfeld managed to be one of the last shows of the old world, where everyone watched the same thing at the same time, while also having a foot in the new world, just as the internet was taking off.

David Rosenthal Yep.

Ben Gilbert The story is really an entrepreneurial one of obsession, craft, and a team that created the number one show in America by doing everything completely differently from the way it had ever been done before, defying all conventional wisdom. It’s one of the best examples we’ve ever studied on Acquired: the creators, Jerry Seinfeld and Larry David, believed so strongly that their product was excellent that they didn’t care what anyone else thought or what the numbers looked like at first. A small, passionate early fan base, with a slow burn, went on to become their greatest asset.

Today, listeners, we’re doing an experiment here on Acquired: the business of Seinfeld.

David Rosenthal Let’s do it.

Ben Gilbert David, where do we begin?

David Rosenthal Well, naturally, even though this is an episode about Seinfeld the show, not Jerry Seinfeld the person, we have to start with Jerry himself.

Ben Gilbert Yes.

David Rosenthal Jerry was born in 1954 in Brooklyn to a Jewish family. When he was young, his family moved to a small town on Long Island named Massapequa. I actually spent a fair amount of my childhood in Massapequa. It’s definitely suburban Long Island. There wasn’t a lot of interesting culture going on there.

Ben Gilbert Great.

David Rosenthal But Jerry’s father, Cal Seinfeld, was known in the family and among his friends as a funny guy who was always telling great jokes, as Jerry would talk about it later. He had the funny gene, and Jerry definitely did, too.

Ben Gilbert Yeah, Jerry insists that comedy is a gene, right?

David Rosenthal Yes. He thinks his kids have it. He knows his dad had it.

Ben Gilbert And that it can’t be taught.

David Rosenthal Yep.

Ben Gilbert Obviously, you can work really hard to hone it and develop more material, but the instinct is actually genetic.

David Rosenthal Yep, yep. He was always making his friends and family laugh. Around the same time, when he was about 12 years old, he fell in love with an album—a record. Not a music album, not one of the great bands of the ’60s or ’70s, but Bill Cosby’s stand-up comedy album, Why Is There Air? And this is—

Ben Gilbert These comedy records used to be a big thing.

David Rosenthal Yeah, stand-up albums on vinyl were a big thing.

Ben Gilbert It’s funny: today we all tune in to Netflix to watch the big stand-up special that just dropped. Albums were doing that same thing 50-plus years ago.

David Rosenthal Yep, totally. After high school, Jerry went to Queens College in New York, actual New York City, where he majored in communications and theater. He was really into comedy, so he set up an independent study where he studied stand-up comedy like his heroes. He went out to the comedy clubs in New York and wrote papers for college analyzing various comedians’ sets. Then he went on stage as part of his college studies to get experience and try out being a stand-up comic. It was just like what he was born to do.

Ben Gilbert And it seems like, from every interview he’s given—and Jerry has given a lot of interviews—

Ben Gilbert Yep, yep. And that is what Sentry does. It takes the thing your users are yelling about and traces it back to the exact change that started it, which release, who was impacted, and the very commit or very golf ball with the developer’s name on it. Then all that context goes straight into whatever writes the fix, whether it’s Claude Code or Cursor or Sentry’s own agent, Seer, which finds the issue and opens the PR for a human to review.

David Rosenthal This is why 200,000 organizations run on Sentry, whether it’s a solo side project or the engineering teams at Anthropic, Vercel, Linear, or GitHub. You can learn more about where software gets fixed at sentry.io/acquired, or click the link in the show notes and just tell them that Ben and David sent you.

So how did it work to actually produce the weekly Seinfeld episode? Thank you to Alec Berg and David Mandel for talking us through this. They were writers on the show, and there are some great interviews with Jason Alexander that share a lot of the detail, too.

The typical sitcom schedule would start on a Monday with rehearsals, leading up to a Friday shoot. On Seinfeld, they realized, “Well, actually, we could start the week on Wednesday and shoot the following Tuesday. When the actors go home for the weekend, that means we can get some extra time to rewrite the episode and make it better.” That was fine, since they weren’t married and didn’t have kids. They had no personal life to speak of. They were obsessed with this, so that’s just what they did.

Day 1 starts with a table read. Everyone is there: producers, writers, NBC executives, and Castle Rock representatives. As Jason Alexander put it, they would then have a big powwow after the table read. They would give their notes, then Larry would quit. The notes would be thrown away, Larry would agree to stay, and then he would come back tomorrow.

Ben Gilbert Sounds about right.

David Rosenthal That’s day 1. The actors start trying to rehearse, but it’s all going to change so materially, and they know it, so they’re not taking that rehearsal that seriously. They’re just familiarizing themselves with the material. Larry and Jerry would then do a bunch of rewrites overnight. The scripts don’t really have stage directions. It’s just dialogue, because they’re comedians. That’s what they write.

Ben Gilbert Right.

David Rosenthal So the actors had to figure it out. Seinfeld had this really unique, collaborative way of working, where the actors would stay on set even when it wasn’t their scene so they could work through it together and trade ideas. They’d say, “Oh, actually, I think it would be funnier if Kramer’s at the fridge right now with the door open, going through it, rather than George,” and try to figure out the blocking together.

Ben Gilbert Yep.

David Rosenthal Then day 3: more full rewrites overnight, more rehearsing, still just internal to the team. The network isn’t there yet. The actors are there, the writers, Larry, and Jerry. This becomes more or less the shape of the final script. Then, at the end of the day, NBC and Castle Rock come in. They watch a full run-through and give their notes. As Jason Alexander says, Larry would quit.

Ben Gilbert Yep.

David Rosenthal Their notes would be diminished, and Larry would come back.

Day 4 is camera-blocking day. This is when the cameramen come in and start learning their shots: who’s taking what. The episode is finalized enough to figure out what shots they need and which cameras they’re assigning. It’s a very difficult thing, because it’s not like the 4 cameras just sit there and don’t change. Let’s say you’re camera 1. You’re responsible for a wide shot. It comes off you and goes to camera 3. You have 5 seconds to scramble, shift, and zoom, and get a two-shot on 2 characters, because when it flips back to you, that’s where you’re supposed to be.

Ben Gilbert Yep.

David Rosenthal It’s a real ballet and art. They all rehearse as a unit, the cameramen and the actors, because the next day they’re in front of a live audience.

Ben Gilbert Yep.

David Rosenthal On day 4, especially as the show got bigger and they were doing more on-location filming outside the permanent sets—the coffee shop and Jerry’s apartment—they’d do things like go to the fake New York street on a different lot for the outdoor street shots, or actual filming locations like the cemetery where George visits Susan.

Ben Gilbert Oh, boy.

David Rosenthal Yeah. Then day 5 is rehearsal in the morning, and they bring in the live audience to film in the afternoon. They’d run the entire show in chronological order. If there were any scenes that weren’t on those permanent sets, the audience—who were sitting in big bleachers in front of the coffee shop and Jerry’s apartment—would watch a rough cut of what was shot outside on a screen they brought down. That way, they could record those laughs, just like we talked about earlier.

If they didn’t get a laugh, do you know what they would do, David?

Ben Gilbert Ooh, no, I didn’t find this.

David Rosenthal If it wasn’t going as expected, even with the live audience there, they would pause production. They’d huddle all the writers, actors, and the director on stage. They’d bring out a live band that was just waiting on set to entertain the audience. They also had comics and other people warm up the audience.

Ben Gilbert Right.

David Rosenthal They’d huddle and try to figure out a better joke.

Ben Gilbert Hmm, yeah. Why isn’t this working? Yep.

David Rosenthal Or how to rewrite it live. The best example of this is in “The Marine Biologist.”

Ben Gilbert Yeah, yeah.

David Rosenthal The episode is supposed to end with George walking into the ocean. If you’ve seen this episode, that is not the end.

Ben Gilbert This is the best story.

David Rosenthal It’s so good. They bring down the screen to show the on-location shot. George walks into the ocean. The audience is confused. There’s been a lot of buildup, but there’s no joke here. So they all huddle and come up with the idea for George to have an additional scene in the booth, where he does a monologue. Then he finally produces the golf ball out of his pocket, which ties in a plot from earlier in the episode, where Kramer’s hitting golf balls into the ocean. That golf ball turns out to be lodged in a whale’s blowhole in George’s storyline, which is why the whale needed a marine biologist in the first place—the role George was pretending to have.

Ben Gilbert So good. It’s so good.

David Rosenthal Larry goes off after their huddle and writes a full-page monologue on the spot. Jason Alexander tells Larry, “Yeah, I can do that. I’m a Tony Award-winning actor.”

Ben Gilbert Yeah.

David Rosenthal I’m a theater actor.

Ben Gilbert Yeah.

David Rosenthal This is “Put me in, coach.” This is what I do. Give me a monologue.

David Rosenthal Yes.

Ben Gilbert So, yeah, he memorizes it and performs it on the spot. It’s incredible.

David Rosenthal In parallel to this entire process is pre-production, where all the writers are paired up in groups of 2 or often just alone in their own offices, writing the next week’s episode, the week after that, the week after that, and then—

David Rosenthal Yeah, the Seinfeld star is burning brighter and brighter and brighter, consuming everybody within it in the fusion reactor at its core.

Yep.

Ben Gilbert

Okay, so my big question for you in analysis, before we get to Powers and Quintessence: We opened the episode by saying this couldn’t happen again today, that this was so anomalous it needed to happen at the exact time it happened, with the exact people who made it. I have a list of things that I think couldn’t happen today, and I’m curious about your thoughts on them.

David Rosenthal

Great. I’ve got a list, too. You want to trade back and forth?

Ben Gilbert

Yeah, let’s do it. My first one: Arguably, the whole show was so creator-led, with essentially no design by committee. I bet that’s pretty hard to find today.

David Rosenthal

Well, it’s easy to find on YouTube or—

Ben Gilbert

Yes.

David Rosenthal

—podcasts or creator media—

Ben Gilbert

And completely outside the system.

David Rosenthal

Completely outside the system. And it is almost impossible to find inside the system because the stakes are too high now. Executives at some organization are involved, whether it’s the streamer, or the production company, or the studio. The budgets are so big. That was my point about the stakes being too high.

Ben Gilbert

Right.

David Rosenthal

You want to make a TV show these days, you need a lot of freaking money. There’s no way something could start like Seinfeld did back in the day, with that budget and that set of episodes.

Ben Gilbert Right. I think It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia did, but that’s now 23 years old or something. I think Tires did, too. Tires was pretty low-budget when it started.

David Rosenthal Yeah. And it was creator-led and independent. So, yeah, I guess it can happen out there. But by and large, you want to make a TV show, you need a lot of money, which means you’re going to have suits weighing in on what’s going on.

Ben Gilbert Which is just going to make everything worse—

David Rosenthal Yeah.

Ben Gilbert —those damn suits.

David Rosenthal Yep.

Ben Gilbert All right, next for you.

David Rosenthal No doubt the independent cap table and incentives associated with Seinfeld made it what it is today. The fact that Jerry and Larry, as creators, got this incredible deal and set of circumstances that let them get huge backend from the production company, and then they made the show artistically what they wanted, but they were always incentivized for the long run, made all the difference in the world.

Ben Gilbert Yes. It is probably impossible today to make a TV show that you, in any way, make $500 million from. You can make it in secondary ways. You can get famous from the TV show and then pick up sponsorships and get to invest in companies and stuff like that. But to truly own enough of a show’s long-term economics to make hundreds of millions of dollars, I think that’s over.

David Rosenthal Yeah.

Ben Gilbert That would only exist in the creator world, like podcasts and YouTube.

David Rosenthal Yep.

Ben Gilbert It doesn’t happen on TV. So the question is: why? Because both business models are totally viable. The old media networks one, where you’re like, “I don’t want to own the long-term upside. I just want to have a profitable business today,” or the one that the Netflixes of the world are doing, where they do want to own all the long-term upside. And follow me on this.

Ben Gilbert I think it’s because the distribution that happens today is on tech companies at their core, not on media networks, which I think were capital-constrained. Tech companies are very used to making big investments up front, the way you would in software, with very high margins when you get to scale. But obviously, you’re way in the hole for a while until you get to scale. Microsoft’s a terrible business with 100 customers but an unbelievable business with a billion customers. The modern media company wants to own all of that risk, like a tech company, and pay for it up front so they can own all the rewards later in the success case, which is the exact opposite of the traditional media business.

David Rosenthal Right. Right.

Ben Gilbert Or the traditional networks business.

David Rosenthal You know, what’s interesting is I sort of expected going into this research to hear over and over that NBC realized their great mistake in not owning any of the back end of Seinfeld, and they let so much value walk. It was this bitter lesson that, especially once Fin-Syn was repealed, they never allowed something like that to happen again. That’s the fact pattern. But actually, back in the day, the executives were fine with it. They were happy with the arrangement: “Yeah, you production companies, you’re essentially the VCs. You take the risk, you make money on the back end. We get this great stuff that we can put on our network, and—”

Ben Gilbert We have a one-year payback period on a multiple of our invested capital.

David Rosenthal “—sell ad units.” We’re super happy. That works great.

Ben Gilbert Yeah. I think it comes down to tech companies being trained to seek operating leverage and attract investors who want operating leverage. That wasn’t a thing when media was distributed by networks. But now that’s the ultimate end state of media distributors being tech companies.

David Rosenthal And back in the day, they were the only game in town, right? You were going to tune into—

Ben Gilbert Yes.

David Rosenthal —NBC, ABC, or CBS, and then eventually Fox, too. That was it.

Ben Gilbert Yep. One other little piece of analysis before we get to Seven Powers. There’s a very real argument here that Fin-Syn being repealed is one of the worst things to happen to the industry in the last several decades.

David Rosenthal Yep.

Ben Gilbert The networks start saying, “We’re gonna pick from the in-house things that we’ve sort of come up with to hit the airwaves.” It just means that you get bad stuff out there.

David Rosenthal Yeah.

Ben Gilbert Whereas if you have this thriving free market of a whole bunch of independently funded small studios coming up with things, and you can buy from any of those, that’s a much better world for content.

David Rosenthal Totally agree. And we heard that universally in the research: “Yep, those were the good days.” Fin-Syn being repealed ended that.

Ben Gilbert Yep, and consolidated where content can come from. Fortunately, the internet changed that, and we have YouTube and the explosion of creator diaspora now.

David Rosenthal Yep. Powers. This is actually gonna be really fun.

Ben Gilbert So let’s see. Normally, the way we do this exercise, Seven Powers are the seven things that could give a company persistent differential returns, or the ability to be more profitable than its nearest competitor on a sustainable basis. Who’s the entity here? The Seinfeld cap table?

David Rosenthal Yeah, I think we should talk about it from the cap table’s perspective.

Ben Gilbert And it’s what lets Seinfeld, the asset of the show, even when it was being produced and today, be more valuable than—

David Rosenthal Other shows.

Ben Gilbert —anything that competes with it, other shows.

David Rosenthal Yep. Yep.

Ben Gilbert Okay.

David Rosenthal I think counter-positioning today might be the biggest one because it’s the last of these huge retention tools left that is not captively owned by a streamer. So it can come to market in a way that Friends and The Office can’t.

Ben Gilbert And you think that’s counter-positioning?

David Rosenthal Well, if you were to say Friends and The Office are its competitors, they are structurally hamstrung—

Ben Gilbert Right.

David Rosenthal —by their ownership situations now.

Ben Gilbert If they did compete with Seinfeld in the free market and were able to go anywhere, it would hamstring their parent company—

David Rosenthal Their parent companies would be making value-destructive decisions to do that.

Ben Gilbert Yep, at least based on their chosen current strategy of needing to have owned-and-operated streaming services.

David Rosenthal Yep.

Ben Gilbert Scale economies all over the place. I mean, the fact that the world has an installed base of 100 million-plus Seinfeld fans—

David Rosenthal Oh, I agree, but I would say this is network economies, not scale economies.

Ben Gilbert Oh, that we’re all like—

David Rosenthal The fact that you know all the memes from Seinfeld is extremely valuable to me.

Ben Gilbert You’re right. I don’t think they’re scale economies, because the definition of scale economies is when I can do something more profitably for the same input than one of my competitors can because I have more scale. But this asset doesn’t actually make any decisions or do anything. Netflix has scale economies. When Netflix decides to pay $500 million, it can make better use of the Seinfeld content and be more profitable on that acquisition than smaller streaming services.

David Rosenthal Yep.

Ben Gilbert But yeah. Branding?

David Rosenthal Eh.

Ben Gilbert Maybe?

David Rosenthal It depends what you consider branding.

Ben Gilbert Right. Is the whole tenor of the show branding? Is it just—

David Rosenthal Yeah.

Ben Gilbert —the logo? I’d much rather watch Seinfeld than The Big Bang Theory, but that’s not because it’s called Seinfeld and I trust Seinfeld more. It’s because I think the intrinsic quality of the show is higher.

David Rosenthal Yep. Yep. I don’t think there are any switching costs here.

Ben Gilbert No.

David Rosenthal I can’t even think of what that would be in this case. Cornered resource, obviously: they have the rights to Seinfeld.

Ben Gilbert And maybe that is the power. That might just all be cornered resource. We have a thing that we can sell that other people can’t sell and make a lot of money on it.

David Rosenthal Yep. And then the last one, process power.

Ben Gilbert Not today, but there was. If you change this exercise to what Seinfeld had when it was being produced that other shows didn’t have, it’s absolutely process power in the way they were making it. It’s absolutely cornered resource in Jerry and Larry, and some of the other writers they had, too.

David Rosenthal I think there was process power clearly in the act of making the show. I don’t think Jerry or Larry individually, or if they were to come together again now, could repeat it. It was a magic moment. And in fact, the evidence is right there in Curb, right? Larry had to run Curb differently than Seinfeld. He couldn’t do again what he did at Seinfeld. Curb was improvised. Larry couldn’t create the scripts and all of the intense effort and alchemy and magic that went into every week of Seinfeld in the same way. You just couldn’t do it.

Ben Gilbert All right. Should we bring this baby home and do Quintessence?

David Rosenthal Let’s do it. I know where you’re headed.

Ben Gilbert So, listeners, the way that we decided we want to do our Quintessence this time is to answer the question: What made Seinfeld such a ludicrously good TV asset to own?

David Rosenthal Yep.

Ben Gilbert What made it durable? What made it continue to get renewed for these really high rates three decades later? And yes, there are comps in The Office, which is actually my preferred thing to watch nightly. I grew up when it was on, so it’s more for me, and it feels more modern. Friends is arguably more valuable but is held captive. So Seinfeld is the one free agent in the top tier that actually can go and trade on the free market.

David Rosenthal Yep. And look, of course there’s a whole list of these, most of which we talked about earlier in the analysis. But I think if you were to ask Jerry, at least, it went out on top.

Ben Gilbert I think the driver is viewership begets viewership. Seinfeld has been everywhere for the last three decades on a bunch of channels and streaming services. Because it has been omnipresent, there’s so much demand today to watch it because we’re so familiar with it. It is today’s comfort food, even though when it launched, it was very uncomfortable. During my childhood, teenage years, college, and adulthood, it was everywhere, and I have all the jokes memorized.

David Rosenthal Mm-hmm. Always on every channel, every night. Yep.

Ben Gilbert It’s passed from generation to generation that way. I talked to my dad about it. In fact, we were prepping for this episode, and my three-year-old son was sitting on the couch with me because we had the DVD on. We were watching. He loves putting the DVDs in the DVD player. He points to the screen and goes, “Is that Jerry Seinfeld?”

David Rosenthal No way!

Ben Gilbert I was like, “Oh my God.”

David Rosenthal That’s awesome.

Ben Gilbert I just passed it to another generation. Then we’re watching the DVD interviews afterward, and he points to the screen and goes, “There, there’s Larry David.” I was like, “I’m so proud of you right now.”

David Rosenthal Wow. Wow. Good for him.

Ben Gilbert I know, right? But it’s this thing. My parents liked it, I liked it, I like it. It’s so in the water in our society.

Ben Gilbert There’s a crazy stat from Nielsen in 2021: 41% of Seinfeld’s then-current audience had either been toddlers or not born yet when the series ended in 1998.

David Rosenthal Amazing.

Ben Gilbert So you have to keep tracing it back. I think you might be right that it’s because it went out on top, but the reason, in my opinion, is the 1995 and 1998 syndication cycles—

David Rosenthal Hmm. Were so ubiquitous—

Ben Gilbert —were so successful and exploded out of the gate—

David Rosenthal Yep.

Ben Gilbert —that they created this “in-the-water-ness” to Seinfeld.

David Rosenthal Yep. I think, at the end of the day, it’s a stew of all these things. But I just think that if they’d milked it for a few more years and the quality had gone downhill, this thing is so hypersensitive to the aggregate cultural assessment and impression of it that, if at the end it didn’t have that “greatest show of all time” vibe in the culture—

Ben Gilbert Yeah.

David Rosenthal —the engine wouldn’t have continued like this.

Ben Gilbert Yeah, totally agree. We’re saying very similar things here. It’s ultimately that, coupled with quality. The situational jokes they set up just don’t feel dated. Even though a lot of these things could be solved with a cellphone, the intrinsic quality of the situations they’re in—

David Rosenthal Yep.

Ben Gilbert —still feels relevant today.

David Rosenthal Well, more than 20% of America agrees with you.

Ben Gilbert 22%.

David Rosenthal There you go.

Ben Gilbert All right.

David Rosenthal On this one, we’ve got some fun trivia that we should include here that didn’t make the episode. Number one: the theme music.

Ben Gilbert Yes, that was mine.

David Rosenthal The bass line.

Ben Gilbert Ba-dum, ba-dum, bum-bum, bum-bum-bum, bum-bum, bum-bum, ba-dum. I wish I had a “beep-beep-beep-beep, beep-beep. Ba-ba-ba-bum.”

David Rosenthal Ben, tell everybody why the theme music is so distinctive.

Ben Gilbert In the pilot on my DVD, you can hear the original pilot with the original theme music, which is not what you’re familiar with. The bass riff composed by Jonathan Wolff is something completely different, and it interferes horribly with Jerry’s stand-up at the beginning. It’s tonally overlapping, and you almost can’t make out his words. So when Jonathan Wolff got the call about it, he said, “Oh, I know exactly what I’m gonna do. I’m gonna treat Jerry’s voice like the lyrics of a song.”

David Rosenthal Yes.

Ben Gilbert “And I’m gonna compose around that,” like he’s carrying the melody. He even felt like there was a tempo Jerry did stand-up to, and it came in around 110 beats per minute. That’s how his jokes were told, in that rhythm. So he didn’t create a theme song. He created a theme-song system where he could uniquely compose on a synthesizer in front of him, with the bass guitar riff mapped to a bunch of different keys, and all of the little sounds, like all the mouth sounds—

David Rosenthal Yep.

Ben Gilbert —that Jerry makes. He uniquely composes a theme for every episode that’s slightly different and fits around Jerry’s jokes in the intro. He has this great quote on this: “Every monologue was going to be a variation of the theme, so whatever I did, I needed to architect it modularly so that it could be shiftable, changeable like Lego music. It needed to not conflict with his voice.”

David Rosenthal So great.

Ben Gilbert So great.

David Rosenthal And so distinctive. I mean, it’s part of what makes the show.

Ben Gilbert Yes. It was so different at the time, too. Of course, like everything else, the network execs hated it because it wasn’t like anything else on the market.

David Rosenthal Of course. That’s a signal of quality, when the network—

Ben Gilbert Yes.

David Rosenthal —executives hate it. All right, that’s number one. Number two: this has come up on Acquired before. Julia Louis-Dreyfus is from that Louis-Dreyfus family, the very large French commodities-trading family.

Ben Gilbert Yeah. Big multigenerational business.

David Rosenthal They’ve made an appearance before on Acquired in the Ferrari episode, because Julia’s grandfather was one of Enzo Ferrari’s first clients and raced his privately owned Ferrari 166—the first cars Enzo made—at Le Mans, back at the beginning of Ferrari.

Ben Gilbert Amazing.

David Rosenthal All right, that’s number two. Number three: NBC had a corporate relationship with Nike.

Ben Gilbert Hmm.

David Rosenthal So any of the stars of any NBC sitcoms could go to the Nike warehouse in L.A. and get all the swag they wanted. So how do you think Jerry Seinfeld started wearing Nikes on Seinfeld episodes?

Ben Gilbert Oh.

David Rosenthal Freebies. We talked about this on the Nike episode: they had their athlete strategy, then they got into entertainment, and this was part of it. Jerry Seinfeld was one of the first big parts of Nike’s “get into entertainment” strategy.

Ben Gilbert All right.

David Rosenthal All right, that’s what I got for trivia.

Ben Gilbert Carve-outs?

David Rosenthal Carve-outs. For this one, appropriately enough, I decided I’ve got to do Seinfeld episode recommendations. The Marine Biologist, number one by far. It’s just the most masterful piece of 22-minute episode crafting I’ve ever seen.

Ben Gilbert It’s great.

David Rosenthal A couple of deep cuts I’m partial to: one, The Jacket, which I already mentioned, and two, the first Seinfeld episode I ever watched. I vividly remember it like it was yesterday. I was 9 years old when this episode came out. I saw it air live on TV. I had a babysitter for the night, my parents were out, and I got to stay up late with the TV on. It was The Dinner Party, which is the episode with the black-and-white cookie. I’ll always remember Jerry eating a black-and-white cookie and talking to Elaine: “Elaine, the world needs to look to the cookie. Racial harmony here in the cookie. What we can learn from the black-and-white cookie.” Then, at the end of the episode, he throws up due to food poisoning from the cookie.

Ben Gilbert Oh, Jerry.

David Rosenthal Oh, Jerry. All right, what you got?

Ben Gilbert For me, I have another Seinfeld-related one. If you have a browser open right now, go to seinfeld.visualizingdata.com. There’s the most insane web project I’ve ever seen, called The Seinfeld Chronicles: An Unnecessary Data Exploration by Andy Kirk. It’s a coffee-table book that the author then put online, a full data visualization of a zillion different ways you could slice and dice Seinfeld. What laughs happened when in each episode? What do the patterns look like? How do they accrue to each character? It goes episode by episode. The thing’s 121 pages, showing when various characters got screen time. It walks through why he thinks the show worked and what makes it unique. But the most wild thing to note is that it’s all hand-labeled. He watched episodes on his couch with a spreadsheet open, pausing every five seconds to label who’s on screen and who’s getting laughs. The whole thing is astonishing: a human did this manually before AI.

David Rosenthal Wow. I have The Marine Biologist up right now. There are 23 scenes in The Marine Biologist.

Ben Gilbert Yeah, it’s crazy.

David Rosenthal There you go. Seinfeld and the internet, made for each other.

Ben Gilbert My second carve-out is Buck’s in Woodside.

David Rosenthal Oh, yeah.

Ben Gilbert Incredible restaurant. David and I just went there for a meeting this week, and I was reminded of just how special that place is, especially if you like Silicon Valley lore and ephemera. They’ve got an Apple I up on the wall. They’ve got a signed Jensen jacket, the first one he ever wore on stage. You can tour around the place and get a history of the tech industry, which is very fun.

David Rosenthal It’s like a Silicon Valley version of Monk’s Café, you might say.

Ben Gilbert Yes. And my last carve-out is a company called Tin Can. My son is obsessed with it. He’s 3, but it’s more for 5-to-12-year-olds. It’s a phone, a landline with no screen that uses Wi-Fi, built for kids. They can call preprogrammed numbers, and if they need to call 911 or an emergency contact, it stays plugged in at home. It’s exactly the type of phone we had when we were kids, and they get to call other kids without all the smartphone stuff. The weird coda to this one is that somehow I ended up being the first investor in this company—

David Rosenthal No, yeah.

Ben Gilbert —because it was a completely different company first. It was the last check I wrote when I was a professional VC.

David Rosenthal You’re like the NBC network executive.

Ben Gilbert It accidentally pivoted and turned into this company—

David Rosenthal Yeah.

Ben Gilbert —and became this massive viral hit. They’re on Good Morning America. It’s the face of this movement around great ways for kids to communicate without screens, and my son is loving it. For a while, I was sitting on it, thinking that at some point I should carve out Tin Can, but I don’t want to be too self-promotional and promote a company I invested in. This thing is just really fun to watch all these kids use.

David Rosenthal Ah, so good.

Ben Gilbert

Among the books we read was Seinfeldia by Jennifer Keishin Armstrong.

David Rosenthal

Yep.

Ben Gilbert

Great, great book. And a few people to thank in particular.

David Rosenthal

Research thank-yous. Speaking of books for the show, first and foremost, thank you to Warren Littlefield, the NBC executive responsible for the decision to officially pick up Seinfeld. Warren spent a great amount of time with us, which was wonderful. He also wrote a fantastic oral history memoir of his time at NBC called Top of the Rock, which is well worth reading. It covers Seinfeld, Friends, Mad About You, Cheers—all the great stuff from NBC in that era.

Famously, right after Seinfeld ended, Warren got fired from NBC and went on to have an amazing second career as a producer. He executive-produced Fargo, The Handmaid’s Tale, Dopesick, and now The Testaments, which is doing incredibly well. It was great to talk to him. Thank you to Alec Berg, David Mandel, and Jeff Schaffer, 3 of the writers behind some of the most legendary episodes of Seinfeld, especially in the second half of the show.

Thank you to Jeremy Zimmer, former head of the UTA talent agency; Michael Lynton, former chairman and CEO of Sony Pictures Entertainment; our friend Ravi Nandan at A24; and Brian McAndrews, a longtime television executive, first at Capital Cities/ABC and then at Disney. And thank you to our friend Jeremy Giuffre for helping inspire this episode with his original recommendation, which I made a carve-out on our last episode: Jerry Seinfeld’s movie Comedian.

Ben Gilbert

Thank you, Jeremy. I’ve got a couple of thank-yous: one to Arvind Navaratnam at Worldly Partners for his great mini-study on Seinfeld for this episode, and another to our good friend Danny Passman, an entertainment lawyer who has spent his whole career around deals in this industry. If you liked this episode, go check out other episodes on TV and entertainment. Taylor Swift, Oprah way back in the day. More recently, much higher quality episode because we got better over time, Disney part one and part two.

David Rosenthal Yep.

Ben Gilbert And, uh, for a tie-in on Coca-Cola.

David Rosenthal That’s right.

Ben Gilbert You can visit library.acquire.fm to get access to all the visuals associated with this episode, charts, tables, and illustrations. You can join the email list at acquire.fm/email. That’s where we will send out behind-the-scenes photos from research, episode corrections, and vote on future episode topics. And come talk about this episode with us and the whole community in Slack after you listen, acquired.fm/slack. With that, listeners, we’ll see you next time.

David Rosenthal We’ll see you next time.

Who got the truth? Is it you, is it you, is it you? Who got the truth now? Huh.

注：BidClub 仅提供原文全文文稿；中文版为标题、要点与摘要的译文。

来源：YouTube

item.title: Comfy Sunday Spaces v37：OAI/Anthropic营收、新云波动与交易哲学
item.description: Flood与Kyle讨论OpenAI与Anthropic营收预期下修后，AI交易如何重新定价。他们认为AI融资需求影响资金边际定价，并谈及现金仓位、比特币与崩盘预案。半导体高倍数与预测市场估值需用现金流验证，而非叙事接力。
item.content:encoded:
thinkingusd · Flood · 2026-10-18 · 106 min · 原语言 EN

Flood与Kyle讨论OpenAI与Anthropic营收预期下修后，AI交易如何重新定价。他们认为AI融资需求影响资金边际定价，并谈及现金仓位、比特币与崩盘预案。半导体高倍数与预测市场估值需用现金流验证，而非叙事接力。

要点 TL;DR

  • 营收预期下修，正在考验一场按超常增长定价的 AI 交易。 Flood 将 OpenAI 传闻中的700亿美元年化收入与公司随后披露的500亿美元相对照；Anthropic 泄露的 Q3 营收约168亿美元，也让市场对1000亿美元 ARR 预期打上问号。这些数字都未经审计，但重新定价已经冲击 Nebius、CoreWeave 和 IREN——据称两周内跌了30–50%。再非凡的技术，也逃不过“金融引力定律”。
  • Kyle 的核心宏观判断是：AI 融资需求正在决定资金的边际价格。 10年期美债收益率一度升至约5.3%，但此后即便 CPI 和 PPI 均高于预期，收益率仍与 AI 股票同步下跌。他的解释是，市场预期 AI 借款减少，资金便能流向其他领域；若 AI 真正反弹，收益率可能重回高点。相信自己在“创造上帝”的开发者会持续借钱，直到融资成本形成约束。
  • Anthropic 即便成功 IPO，也可能从现有 AI 持仓中抽走资金。 Kyle 预计，未来一年大型新股发行及后续解禁合计将带来约5万亿美元股票供给，争夺有限的风险资本。Circle IPO 后股价大涨，体现了他的逻辑：投资者为了买入“纯 AI 标的”，可能卖出基础设施代理股，即便这些公司的基本面并未恶化。
  • Flood 的防御仓位主要是现金，但如果投资逻辑改变，他愿意迅速转向。 他称目前约70%为现金；在缺乏强烈判断时，他通常维持80%左右的净多头仓位，同时保留较小的 Bitcoin 和 Hyperliquid 仓位。Flood 说，股市大幅回撤时，他没见过 Bitcoin 明显跑赢；Kyle 补充说，他从没见过 Bitcoin 在这种行情里持平，更别说上涨。若他重新看多股票，或通胀性融资利好 AI，Flood 可能改变看法。“我会等下一个好球。”
  • 为暴跌做准备，关键是在价格失序前备好可动用资金，并预演应对决策。 Kyle 将买入强平引发的反弹，与逐步积累长期持有资产区分开来；Flood 则提醒，山寨币跌60–70%时，挂在市价下方10–20%的买单仍会把杠杆交易者全部爆掉。Flood 举例说，HYPE 到40美元时，他会开始分批买入。他们的说法是：“市场会突然出考题。”
  • 半导体估值便宜，可能反映的是盈利已见顶，而非市场漏看了价值。 Flood 说，存储厂商毛利率惊人，但终端 AI 业务的经济性仍很贵；市场可能正确预判了上游利润将回归常态。他提出的估值检验刻意直白：“地球上每个人都会每年花3000美元用 AI 吗？”更广义的投资纪律，是分清哪些现金流足以支撑持仓，哪些只是吸引下一个买家接盘的故事。
  • 利率走高，最终可能强化货币贬值逻辑，而非削弱它。 Kyle 沿用 Jeffrey Gundlach 的框架：主权债务高到一定程度后，有吸引力的美债收益率反而会成为财政可持续性的警讯，可能削弱美元，并利好黄金、Bitcoin 和房地产。AI 困境也可能引来以对抗中国为名的通胀性干预；在他看来，这“对 Bitcoin 和货币贬值交易极为有利”。
  • 预测市场的增长，并不能解决估值或法律地位能否持久的问题。 Flood 认为 Polymarket 200亿美元的估值过高，即便按100亿美元看也一样；他更倾向用传统交易所的估值倍数。Kyle 则指出，监管前景不明，难以有把握地估值，并认为博彩公司是相关可比标的。Flood 认为，加密行业需要把保护措施“写入法律”，以应对2028年可能出现的政治反转。

摘要 Digest

1. 私人 AI 实验室带来公开市场信息风险

  • Flood 开场表达的不满，核心是信息不对称：大量公开市场仓位的价值，取决于两家私人公司的营收、支出和资产负债表，而外界无从查证。甚至有些投资者也没有获取信息的权利。若有人提前得知实验室营收正在放缓，就能在其他人反应过来之前，交易公开市场上的受益公司。他批评的是“巨大的信息不对称”，并非指控任何一家公司造假。
  • Flood 提出，若公司以如此规模从外部融资，或许应该满足一些披露要求：营收达数百亿美元、融资额达数千亿美元，可能足以构成上市并公开披露信息的理由。他也建议允许公司按年披露，以减轻短期压力。Kyle 明确表示不同意：“我完全不在意。”他认为，一家万亿美元估值的家具制造商也应该有权选择保持私有。
  • Kyle 关注的则是这项技术带来的外部性：实验室将公共网络上的知识变现，产品却可能影响所有人。他提到，Anthropic 提议将最多20%的股份捐给 Trump Accounts，试图在不赋予投票权的前提下，让更多人分享经济收益。另据 Flood 所述，潜在外部性和危害还包括加密技术面临的风险、有关黑客攻击的报道，以及 REA 这款逆向工程工具——他称其能利用 AI 拆解编译后的程序。

2. 年化收入数字留下营收与利润率疑问

  • Flood 强调，讨论中的数字都是传闻或未经审计的披露。OpenAI 传出的700亿美元 ARR，后来变成公司披露的500亿美元。年化算法本身也值得审视：某天收入100万美元，按日年化就是3.65亿美元，但这并不能证明未来一年真能实现同等收入。市场最初对这次下修反应平淡，之后 AI 概念股才走弱。
  • Anthropic 投资者会议内容泄露，显示 Q3 营收约168亿美元，也就是约170亿美元；此前市场讨论的 ARR 则达到1000亿美元。Flood 提出一种可能的解释：Q4 营收约250亿美元，就足以支撑这个年化水平。这意味着环比还要再增约50%，与 Q2 到 Q3 的增幅相近，但此前那段增长包含“token maxing”。他还区分了两件事：重度使用 API 会推高成本，但每个 token 的价格在下降。
  • Flood 将多头逻辑讲到最强：这些可能是“地球上最好的生意”，只是预训练成本掩盖了盈利能力。他提到，推理只占数据中心使用量的37%；如果这一比例升到90–100%，就可能形成规模巨大的高毛利业务。问题在于，一旦停止投入以维持前沿模型表现，这种经济性还能否成立。
  • 空头逻辑是商品化：如果不持续预训练，用户可能转向免费的开源模型，或得到补贴的竞争对手。Flood 用经济舱航空作比：乘客大多只在乎能否到达同一目的地、服务是否过得去，而不是搭哪家航空公司。如果购买决策取决于“最终产品、最终状态”，前沿智能就可能难以在日常任务中维持溢价。

3. 新云处于被放大的支出链条中

  • Kyle 将 AI 产业内部交易与产业外部客户需求区分开来。他估算，产业外部客户的年化支出约为2500亿美元，但公司之间相互采购，会把这笔支出放大到数万亿美元。Nvidia 硬件进入 CoreWeave 机房，网络设备来自 Broadcom，服务器则消耗 AMD 或 Intel 的 CPU 和内存。这种“放大效应”让许多证券都对同一底层需求敏感。
  • Kyle 认为，早先部分增长来自中国模型蒸馏，而实验室明知这一情况仍予以容忍，因为它既带来营收，也有利于融资。按他的解释，随后封堵这些客户，令增长趋平，并扰动了下游供应商。这是他对营收走势的解读；讨论中没有提供能证实这一说法的公司内部证据。
  • Flood 称，Nebius、CoreWeave 和 IREN 两周内下跌约30–50%，同期大盘年初至今仍上涨约15%。Kyle 指出，CoreWeave 和 Oracle 的信用违约互换保护成本上升，说明投资者正在辨认潜在受害者。他担心的是，如果这些实验室“只有我们原来以为的七成那么强”，接下来会发生什么。
  • 两人都不认为自己在这些标的上有交易优势。他们表示，融资结构、建设延期、政治阻挠和合同责任都需要他们不具备的专业知识。

4. AI 融资需求可能正在决定资金成本

  • Kyle 回忆，10年期美债收益率一度升至约5.3%，同期还有一次加息，但股市起初顶住了压力。随后 CPI 和 PPI 双双高于预期，AI 股票却下跌，美债收益率也随之走低。他提出一个颇具争议的解读：目前决定资金边际定价的主导变量不是通胀，而是市场对 AI 融资需求的预期。
  • 在 Kyle 的框架里，关键区别是明年 AI 需要借5000亿美元，还是1万亿美元。需求强劲会推高融资成本，并与其他借款人争夺资金。AI 放缓则会减轻这种竞争，让政府和行业外企业更容易获得资金。因此，收益率下跌可能反映的是 AI 前景变差，而不是通胀数据变好。
  • 他的条件判断很具体：如果这轮抛售只是基金清算所致，AI 股票随后反弹，美债收益率可能重回此前高位；如果 AI 持续走弱，融资成本就会继续下降，甚至影响2年期美债收益率，以及市场对不再加息的预期。两种结果都不是确定判断。
  • Kyle 认为，相信自己在“创造上帝”的开发者会把能借的钱都借来加速进度，无论动机是实现 AGI，还是与中国竞争。融资成本升高，最终会划出一条上限。这也是他认为固定收益投资者目前“掌握方向盘”的原因：他们对违约风险和融资成本的定价，决定了这场交易还能承受什么。

5. AI IPO 可能上涨，却抽走代理股资金

  • Anthropic 的 S-1 仍是尚未落地的关键催化剂。Flood 承认，文件可能揭示“地球上最好的公司”，令空头遭到挤压。Kyle 则更怀疑 IPO 延迟背后的原因：Polymarket 对当年 IPO 的预测概率从9月初约94%降至约70%，而在11月底前完成的概率只有约50%。他还提到，公司间信息共享有限，以及安全方面的担忧再度升温。
  • Flood 提到，市场传闻 Anthropic 估值为1.5万亿美元，低于此前2万亿美元的目标，融资规模约2000亿美元。Kyle 将 Anthropic 和 OpenAI 可能发行的股票、后续解禁，以及 SpaceX 的潜在供给合并估算，认为未来一年约有5万亿美元股票待买家承接。这些是对未来供给的估算，并非已经完成的发行，但也构成他对风险资产保持谨慎的依据。
  • Kyle 最看好的类比是 Circle：投资者想要的是纯粹的稳定币业务，而不是通过 Coinbase 或 PayPal 获得部分敞口；Circle 股价在3周内大涨。主题投资的资金配置可能压过估值考量。他预计“纯 AI 标的”也会迎来类似需求，Anthropic 可能表现亮眼，而投资者会卖出相关基础设施持仓来腾出买入资金。
  • Flood 也在关注现有公司发行股票为资本开支融资。管理层选择出售股权，而不是继续增加借款；这种对手方决策值得留意。他并不认为这就意味着应当立即清仓，但市场仍在摸索 AI 最终的经济性，这又给重新审视仓位提供了一个理由。

6. Flood 的现金仓位跟随他的股票判断

  • Flood 称自己目前约70%持有现金，同时保留规模小得多的 Hyperliquid 和 Bitcoin 仓位。理解背景很重要：缺乏强烈判断时，考虑到他对加密资产的长期热情，通常会维持约80%的净多头仓位。他还说，减仓时卖出的 Bitcoin 每枚带来了近2000美元收益。现金就是他当前的配置选择：“我会等下一个好球。”
  • Flood 说，在近15年的加密从业经历中，他没见过股市大跌10%、15%或20%时，Bitcoin 还能极强地上涨。Kyle 补充说，他没见过 Bitcoin 在这种跌势里保持平盘，更别说上涨。由于 Bitcoin 全天交易且流动性强，它的跌幅往往更大。因此，押注它能罕见地与股市脱钩，不足以成为 Flood 维持常规仓位的理由。
  • 若股票转为看多，Flood 很可能迅速买回加密资产；若出现高度通胀性的 AI 优先融资，他也可能改变看法。他们的防御仓位还包括低两位数百分比的做空仓位，并非押注市场崩盘的大额空头。Flood 认为下周市场跌10%的概率极低；Kyle 强调，他们的股票判断周期约为6个月。

7. 投资逻辑需要明确的失效条件与匹配的时间周期

  • Flood 希望每个投资判断都能对应一个明确的价格、事实或状态变化，出现时就说明逻辑错了。否则，等到认错时可能已经亏损惨重。他对利率上升格外敏感，源于2022年的自满令其投资组合“被彻底打残”。他还提醒，社交媒体信息流会强化既有仓位：他只点赞了一条看空 CoreWeave 的帖子，信息流里就开始充斥类似论点。
  • 经常判断正确，与最终赚钱是两回事。Flood 提到，同行交易员 Basics TNZ 称自己的胜率约30%，但利润仍然可观；重仓最有把握的机会，可能比胜率更能决定结果。他强调，交易者需要情绪上的灵活性：不肯承认判断错误、调整仓位，亏损就会更严重。
  • Kyle 提醒，6个月的投资判断可以伴随短期痛苦反转，包括3–4%的反弹和单周上涨10%。Flood 以 Hyperliquid 为例：个位数买入、约30美元卖出，这笔交易做成了；但当价格逼近100美元时，投资者需要经受多轮考验，包括 Jelly Jelly 和 Lighter 的竞争。短线交易规则可能打断长期投资逻辑。
  • Flood 和 Kyle 分别管理不同的投资组合，也可能意见相左，因此一个公开钱包并不代表所有仓位或观点。Flood 也拒绝为了维护网上声誉而交易。“能赚钱，靠的是保持灵活、根据状态变化及时应对”，而不是让社交压力替自己决定仓位。

8. 暴跌前先备好真正能动用的资金

  • Kyle 的第一条规则是，暴跌当天不能让自己失去行动能力。锁在7天或30天质押解锁期里的资金，无法用于抓住即时机会。接下来要区分两种策略：买入强制去杠杆造成的超跌，比如杠杆 ETF SOXL；或买入打算持有1到3年的资产。两者需要不同的选标和退出决策。
  • 他会预演一条极端情境：Anthropic 的 S-1 糟糕、支出承诺未兑现、新云公司陷入困境、Oracle 出问题，而 Nvidia 的兜底安排又引发传染效应。预演的目的，是在冷静时先决定如何应对。他明确说，这种戏剧性情境“几乎肯定不会发生”；做准备有用，但不代表这是预测。
  • Flood 提醒，有些交易者在市价下方10–20%挂着买单，山寨币跌60–70%时，连2倍杠杆仓位也被强平。逐仓之外的交叉保证金账户，甚至可能因瞬间下跌90%而爆仓。交易平台宕机和链上拥堵也各自构成风险，与偿付能力无关：资金放在不合适的平台，关键时刻就可能无法操作。
  • Flood 举例说，HYPE 到40美元时，他会开始买入，每分钟买入一笔预设金额；价格越低越好，因为他认为更低的价位有吸引力。有一份买入清单，不等于必须挂上无人看管的限价单。“市场会突然出考题”：提前准备，可能决定罕见的错价带来两位数收益还是亏损，也可能决定交易者是果断行动，还是僵在屏幕前。

9. 市场下跌会迫使故事重新回到现金流

  • Kyle 描述一只股票20周里有18周下跌后，持有人会开始厌倦：“我他妈为什么要持有它？”他的框架是，市场在现金流和故事之间摇摆。只要未来故事足够诱人，股价就能涨得很高；但要形成持久的底部，投资者必须有理由相信，这家公司能在合理时间内、以可接受的风险回报股东。
  • Zoom 是他举的历史案例：办公室、教室和商务沟通永久迁移到一个远程平台的叙事，曾经支撑了极高预期。“故事管用，直到它不再管用。”在长期下跌中，投资者可能转而偏好不那么依赖叙事的企业，哪怕因此放弃一部分上涨空间。
  • Flood 发过一条推文，提到有公司估值在几个月内从5000万美元升至100亿美元。他说，这相当于一个规模不大的团队创造了99.5亿美元价值。Kyle 认为，这是高明的讲故事。Flood 还指出，风投声称的1倍下行保护，前提是公司确实能被收购。他们建议，要学习长期资产配置判断，可以读 Buffett 和 Howard Marks，而不是依赖每周市场预测。

10. 债务压力可能逆转利率上升的通常反应

  • 被问到1970年代石油冲击、加息和黄金涨逾10倍是否可作参照时，Kyle 说，历史类比很可能不适用于当下。他参考 Jeffrey Gundlach 的框架：通常，美债收益率上升会吸引投资者从不生息的黄金转向美债；但政府债务足够庞大时，利率上升可能不再显得是投资机会，反而成为财政可持续性的警讯。
  • 如果偿债成本占税收收入的比例高到令人担忧，Kyle 认为，结果“可能是美元下跌”，并利好黄金、Bitcoin，甚至房地产。另一方面，若 AI 困境加剧，也可能引来以战胜中国为名的特别支持。他认为，这类干预利好货币贬值交易，也解释了为什么他对加密资产的长期前景不如对股票那么担心。

11. 预测市场的估值，既取决于增长，也取决于法律

  • Flood 认为 Kalshi 还算合理，但他公开看空 Polymarket：200亿美元估值太高，即便按100亿美元看也一样。他拿交易所作比较：Nasdaq 约为8倍，合理区间可以是5–10倍，而不是20倍、40倍或100倍。这个行业可能会增长，但落地和竞争问题令他对现有公司的估值总体持中性略偏空态度。
  • Kyle 反驳说：“我不确定它是不是严重高估了。”法律前景不明，连这门生意本身都难以估算：运营商两年后可能就没有业务了。Robinhood 的预测市场收入引发了增长预期，但 Kyle 认为，不少交易活动只是从交易所或体育博彩转移过来。因此，MGM 和 DraftKings 也是相关可比公司，意味着估值可能低于私募市场目前给出的水平。
  • 谈到中期选举，Flood 将一般政治僵局——市场往往乐见其成——与加密行业需要明确法律保护区分开来。若没有 CLARITY Act 之类的立法，2028年若由民主党总统执政，当前的宽容态度可能逆转；预测市场尤其容易受影响。Flood 直觉上认为民主党大概会赢得中期选举，随后也会成为2028年大选的热门，但这两种结果都不是确定的。

12. 芯片盈利便宜与 AI 服务昂贵可以同时成立

  • 被问到机构投资者是否只是在追逐故事、和散户没两样时，Flood 说，估值要看具体标的。他提到 SK Hynix 和 Micron 创造了惊人的利润，净利率约90%，按当前股价计算，赚到的利润大约3年就够回购全部股份。Kyle 先前还提到，有些芯片股的市盈率约为3–4倍。这些股票看起来确实非常便宜。
  • 问题在于超额盈利：产业链内部循环支出可能令供应商利润异常强劲，而低市盈率也说明市场不相信这些盈利能持续。Flood 认为，市场给芯片公司便宜的定价，可能是对的。反过来，如果只看 Google、Microsoft、Amazon 或 Meta 的 AI 营收相对于 AI 支出，这些业务看起来会非常昂贵；其他业务则稀释了整体成本。

ARR is different from revenue. It’s a bit of a confusing metric. It’s annualized run rate. What does that mean? You could take the last day of revenue and project an ARR. If you made $1 million that day, your ARR would be $365 million over the course of a year. If you take the last week, then multiply it by 52, and so on and so forth.

It’s not disingenuous, but it’s non-GAAP accounting. It’s kind of saying, “We make this amount of money, and if we continue to make money at this rate, this is what we would make for the rest of the year,” or something like that. Typically, it’s year or year to date.

It came out recently that Anthropic—or, excuse me, OpenAI—walked its numbers down from $70 billion to $50 billion. This happened, I believe, on Monday or Tuesday of last week, and the market didn’t really care. The market kind of shrugged it off, and the S&P closed kind of green on the day.

Speaker 1 Yeah. Okay. When you come into a day like that, the first thing you want to do is make sure you don’t get your ass kicked that day. What does that mean? It means you don’t want your capital tied up in things that are illiquid, where you can’t realize any cash from them.

In a crypto sense, if you’re behind some sort of staking unlock where your capital is always 7 or 30 days away from you, tough shit. You’re not going to be able to participate in a productive way. You want to make sure you have very instant access to your money. That’s how you’re going to be able to capitalize.

Beyond that, I think it’s really an asset selection game. You have to say, “Look, what do I want to buy here?” There are going to be a lot of things that go down by an amount that’s clearly wrong. They’re clearly going to reach their terminal price through some sort of forced deleveraging. Then you’d expect that when the deleveraging occurs, they snap back to something more reasonable, albeit at a price substantially lower than where they started.

You have 2 strategies. You can bottom fish for these things and say, “Look, good shot that something like SOXL, a leveraged ETF product, ends up way overshooting,” and then buy something like that. Or you can say, “Look, I have durable views on a couple of assets in this space. I have a few things I want to buy here that I intend on selling for long-term capital gains in a year or 2 or 3.” Then you just buy them at a good price.

You have to make sure you run that playbook for yourself ahead of time, before anything like this ever happens, because you’re not going to feel calm or in control. You’re not going to feel like you have a lot of time to sit down and contemplate these things when it’s happening. I think it’s a good drill to rehearse the what-ifs. Just say, “Look, what if we had a lot of stuff? What if the Anthropic S-1 comes out and it’s horrific, and investors panic, and the debt guys sell stuff down, and there’s this domino effect where the neoclouds look like they’re going to default, OpenAI and Anthropic aren’t going to make their spending commitments, Oracle’s in a tough spot, Nvidia backstopped a lot of these guys, and there’s this contagion?” In that moment, how would you respond?

Just running that playbook as a rehearsal will bring you a lot of calm, because as markets go down, you say, “Look, I’ve prepared for this. I’m ready for this.” If it doesn’t happen—and it almost certainly won’t happen, at least not in any sort of dramatic capacity—then no harm, no foul.

I own something because it really is worth this much.” It’s a very different way of looking at your portfolio.
