item.title: 第199期｜2026年10月16日
item.description: XBI年初至今仍涨20%，却从169跌至约146；对冲基金累计减持生技风险敞口为5年多来最大。IPO窗口仍开，但资金偏好临床催化剂和可防守IP，并购或能重启买盘。Bristol的admilparant仅低剂量显著，支持LPA1用于IPF，剂量反应仍待厘清。
item.content:encoded:
Biotech Hangout · Graig Suvannavejh、Paul Matteis、Brian Skorney、Yaron Werber、Jake Becraft · 2026-10-16 · 59 min · 原语言 EN

XBI年初至今仍涨20%，却从169跌至约146；对冲基金累计减持生技风险敞口为5年多来最大。IPO窗口仍开，但资金偏好临床催化剂和可防守IP，并购或能重启买盘。Bristol的admilparant仅低剂量显著，支持LPA1用于IPF，剂量反应仍待厘清。

要点 TL;DR

  • 指数走强掩盖了大量成分股的疲弱，也掩盖了一轮历史性的降总敞口。 XBI年初至今仍上涨20%，但已从8月高点169回落至约146；XLV年初至今的涨幅则从7%加速至15%。高盛主经纪商数据显示，对冲基金在过去8周中的6周减持生物科技风险，累计降总敞口为5年多来最大。
  • 眼下的问题在于资金流和市场情绪，而非整个板块估值泡沫。 拥挤多头被抛售、拥挤空头被回补，形成自我强化的循环；没人愿意去“接飞刀”，因为股价还可能再跌10%-15%。Skorney的估值判断是，市场早已远离投资者还能“拿一张餐巾纸上的临床前构想，就以10亿美元IPO”的年代。
  • 并购仍是最明确的潜在转折点，但利率和基金结账周期或许得先过关。 Matteis认为，收购能带来外部验证和FOMO情绪，推动买盘回归；Werber则指出，许多基金10月31日年度结账、中期选举以及再度加息，仍是悬在市场上的压力，后者可能发生1次、甚至2次，年内至少会有1次。与此同时，ETF表现强劲，反而加剧了专业基金的压力，因为它们持有的个股表现落后。
  • IPO窗口仍然敞开，但越来越青睐临床催化剂和差异化技术。 TRex Bio融资1.17亿美元，Iambic Therapeutics融资1.5亿美元，City Therapeutics将融资额上调至2亿美元，2026年生物科技IPO的非官方数量由此达到约28家。Becraft明确表示，投资者看重的是IP和执行壁垒，以及能够降低风险的临床证据。
  • Bristol的admilparant III期试验支持LPA1在IPF中的作用，但剂量反应仍未完全厘清。 低剂量达到统计学显著性，高剂量则没有；小组仍认为药物很可能获批，市场规模也可能很大，因为更好的耐受性或允许联合用药。Contineum股价盘前一度上涨20%，随后转为下跌逾25%；投资者质疑更广泛的受体覆盖能否带来差异化，而公司自己的读出要等到2028年。
  • 免疫学领域既有平台验证，也有对“不要把II期生物学外推过头”的警示。 Mirum的Livmarli在更多儿童胆汁淤积性疾病中持续降低瘙痒；3个竞争中的乳糜泻项目也都显示出早期组织学和症状改善。相比之下，argenx在III期无效性分析后终止了Vyvgart治疗干燥综合征的项目，印证了Werber的判断：“驱动生物学的不是某一个单独因素。”
  • 中枢神经系统递送和癌症疫苗带来了本周上行空间最大、但仍待验证的技术读出。 Arrowhead通过转铁蛋白siRNA药物偶联物使脑脊液tau降低超过80%，但脑脊液指标下降未必能预测tau-PET或临床获益。Moderna/Merck即将公布的ESMO数据让“mRNA重新回到讨论桌上”，但Becraft强调，试验缺少非特异性mRNA对照，也仍需证明获益不止于已切除的黑色素瘤。

摘要 Digest

1. 被迫降总敞口，让拥挤仓位陷入恶性循环

  • Suvannavejh点出了矛盾：XBI年初至今仍上涨20%，但目前约在146，较上一期节目时又回落约700个基点，远低于8月下旬169的高点。与此同时，XLV涨幅从7%加速至15%，显示资金正从生物科技轮动至其他医疗保健子板块。
  • Skorney将降总敞口定义为多空基金缩减整体风险敞口，例如把20亿美元的投资组合降至15亿美元：卖出多头、回补空头，未必是出于基本面判断。专业基金仓位过于拥挤，使这一机械过程的冲击格外剧烈。
  • 一家基金减仓时，拥挤多头下跌、空头上涨，拖累持仓相似的其他组合，进而促使更高层级的风险管理人员也削减总敞口。即便是只做多的投资者也可能加入抛售，而潜在买家则选择观望，不愿“接飞刀”，因为股价还可能再跌20%-30%。
  • Skorney开玩笑说，从6月以来，市场每隔两周就让人觉得压力快结束了，像电影《The Money Pit》里的施工队一样没完没了。高盛主经纪商的一张图表更凸显了这一点：对冲基金在过去8周中的6周减持生物科技风险，累计降总敞口为5年多来最大。

2. 仅凭便宜，扭不转由恐惧和资金流主导的市场

  • Matteis描述了投资者的行为僵局：大家喜欢这些持仓时，股价比现在高30%；如今又看到了有吸引力的催化剂，却担心资金流驱动的下跌还会再带来10%-15%的跌幅。“大家都在等别人先动”，因为没人知道这场抛售何时才会停止。
  • 并购可能成为那个先行动的信号：它能验证优质公司已变得便宜，并触发FOMO情绪。Matteis称“并购治愈生物科技熊市”是老生常谈，但除了交易落地或单纯等时间过去，他看不到同样明显的催化剂。
  • Werber认为，许多基金10月31日年度结账后，压力可能有所缓解，之后还有中期选举；但他强调，利率一直是板块反复承压的来源。他认为再加息很可能发生，甚至可能加息2次；年内至少会有1次。综合型投资者也在讨论民主党若横扫选举，是否会带来AI监管并改善生物科技情绪；围绕Isomorphic Labs估值可能达到500亿美元的猜测，则让这场讨论进一步升温。
  • Skorney认为，股票确实比以前便宜，虽然还没有便宜到2023年的程度，但“离泡沫很远”：市场已不可能再把“一张餐巾纸上的临床前构想”拿去IPO，估值10亿美元。可没有近期催化剂，光有价值很难吸引资金；Werber还指出，ETF驱动的交易很大程度上不看估值，即便数据不错，股价也可能原地踏步甚至下跌。
  • Werber还提到，XBI市值最大的25家公司表现不错，部分受Twist带动；Twist是一家由AI驱动的诊断公司。但与此同时，许多基金的底层持仓并未跟上，基金经理不得不向LP解释：为什么自己的业绩没有反映出板块指数看起来那么强劲的表现。

3. IPO市场仍在运转，开始筛出真正有差异化的公司

  • TRex Bio融资1.17亿美元，围绕其Treg I期项目及与Lilly、J&J的合作展开。以AI驱动肿瘤研发的Iambic Therapeutics融资1.5亿美元，公司有一项针对HER2突变癌症的I期项目，并与多家制药公司建立了合作。
  • City Therapeutics将发行规模上调至2亿美元，Suvannavejh统计的2026年生物科技IPO非官方数量由此达到约28家，市场正朝着30多家迈进。City已分别与Bausch + Lomb和Biogen合作开发临床前眼科和神经科项目，另有一项自有的I期血栓栓塞性疾病候选药物。Frazier Life Sciences旗下一个新SPAC也已上市，尽管已公布的战略并购近期趋于沉寂。
  • Matteis说，7月和8月私营公司的融资沟通开始让人想起2020年：非常早期的公司也在问“为什么不能是我们？”，并考虑反向合并。6周后，随着公开市场环境骤变，这类电话已经少了很多。
  • Werber将仍在排队的公司分成几类：有新数据、正处风口的公司；项目已经推进太远、无法停下来的公司；以及缺资金、不得不试探窗口的发行人。Becraft认为它们的共同点是“质量与创新兼顾”：技术有差异化、有可防守的IP和执行壁垒，并且有近期临床催化剂，而不只是平台听起来有意思。

4. Bristol验证了LPA1在IPF中的作用，但剂量反应争议未解

  • Matteis认为，Bristol的admilparant III期结果对公司是利好，科学上却有些棘手：低剂量达到统计学显著性，高剂量没有。考虑到IPF仍有大量未满足需求，他认为很难排除药物获批的可能；但Bristol没有公布具体临床数据，要等到可能在春季召开的医学会议才能作出完整判断。
  • 商业机会可能相当可观：IPF药物的年销售额有望达到数十亿美元，但现有治疗仍无法阻止患者病情进展，而且耐受性也可能不佳。耐受性更好的LPA1药物或许能与其他药物联用；目前的吡非尼酮和尼达尼布等药物则很难叠加使用。
  • Contineum股价盘前一度上涨20%，最终收跌逾25%。公司的逻辑是，更广泛的受体覆盖可能提升疗效；但Bristol看似出现的“剂量反向反应”——也可能只是反应趋平或统计噪声——让投资者开始质疑这种差异化，而Contineum自己的试验要到2028年才读出。Matteis说，公司每日一次的给药方式至少可能构成优势。
  • Skorney提醒，IPF的病理生理机制仍未被充分理解，II期结果向III期转化也屡屡失败。他在吡非尼酮监管问题上吃过苦头，Werber则回忆起Galapagos的自体毒素项目在2项III期研究中都出现死亡率失衡；这些经历都说明，不能说这一类药物的风险已经完全排除。与囊性纤维化不同，IPF并没有同样清晰的遗传学和药理学图谱。

5. Mirum扩展已验证的症状药物布局，乳糜泻则开启新战场

  • Mirum的Livmarli在一项覆盖多种儿童胆汁淤积性疾病的III期篮式试验中，持续降低患者瘙痒程度，其中胆道闭锁患者占比最高。Skorney估计，美国和欧洲约有2,000名胆道闭锁患者可能适用，其他较小亚组合计或再增加约2,000人。
  • Skorney认为，更广泛的证据表明，IL-10抑制剂能够缓解胆汁淤积性瘙痒。Mirum的成人候选药物volixibat针对PBC的关键性试验将在未来数月读出；公司还计划明年上半年提交PSC的新药申请，Skorney称目前尚无获批疗法。
  • Werber称乳糜泻是“生物科技里最好的机会”：Teva靶向IL-15配体；收购了Forte Biosciences的argenx，以及First Tracks，则靶向IL-2受体的一部分CD122。3家公司的小型研究都显示，上皮内淋巴细胞减少、组织学改善和症状获益，预计将在11月于墨尔本举行的国际乳糜泻研讨会上集中亮相。Teva的药物每3个月皮下注射1次。
  • 生物学或许比市场更清晰。目前没有获批路径，试验采用的麸质激发方案各不相同，开发者还得弄清终点应是组织学还是症状、治疗要持续多久，以及支付方愿意为药物支付多少、相较无麸质饮食有何优势。多头认为市场巨大，空头则觉得“没人会愿意为它付钱”。早期白癜风数据、即将公布的argenx斑秃数据，以及First Tracks的EoE研究，都可能拓展这类药物的机会。

6. argenx干燥综合征项目失败，暴露单一路径推理的局限

  • Werber刚结束一场看多的医生圆桌讨论，argenx就宣布在无效性分析后终止Vyvgart治疗干燥综合征的项目——圆桌嘉宾此前都不知道这项分析。此前II期数据令人鼓舞，这一意外消息打压了股价，尽管小组仍认为干燥综合征可能是一个大市场。
  • 他从生物学中得出的教训是，炎症往往依赖B细胞与T细胞的相互作用，而不是某一个孤立因素。Vyvgart降低自身抗体的做法未能在III期奏效；Amgen调节这一相互作用的CD40配体疗法，则从有力的II期证据推进到III期阳性结果。小组也看好BAFF/APRIL路径，但认为Novartis的药物不如Vera的。
  • Matteis指出，argenx股价与去年同期大致持平，而Alnylam和Insmed都大幅下跌。Werber将其韧性归因于强劲的执行、预期中的Q3/Q4表现，以及广泛的综合型投资者持仓——“几乎所有人都持有它”。即将公布的C2拮抗剂治疗MMN数据，将帮助判断机会是通过对IVIG非劣效、进入二线治疗，还是凭借优效、进入一线治疗。

7. 转铁蛋白穿梭递送正成为平台，但tau才是真正考验

  • Arrowhead的转铁蛋白siRNA药物偶联物使脑脊液中的tau降低超过80%，成为首个公布转铁蛋白递送siRNA药物偶联物临床数据的项目。Matteis认为，这一执行尤其值得注意，因为Arrowhead在转铁蛋白上的经验不如Roche或Denali丰富。
  • 核心疑问在于不同体液和组织间的差异：脑脊液tau未必能代表相关脑区的病理变化，因此tau-PET是否下降仍然重要。Biogen此前显示，脑脊液指标的变化远大于PET变化；其鞘内给药的IIb期试验在最低剂量下就产生临床获益，同时出现剂量反向反应，高剂量还伴有毒性。
  • Matteis猜测，Biogen的毒性可能是ASO本身的特殊问题，因为各剂量的tau下降程度相似；但他也承认，只有Arrowhead、Denali等公司的下一代项目才能回答这个问题。转铁蛋白开始让人想到肝脏里的GalNAc——“我不想说它已经商品化了”（“I don’t want to say it’s commoditized”）——多家团队正同时攻克相关科学问题。
  • Suvannavejh还介绍了Alector的ABC（Alector Brain Carrier）平台：其先导靶向β淀粉样蛋白的抗体为AL-137；tau-siRNA项目在临床前实现了约75%-80%的mRNA敲低，但最快也要明年、也可能到2028年才进入临床。公司在研发日后融资7,500万美元，此前因后期临床资产失败而调整了研发方向。

8. 肿瘤领域热情回归，但对照组设计仍然重要

  • Suvannavejh重点提到Verastem针对KRAS G12D的突变选择性抑制剂在多个癌种中公布的“非常、非常出色”早期I期和II期数据，尤其是胰腺癌。相关读出与市场对Revolution Medicines泛RAS抑制剂的持续关注相呼应；该药刚获得CHMP的积极意见。
  • Becraft称，Moderna/Merck的项目可能是癌症疫苗领域首次重大突破，数据显示其在黑色素瘤中似乎能改善无进展生存期。但最初研究针对的是可完全切除的肿瘤；BioNTech取消结直肠癌和头颈癌单药试验，也提醒市场不要把结果轻易外推到其他癌种。
  • 他最主要的质疑在于试验设计：对照组是安慰剂，而非非特异性mRNA疫苗；但越来越多证据显示，包括COVID疫苗在内的mRNA可能不依赖选定的癌症抗原，也能刺激T细胞。“如果能看到”这一对照就好了，Becraft说，在此之前不应轻易把结果归功于AI衍生的抗原算法。
  • ESMO的最新突破性研究将提供完整数据。Becraft透露，自己经营的是一家mRNA疗法公司，而非疫苗公司；他表示，“mRNA又重新回到讨论桌上了”（“mRNA is back on the menu again”）。但更大的目标——从疫苗和治疗性疫苗走向成功的mRNA疗法——在被期待了约10年后，仍未实现。

全文文稿（原文）

Graig Suvannavejh

You’re listening to “Biotech Hangout,” a live and unedited weekly discussion of all the latest news in our industry with a group of biotech leaders and experts. I’m Graig Suvannavejh, and my co-hosts today are my fellow sell-side biotech analyst Paul Matteis, Brian Skorney, and Yaron Werber, as well as Jake Becraft, a private biotech company CEO. For more information about our hosts and guest speakers, or to listen to the most recent episode, please go to biotechhangout.com.

So happy Friday, everyone. It’s cold and somewhat rainy where I am in New York, and some might say it’s a bit miserable out. I guess the same can be said of the current state of the public biotech market, which is again trending downward. The XBI is under pressure again today.

Markets Weigh IPO Strength

With that in mind, let’s quickly review where things stand in biotech. I’ll touch on performance, IPOs, and deal activity. The XBI ETF is still up a very healthy 20% for the year, especially relative to the dark period that stretched from 2022 to 2024. That said, at the current level of around $146 flashing on my Bloomberg, the XBI has come down considerably—some 700 basis points since our last podcast 2 weeks ago—so that’s not a great sign.

Further outperformance versus the broader XLV ETF has narrowed significantly. Recall that XLV includes pharmaceuticals, healthcare equipment and supplies, healthcare providers and services, life science tools and services, and healthcare IT, in addition to biotech. Two weeks ago, XLV was up 7% year to date; it’s now up 15% year to date. That suggests to me that investors are rotating out of biotech into these other healthcare subsectors. In the context of the XBI’s late-August high of $169, we are now definitively in a correction of sorts.

I’ll return to the markets in a few moments, but I want to point out that, at least on the IPO front, we’re seeing pretty good momentum. We saw 3 new names come to market. TRex Bio is focused on Treg-targeted biologics for immune-mediated diseases. It has a Phase 1 asset for atopic dermatitis and partnerships with Eli Lilly and J&J, and it raised $117 million in gross proceeds earlier this week.

We also saw Iambic Therapeutics, an oncology-focused biotech leaning heavily on AI. Its lead pipeline asset is in Phase 1 and targets HER2-mutated cancers. It has partnerships with AbbVie, Bayer—“Buyer,” as I think it’s more properly referred to—Lundbeck, and Takeda. It raised $150 million in gross proceeds.

Today, City Therapeutics is making its debut. It’s an RNA interference, or RNAi, drug developer with preclinical ophthalmology and neurology candidates partnered with Bausch + Lomb and Biogen, respectively, as well as a proprietary clinical-stage candidate for thromboembolic diseases that’s in Phase 1. City’s IPO was upsized to $200 million in gross proceeds, so that’s a nice sign for the company.

By my unofficial count, we’re now at around 28 biotechs that have made their debut in 2026. At least from an IPO market perspective, things seem to be tracking along very nicely, and it looks like we’re definitely on pace to see perhaps 30 or more new issues this year. As additional momentum, just today we saw the market debut of a Frazier Life Sciences special purpose acquisition company, or SPAC. Let’s see how things end up with that one. I was doing some research for this podcast, and it looks like Frazier’s last SPAC merged with NewAmsterdam Pharma, which has been a success overall.

That being said, announced M&A deal flow does seem to have quieted down considerably. Perhaps this lull reflects an acutely rising interest rate environment, which makes borrowing more expensive for strategics, but perhaps it’s also a temporary pause as we approach next month’s midterm elections.

I’m going to stop here on my take on where we are in the markets. What I’d like to do now is bring back our co-hosts for a roundtable discussion about what’s really happening more broadly in the biotech market. There’s been a lot of noise given all the volatility. We’re going to touch on things like degrossing, which is what we’ve been seeing from the buy side, current biotech valuations, and what it takes to turn this market around.

Why Funds Are Degrossing

To start, I’ll go to our sell-siders, who talk with biotech investors every day. Brian, can you start? For our audience who may not know what degrossing is, can you briefly explain what we’re talking about here? I’d also love to get a sense of what you’re hearing from investors, and then I’d love to have Paul and Yaron offer their perspectives as well. Brian, why don’t you go ahead?

Brian Skorney

Thanks, Graig. Degrossing has been the big buzzword of the last couple of weeks. It seems to be everyone’s explanation for some of the pain since we got back from the summer, into Labor Day, and the pressure from degrossing events.

Technically, I don’t know that there’s a very specific distinction between degrossing in biotech and fund flows out of biotech. They could be used interchangeably. In practice, degrossing is thought of more as hedge-fund terminology, where a long-short fund takes down its entire position from some level. If you think about a very strict 50/50 long-short fund, it would be selling its longs and buying back its shorts, not necessarily for a fundamental reason, but simply because it has, say, $2 billion of exposure and wants to cut that down to $1.5 billion. Within any individual fund, there should be some nuance to what gets traded out of, but generally it’s about broadly lowering those positions.

The thing to think about, and why this affects valuations, is that biotech is a small world of investors. There’s a tendency to see a lot of crowded trades: names that are very well loved by specialists and names that are very much hated by specialists. When those positions get crowded, particularly in names with low floats, a degrossing event can mean that a fund’s positions are broadly taken down. That causes its long names to go down as there’s selling pressure, and its short names to go up as there’s buying pressure.

That can lead to a vicious cycle. Another fund sees its longs go down and its shorts go up because a fund with the same trades is being forced to lower its positions. Everyone sees their performance get hit, and as the risk profile goes up—especially at more of these 50/50 shops—the people higher up in the firms take down gross exposure.

This can bleed beyond the pure, large 50/50 hedge-fund groups we see. I think it can also be fundamental. If there’s a view that the overall market is going down, someone with a big dedicated position, whether in a 50/50 long-short fund, a 70/30 fund, or eventually even a long-only fund, might choose to take some of the position down because of the forced selling pressure. It also makes it hard for people to lean in and buy into that pressure. “Catching a falling knife” is one of the phrases investors like to use when things start getting sold off. They don’t want to be the one buying when there could be another 20% or 30% to go down, so they view it as a risky endeavor.

In terms of investor conversations, it’s funny: we’ve really seen this become a more pronounced pain point across the entire sector over the last month or so. But a lot of my hedge-fund investor conversations make it feel like they’ve been getting hit by degrossing issues going all the way back to June. I remember conversations with a bunch of hedge-fund PMs who were saying, “We’re getting hurt by these squeezes from degrossing. It’s probably another 2 weeks of this.”

It reminds me of the construction crew from Tom Hanks’ The Money Pit. Every time he checks, it’s “another 2 weeks.”

I think in the hedge fund world, that pressure has been on since early summer, and now it’s starting to bleed over, where long-only or more heavily long-focused funds are also feeling that pressure. I don’t know if the rest of the crew has thoughts on what they’re hearing from investors.

Paul Matteis

Yeah, Brian, I’d echo all of that. Another angle is: where do we go from here? Are people starting to feel like stocks are cheap? Graig touched upon the lack of M&A. I’ll hit on 2 quick things, and then I’d love to hear your perspective as well.

I think we’re at the point in this market where it’s become just as much behavioral and psychological as anything else. My sense is that people I talk to see a lot of interesting opportunities, both with stocks they own—where they liked them 30% ago and now they’re down a lot, so they’re asking, “Should I buy more of this?”—and with companies they’ve been watching that have traded off and now have a great risk-reward catalyst.

But what I’ve been hearing from people is that no one really knows when this carnage is going to stop. I think people are afraid of being too early, buying something that’s down X% on nothing, or down X% on fund flows and little sector or macro issues, when it could go down another 10% or 15%. I almost feel like people are waiting for others to make the first move and decide that this is done.

I think that’s where the whole M&A piece comes in. If we start to see a string of M&A, I feel like—it’s a cliché to say that M&A cures bear markets in biotech—but it could create a little FOMO or external validation: a lot of good companies are trading at a bargain now, and if I don’t start buying stocks I think are interesting, I could miss out.

I think that’s where the narrative seems to be shifting on a forward-looking basis: what’s going to turn this around? Unfortunately, I think it’s hard to find a catalyst—

Brian Skorney

Other than M&A, or maybe just time, I’m not totally sure. What do you think, Yaron?

Yaron Werber

Yeah, I think this is an amazing discussion. We’ve been marketing, and as you can imagine, people are really struggling. I think there are 2 things going on. The de-grossing, theoretically and hopefully, is going to start abating after the October 31 annual close for many funds. I think a lot of people are looking at that as a potential source of resolution.

Then, right afterward, there are the midterm elections. Even though they’re not a huge overhang on biotech—on therapeutics, probably not an overhang at all—what’s really interesting is that we’re increasingly getting questions from generalists about whether, if the Democrats sweep Congress, which is now increasingly a risk or a possibility, they’re going to move to regulate AI, and whether that could actually be positive for sentiment in biotech.

People are looking at it with fresh eyes. It’s amazing how many questions we get about AI, either from generalists worrying about Isomorphic Labs and speculation that it has a $50 billion valuation, and the implications for biotech, or about the trade of AI versus biotech. There’s a lot of macro, and many funds are basically telling us this is the worst environment they’ve ever seen in their careers.

What’s remarkable, and I think you’ve mentioned this, is that if you look at the 25 top stocks in the XBI, they’re performing very well. The XBI is doing very well, partially driven by Twist, which is an AI-driven diagnostics play. So it looks like biotech is doing well, while many of the underlying investments are not. That puts a lot of pressure on fund managers whose LPs are asking, “Biotech is doing extremely well, and your fund doesn’t seem to be following the same trend. What’s going on?” That’s fairly routine now for everybody.

It’s a tough environment right now. But honestly, I don’t think we can ignore that this was also very much driven by the increase in interest rates. There’s probably going to be another rate raise, maybe even 2 from here—certainly one by the end of the year. We feel like we need to get through that again, and that’s probably one of the things we all need to follow very closely. Rising rates were what put pressure on the sector before.

Graig Suvannavejh

Yeah, thanks, Yaron. I want to flag a really interesting post I saw this week on X by Rod Wong, an investor, who posted a snapshot from a Goldman Sachs report. For those of you who can look it up, it was a graph showing Goldman’s view of recent de-grossing in biotech, according to its prime brokerage book.

The punchline is that hedge funds have unwound risk in biotech stocks in 6 of the past 8 weeks. In cumulative percentage terms over the past 8 weeks, the recent de-grossing is the largest in more than 5 years. Whether it’s interest rates, continued inflationary concerns, lack of M&A, or funds needing to de-gross, it’s just not a great picture right now.

We’ve got the elections, and Yaron, you put it so well in terms of the uncertainty around them. It just seems to be a more nervous time. That being said, the IPO market does seem to continue to hum along. Companies are able to raise money, but perhaps in a different kind of way, and I’ll touch upon that later.

Valuations And IPO Appetite

Maybe we can talk about valuations right now. Many of us have been in the industry on the sell side for quite some time. Does anyone have a comment on where valuations are right now? Are they stretched? Are stocks cheap? Brian, do you want to start?

Brian Skorney

They’re cheaper. They’re not as cheap as they were in 2023. Obviously, we’ve had a big move up. I think a lot of that move up has been more catch-up than anything else. I don’t think we’re anywhere near a bubble. I don’t think you can IPO a preclinical idea on a napkin for a billion dollars anymore.

I think a lot of the signals—and we’ve talked about this a lot on the IPO side of things—indicate that we’re not in an overvalued sector. There are certainly names that are overvalued, but I think there are a lot of names that are undervalued. I find more opportunities on the long side than on the short side. That’s probably most of what I hear from investor sentiment right now as well.

Everyone lived through the post-COVID fallout, so everyone knows how far down it can go, and you can see value now. One of the arguments I hear a lot when I try to pitch ideas to investors is that there’s a focus on near-term catalysts. I think there’s a fear that value alone can’t correct in a short enough timeframe for investors who want to buy.

There are certainly exceptions. We’re very long-term focused and see this as a way to find opportunities now. But by and large, people have gravitated toward shorter-duration catalysts to drive value. Again, I think there are a lot of those opportunities.

What I’ve always found most attractive about the XBI, whether it’s a great value for biotech in general or even overvalued for biotech in general, is that stocks with positive clinical data, where there’s some doubt about the outcome or the regulatory or commercial picture, go up a lot when sentiment isn’t fully baked in. That’s the nice thing about the sector.

The argument that’s so hard for the sector right now is that people who pride themselves on calling events and making money on them are particularly hurt by this de-grossing event. It takes away that argument around alpha performance versus taking a view that all of biotech is overvalued or undervalued.

Graig Suvannavejh

Paul, Yaron, any comments on valuations from your perspective?

Yaron Werber

I completely agree with Brian overall.

You know, it’s funny because when you look at large caps, people very rarely talk about valuation these days. You guys remember that years ago, valuation was very important and things traded within a certain band. So much of it now is that things are trading on M&A in lower-cap land, and in general, 99% of the volume is ETF-driven. ETFs are not exactly valuation-sensitive.

We look at valuation a lot more in stride these days, because we can totally get run over by being too conservative about where things can go. But things are fairly reasonably priced. We’re back in a market where, if you have data and the data’s great, the stock is flat or down the next day, and if the data’s not good, the stock’s down a lot. So valuations are fairly reasonable overall. Certainly not cheap, we agree.

Graig Suvannavejh

Maybe I can bring in Jake here. Jake, nice to meet you on the podcast. As a CEO, how do you make sense of what’s happening right now as you think about your own company, your peers, and whatever aspirations you might have as a company for thinking about the public markets?

Jake Becraft

Well, thanks for bringing me in. When I speak both to investors and other CEOs, I think the general sentiment is there’s a flight to both quality and innovation right now. We talked about the general de-grossing in the market. I think there are all sorts of things affecting the public markets right now that seem very transient and disconnected from underlying fundamentals.

There are even some folks blaming Moderna’s stock run-up, which was just about 8 weeks ago now, for being a driving force behind this. A lot of specialty investors were short Moderna, thinking their vaccine business was in trouble and their cancer vaccine business wasn’t nearly enough to justify an uptick in price. Of course, I think AI and other sorts of excitement around finally winning in cancer vaccines took their stock up, and some folks had to cover those short positions.

When I talk to specialty healthcare investors, whether they’re crossovers, public-only, or public-majority investors, the focus seems to be on both near-term catalysts and innovation. Whether it’s the general competitive dynamic, pricing pressures in the commercial market, or, perhaps more importantly, the threat of fast followers from China, the question is: How are you fundamentally and technologically differentiated in this space, with both an IP moat and a technical execution moat?

We saw that with City Therapeutics going public very recently: a clinical-stage company with a very innovative technological offering, and what I think is a very nice valuation for a company at that stage to get out in the public markets. There’s definitely price pressure, which I think is a fundamental theory and thesis of biotechnology specialty investors. There’s always going to be price pressure around how you justify a given valuation. But if you’re technologically differentiated in the space and have a near-term catalyst to de-risk that technological differentiation—and that catalyst needs to be clinical—I think you need to show some amount of clinical differentiation and de-risking of your technology. The appetite among later-stage investors, whether it’s later-stage growth crossover capital in the private markets or investors getting into the public markets, is still incredibly strong for a differentiated story.

Graig Suvannavejh

Brian, and also Yaron and Paul, we all talk to private companies a lot. I’m wondering if, based on your conversations over the past month or so, you’re hearing any shift in how they’re thinking about things, given the weakness in the XBI, even though we’ve had momentum in the IPO market. You may not be, but I’m curious.

Brian Skorney

I thought in the summer, like July or August—can you guys hear me, by the way, Graig?

Graig Suvannavejh

Yeah, we can hear you.

Brian Skorney

Okay. I had to update X for a second because I was having issues.

Paul Matteis

The list of private companies that were reaching out to me to talk and get a perspective on what they were doing, and contemplating their next steps toward becoming public, was starting to feel a little bit like 2020, just in terms of how early-stage some companies were and how viable they thought they could be as public companies.

It felt a little like the whole “Why not us?” dynamic, where they’d say, “Hey, we’ve seen all this happening, and we think we’re special. I talked to this board member or that board member, and they said, ‘You should look at a reverse merger.’” That wasn’t that long ago. That was early August. It feels like the past couple of months, or the past 6 weeks, have been a lifetime. We’re in a completely different world than we were in the summer.

So it’s hard for me to say if those types of companies are suddenly flipping, but maybe I just haven’t had as many of those calls in the past couple of weeks. I was having a lot of them. I’m sure, Yaron, you were too.

Yaron Werber

Yeah. I think we’re seeing three dynamics, and I want to pressure-test them against what you’re saying. One, we know that when the markets were strong, everybody on the other side started getting ready to gear up. All the motions, all the wheels were in motion. Then, when the window starts tightening and closing, the good ones, or the ones that really need capital, try to rush it out. We’re seeing a lot of that right now.

Second, there are companies doing really well that have new data in hot areas that are very vogue, topical, and innovative. Those are probably going to try to go out even in this window. There’s demand for those kinds of companies, and it’s a question of valuation and whether they really want to go out.

Then there are the other companies that sort of need to go out, were already in motion, and can’t really stop now. Frankly, they need capital, and they might try to test the market too. A lot of the feedback to all of us is: only go out if you have a catalyst coming up. You could be an amazing company going out into a vacuum of catalysts, and inevitably, at some point, I think you’re going to get forgotten. We’re definitely seeing that dynamic. There’s still demand, and you are seeing deals get done. It’s a question of how they trade ultimately.

IPF Data Tests The Thesis

Graig Suvannavejh

Okay. Thanks for that perspective. We’re going to pivot the conversation to data from the week. We’re going to start off in the IPF space, where Bristol Myers Squibb had a drug—I think it’s called admilparant? Sorry about that. They had a successful Phase 3 study, but maybe not so successful a Phase 3, and there are some read-throughs to other companies. With that in mind, I’ll turn it over to Paul or Brian, whoever wants to lead off the discussion on the IPF data.

Paul Matteis

I’m happy to kick it off, and I’d love to hear Skorney’s view. Bristol reported data that they’re describing as 100% positive, and I think they’re probably right that it’s positive for them in terms of getting a drug likely approved, and a drug that could be a big product. The drug is an LPA1 receptor antagonist for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

IPF is a fatal lung disease. There are a number of drugs approved, but none of them are really that great or solving the unmet need, per se. Patients still progress, and tolerability is tough. LPA1 receptor has been a very interesting biological target, but it’s been somewhat controversial because we’ve had mixed historical success. We’ve had some failures, including failures of approaches that people looked at as orthogonal, such as pursuing autotaxin.

For Bristol, this study was not at all seen as a slam dunk. I think the nuance Graig is alluding to in terms of whether these data are positive is that the low dose had statistical significance and the high dose did not. In the grand scheme of things for admilparant, you probably just need to get on the market with this class. Even if the dose response is a little odd here, and even if the effect size ends up not being as big as some other things we’ll ultimately see, these drugs do seem to be much better tolerated than other drugs in IPF.

We’ve done a number of calls with specialists in this space who’ve been interested in this class of drugs because they could theoretically be combined with many other agents. Right now, it’s hard to stack agents because of tolerability.

And just for anyone listening for context, when we’re talking about IPF drugs, we’re talking about drugs that could potentially sell billions in revenue per year. What’s interesting here is that Bristol stock was volatile. It was up and down. I’m sure people are trying to make sense of the filing strategy, too. Is it okay that the high dose didn’t hit and the low dose did?

I think, given the unmet need in IPF, it’s hard to see the FDA not approving this. But Bristol didn’t give any hard clinical data, so you have to reserve some judgment until we see the full data, likely at a medical meeting next spring. The other orthogonal trade came from Contineum, a company I cover that’s also developing an LPA1 receptor antagonist. Contineum was up 20% in the premarket, then ended up down more than 25% on the day as people tried to make sense of what this means for the company.

Contineum’s drug may be more potent than Bristol’s, and part of its thesis is that it can achieve better receptor coverage than Bristol. But looking at Bristol’s dose response, which some people might call an inverse dose response, my guess is that it’s probably more of a flat dose response, or just noise, because these doses don’t seem that different in terms of receptor coverage. I think people not seeing this dose response has led to more questioning of whether greater receptor coverage can drive greater efficacy for Contineum.

In this biotech market, which is very anxious and not very patient, IPF trials take a long time, and Contineum’s trial isn’t expected to read out until 2028. The stock traded off on this sort of unanswerable question around clinical differentiation for these drugs. I think people are also wondering how clear-cut the Bristol data is, how big the effect size is, and how robust the p-value is. As we think about the orthogonal read-through, are these drugs de-risked?

Our perspective is that the unmet need in IPF is so significant. If Bristol’s data is real, as it looks like it is, and this ultimately becomes a big commercial product, there’s likely room for a number of these drugs. Contineum’s drug should, at the very least, have a dosing advantage with once-daily dosing. But a lot remains to be determined until we see the full data in the spring.

Investors tend to look at IPF as one of those conditions where the translatability from Phase 2 to Phase 3 isn’t that great. In the context of the Contineum discussion and this orthogonal read-through, people will be looking closely at this top-line readout that is “positive,” but perhaps a little nuanced. How nuanced is it, versus how confident can we be that this target is de-risked for others beyond Bristol? I don’t know, Skorney. What else did you want to add there?

Brian Skorney

I think we share a lot of the same thoughts. IPF is a terrible disease. I don’t want to totally equate it to lung cancer, but there are slight similarities. It’s a very progressive, fatal disease, and these patients quickly lose the ability to breathe. Clinical trials here have been really tough. Part of it is the nature of the disease being idiopathic: there isn’t a great understanding of its pathophysiology. You can recognize what IPF looks like in a patient, but the underlying biology is totally uncertain.

Even when you think about the approved drugs, like nintedanib or pirfenidone, they have kind of weird mechanisms. It’s not a case where you say, “Oh, there’s this clear biological plausibility.” That’s not always the case for effective drugs, of course, but I certainly think the unmet need is here. I think this would be an area of flexibility. I have battle scars from watching the FDA reject pirfenidone on its first go-around, despite what I thought was pretty good data. I thought they were going to approve it, but they made the company run another Phase 3 study to recapitulate what they had already seen in the prior study.

It’s not necessarily an easy indication from a regulatory perspective, and it’s very hard from a clinical trial perspective. As you said, Paul, it’s hard to say what’s noise and what isn’t. Certainly, the hypothesis should be that there would be at least a flat dose response or a dose-related relationship here. Inverse dose responses probably aren’t something you’d predict in a disease like IPF with this mechanism.

One question I’d have—and Bristol didn’t really address this yet—is whether there were more tolerability issues. It didn’t seem like there was a big tolerability issue overall, but if there were more discontinuations on the high dose and patients weren’t getting the drug, that would be something to consider. In general, I think people are looking at this data very skeptically and asking what it really means for the mechanism.

Given the dozen or so drugs with early positive data that ultimately went into much larger studies and failed to show a clear signal, I think there’s a certain psychology around IPF’s history. There isn’t a lot we’ve seen that you can bank on moving from Phase 2 to Phase 3.

Yaron Werber

Brian and Paul, on the IPF space, I have some battle scars of my own. I used to cover a company called Galapagos, which has now been rebranded as Lakefront Therapeutics. Galapagos had an autotaxin modulator that ended up failing in 2 Phase 3 studies, I think mainly because of an imbalance in mortality, which obviously wasn’t good for the drug.

I’m wondering, as we think about the IPF space, if anyone is investigating combination approaches, like in cystic fibrosis.

Brian Skorney

I think that would be the hope with this mechanism, as Paul alluded to. There are anecdotes of people using pirfenidone and nintedanib together, but those are really toxic drugs. The treatments available in the IPF space to move the needle have been pretty tough to combine. Part of the hope was that you’d have a very tolerable mechanism, and it would be a great advance if you could stack additional tolerable mechanisms to add up to a benefit.

With cystic fibrosis, the problem is that, unlike idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, where the pathophysiology is very uncertain, we have a very good understanding of the underlying genetics, how those genetics result in a specific phenotype, and where to target with pharmacology to correct or potentiate it. We’ve seen that with Vertex’s drugs.

Yaron Werber

Thanks for that. Brian, we’re going to stay with you. Two weeks ago, we talked about Mirum and another drug that got approved. It looks like Mirum had some Phase 3 data this week that you wanted to highlight.

Brian Skorney

Yeah. Just really quickly, they had a Phase 3 data set for their commercial drug, Livmarli. Livmarli is approved in 2 pediatric cholestatic liver diseases to improve pruritus, which is the main symptom here. This was an interesting basket study in other pediatric cholestatic liver diseases where pruritus is occurring. It was mostly made up of patients with biliary atresia, but there were also a number of much smaller ultra-orphan subgroups.

It showed what I’d call very consistent placebo-adjusted reductions, with a good magnitude of reduction in pruritus from baseline. They’re going to file for this indication, which could potentially add another 2,000 patients in the U.S. and EU just on the biliary atresia side. The cumulative numbers for the other groups are a little more uncertain, but probably add another 2,000 patients.

Brian Skorney

This is a pretty meaningful potential expansion. I think it also builds upon Mirum’s evidence for IL-10 inhibition. This drug is an IL-10 inhibitor. They also have another drug that they’re planning to file for adult cholestatic liver disease.

I think the bulk of the evidence is that if a person has pruritus due to cholestasis, giving them an IL-10 inhibitor will dramatically reduce that pruritus. They’ve shown that in a number of studies now. I think this feeds into a lot of their long-term opportunity: they continue to show growth with Livmarli in the pediatric indication, and their very late-stage adult IL-10 inhibitor, volixibat, has a pivotal study readout in PBC in the next few months. They’re planning to submit an NDA for PSC, where there is no approved therapy, in the first half of next year.

Graig Suvannavejh

Okay, great. Thanks so much. Let’s turn to Yaron. Yaron, you’re going to talk about a company that I don’t know of. It’s called First Tracks Biotherapeutics, and then you’re going to talk about maybe 1, if not 2, datasets from a company that everyone knows about. That’s argenx.

Yaron Werber

argenx.

Graig Suvannavejh

I’ll turn it to you.

Celiac And Sjögren’s Data

Yaron Werber

Yeah. Everybody, if you’re not following celiac disease, it’s time to do so, because this is like the best of biotech. It’s going to be controversial. There’s a lot of competition, and there are going to be lots of fireworks, with questions about mechanism of action. You start drilling down into very, very specific activity and inflammation. Frankly, as we all know, we don’t know everything about immunology.

There are 3 companies here: Teva, argenx, and First Tracks. The good news is that Teva is hitting the IL-15 ligand, while argenx and First Tracks are hitting the receptor. All of them show really good data. They’re showing a reduction in the attack on the epithelial lining by lymphocytes, so a reduction in intraepithelial lymphocytes, or IELs. They’re also seeing histological benefits and symptom benefits in very small studies, and all of them look fairly similar.

argenx, which bought Forte Biosciences, is technically in the lead. They just released positive data literally last week, and they didn’t release the full data. The main event for all these companies is probably going to be the International Celiac Disease Symposium in Melbourne in mid-November. If you haven’t been to Melbourne, that’s a great chance to visit. I think many of us are trying to figure out what it’ll cost to get there, because we sort of need to be there. It’s going to be the coming-out party for celiac disease.

There are nuances. As I mentioned, Teva is hitting the circulating cytokine. Its drug is administered subcutaneously every 3 months. First Tracks and argenx are hitting the receptor where IL-15 binds. It’s called the CD122 receptor, which is also part of the IL-2 receptor. As soon as many of us hear IL-2, we know there’s going to be a lot of activity here, both good and bad, that we need to be very cognizant of. They’re essentially shutting down the activity that you don’t want to have. It seems to be fairly safe and active.

The data looks good. There are subtle differences in trial design. Nothing is approved, and there’s no “pathway” yet to getting drugs approved. They’ve all done slightly different studies in terms of the gluten challenge patients have to undergo. How hard do you go? How long do you go with the challenge? Then come the biotech debates: the gluten-free diet is not expensive, so what do you charge for a drug that reduces gluten intolerance? What’s the endpoint going to be: histology or symptoms? How long do you treat for? How hard do you go? All of this needs to be ironed out. The bulls say the market is going to be huge; the bears say it’s going to be very small because no one’s going to pay for it.

The good news is these drugs also work so far in vitiligo. We’ve seen data from Forte/argenx and Teva. We’re waiting for the alopecia data from argenx imminently, and First Tracks is also doing an EoE, or eosinophilic esophagitis, study. Lots to look forward to: unlocking a whole new area of biology, which is super cool.

Paul Matteis

Mm-hmm.

Yaron Werber

We were hosting our therapeutics conference in Boston, which is a 2-day symposium with physicians, and we literally wrapped up a very bullish Sjögren’s disease panel. Amgen, as you know, is going to have its Phase 3 data coming up at ACR, and the next dataset expected was argenx’s Phase 3 Vyvgart data in Sjögren’s. The panel was basically very positive on Amgen and very positive on the BAFF/APRIL modality. The first one is going to be Novartis with the weakest drug; Vera is coming behind with a better drug, and then there are the FcRn drugs from argenx. They viewed them as active, but fourth in potency.

Fast-forward 12 hours, and we all wake up to argenx terminating development after failing a futility analysis. None of us even knew there was a futility analysis in that Phase 3 study, and of course argenx immediately sold off. Again, that was surprising. We do think Sjögren’s is going to be a big market with innovation, and we’re already seeing success with the upcoming Phase 3 data at ACR from Amgen for the first study. They have a second Phase 3 study coming by the end of the year.

The more we learn about biology and inflammation, the more we realize it’s not one specific factor that drives the biology. A lot of times, it’s the B-cell/T-cell interaction that’s probably most important in regulating disease. That was an example of Vyvgart specifically reducing autoantibodies: great Phase 2 data, but it failed in Phase 3. Meanwhile, the CD40 ligand from Amgen, which had great Phase 2 data, now also has positive Phase 3 data by regulating the B-cell/T-cell interaction. Lots to study in immunology.

Paul Matteis

Yaron, are you surprised that argenx is flat compared with a year ago, even after the market and this setback? Honestly, as you were talking, I was looking at the chart of this versus Alnylam and Insmed. People were putting these in the same bucket. Alnylam and Insmed are both down a lot. argenx is still hanging in there. What do you think?

Yaron Werber

Good point. There are puts and takes, right? Insmed was supposed to get acquired, but it didn’t, and then the question is whether the launch is crushing numbers or not. Alnylam is not crushing numbers. Of course, BridgeBio is doing very well. There are concerns about market dynamics.

argenx was a high flyer this year, crushing numbers, with good data. Lots of generalists are involved globally, and I’ve got to be honest: this is the one stock where we feel like everybody owns it. Literally everybody owns it. So it always overreacts to the upside and, frankly, to the downside with any data—even data that, to us specialists, doesn’t matter. I’m not talking about the Sjögren’s data.

Am I surprised it’s flat, as opposed to being down a lot? We’re expecting another good quarter in both Q3 and Q4, and then they have very important Phase 3 data coming up in MMN, or multifocal motor neuropathy, with their C2 antagonist. This is all first-in-class new biology, and that should work. The question is whether it’s going to be non-inferior to IVIG or superior. That makes a big difference to peak sales, depending on whether you go second line or front line, and that will determine how the stock does by the end of the year.

Are we shocked? No. But, to be honest, argenx has performed better than we expected this year, too, and I think a lot of it has honestly been driven by generalists coming in. We’re pleased, and there’s obviously important data coming imminently that we’re constructive on.

Graig Suvannavejh

I think the argenx story is remarkable. I remember at a prior firm, we initiated coverage in late 2018, at €89, I think. To see how far the company has come is great, and I think it’s great for European biotech, too, which sometimes gets a bad rap. Yaron, thanks so much for that summary. Great stuff there.

Brain Shuttle Data Builds Momentum

Paul, I want to turn it over to you, and we’re going to switch to neuro now, a place that’s near and dear to both of us. Arrowhead had some data for a tau asset this past Wednesday, so it would be helpful if you could summarize that data and what you think it might mean for the brain shuttle space.

Paul Matteis

Yeah. Thanks a lot, Graig. Arrowhead had clinical data for its transferrin siRNA drug conjugate. Transferrin conjugates have been used to deliver drugs in the brain. We’ve seen success with transferrin in increasing antibody penetration, in the case of trontinemab, Roche’s drug for Alzheimer’s that’s in Phase 3, and with Denali and JCR, with enzymes. The space is quickly moving towards all kinds of cargo.

I think it’s not just a delivery thing, either. For CNS, transferrin could increase the probability of success, depending on the target, because sometimes you can’t get enough drug into the brain, or you can’t get it to distribute to the right areas of the brain when you go intrathecal or use another approach.

This was interesting for a few reasons. First, Arrowhead, which doesn’t have much history with transferrin expertise compared with Roche or Denali, apparently executed very well and became the first to show clinical data for an siRNA antibody-drug conjugate. Second, the data were good. They showed data for their tau-lowering drug, with up to more than 80% tau lowering in the CSF. We’ll obviously see more details, but at a high level, it looks pretty promising.

The discussion around tau has become more nuanced for a couple of reasons. One is that CSF tau may not equal tau burden in the areas of Alzheimer’s pathology. Ultimately, that’s where this is the most exciting target in Alzheimer’s: you have to show a reduction in tau PET. We saw with Biogen that the CSF reductions were a lot bigger than the PET reductions.

Second, Biogen had data from a big Phase IIb study this summer for its tau-lowering drug, which is given intrathecally. The distribution and efficacy profile may be very different from Arrowhead’s. Biogen was able to lower both CSF tau and tau PET, and showed clinical benefit at the lowest dose, but there was an inverse dose response and toxicity at the higher dose. That’s led people to question whether the Biogen efficacy is real and what the dose relationship is with tau lowering. Our thought was that, at least on the safety side, the tau lowering across all the Biogen doses was close enough together that it’s hard to believe the toxicity was driven by tau. It seems more likely that it was idiosyncratic toxicity from the ASO. Until someone like Arrowhead or Denali tests this hypothesis with a next-generation tau drug, we won’t really have the answer.

There’s still tremendous promise here. It’s really cool to see Arrowhead succeeding in a new tissue. I don’t cover Arrowhead, but I remember that, a number of years ago, the company got the rap of having a lot of me-too products and pipelines that overlapped with Alnylam and Ionis in the liver space. You’ve really seen the company break out, not just by innovating in an area like tau, but also with its triglyceride drug.

Graig, I think you had another angle on transferrin more broadly. For me, it’s interesting that we’re seeing so many companies succeed with transferrin. It feels like it’s become like GalNAc in the liver relatively quickly. I don’t want to say it’s commoditized, because I’m sure there’s a lot of art and nuance in doing this, and you have to give credit to companies like Denali that have gotten a drug approved and really figured out the safety margins. But there are a lot of players in this space, and it feels like a lot of companies are figuring out the science at the same time.

Graig Suvannavejh Yeah, that’s a great segue. I cover a company called Alector. We’re neutral-rated on it, but they had an R&D day that I thought went really well. They’ve had a pivot of sorts. They had some clinical-stage assets that unfortunately didn’t work in late-stage clinical trials, and they’re focused on neurodegenerative diseases. Now they’re developing a proprietary technology that they’re calling ABC, short for Alector Brain Carrier.

This is against the backdrop of a very competitive landscape. You mentioned Roche and Denali, Paul, but there’s also AbbVie in this space. There’s Corsona [?] in this space. BioArctic is supplying its technology to a couple of companies, including Acumen and Prothena. Alector made a bigger splash with its ABC technology, and its lead asset is a beta-amyloid-targeting antibody called AL-137. We don’t have any clinical data yet, but they made a really interesting and persuasive argument as to why their construct may prove superior.

They’re using transferrin, and they also have siRNA-based approaches, including one that targets tau. That won’t get into the clinic until next year, or perhaps not until 2028, as I think about it. But they’ve shown preclinically tau mRNA knockdown of about 75% to 80%, so it’s in the ballpark. Tau has been a challenge for many companies because the view is that tau is perhaps more intracellular, and traditional antibody approaches won’t particularly work if you’re trying to target it intracellularly.

Keep an eye on Alector and the space. It has heated up quite tremendously, and we’ve seen a lot of deal activity. Interestingly, the company raised $75 million this morning, even though its event was on Tuesday. Good for Alector, and we’ll see continued progress in that space.

I also wanted to briefly mention Verastem, a company I cover, which is in the red-hot RAS inhibitor space. They had very, very excellent data for their mutant-selective KRAS G12D inhibitor. It’s still early days; this is Phase I and early Phase II data across multiple cancers, particularly pancreatic cancer. That has gotten all the attention because of what’s happening with Revolution Medicines and its pan-RAS inhibitor, which, I think, just this morning or yesterday got a positive CHMP opinion for approval.

There’s good momentum in the KRAS space, which continues to be very hot, and lots of entrants are coming into the space. We’ve got a couple of minutes left, but I wanted to turn it over to Jake, who we haven’t heard from in a little while. We want to talk about upcoming ESMO data, especially in the context of the Moderna candidate. Jake, I’ll turn it over to you.

Jake Becraft Yeah. This has been a hotly watched area. In my opinion, in a certain context, we’ve had the first big breakthrough in cancer vaccines, with Moderna and Merck announcing eight weeks ago that they seem to be able to show a significant benefit with their vaccine. It’s been a hotly contested data point. I’ll say that there’s growing evidence that mRNA vaccines, even COVID vaccines, can provide an immunotherapy benefit on their own, probably from a general T-cell stimulation effect.

Notably, I believe the Moderna-Merck data are controlled against a placebo, not another cancer vaccine. So there’s this overarching question, further confounded by BioNTech having now canceled, I think, 2 of its non-melanoma monotherapy cancer vaccine trials: first in colorectal cancer, then more recently in head and neck cancer. Moderna and Merck have a combination with Keytruda and a cancer vaccine whose antigens, Moderna says, are derived from an AI algorithm.

A lot of the stock trading around that move was probably general fervor around the idea that AI has finally cracked cancer. We’ll see at ESMO. I think the general industry take from the press releases that came out eight weeks ago, and the general buzz around that data, is that there’s certainly an ability to increase progression-free survival among melanoma patients. It’s a very small market, and they’ll need to prove that out much more broadly. There have been some Twitter fights between reporters, analysts, scientists, and others about the impact of this data. But it gives us all a lot of hope that there’s a lot more work and progress to be made in cancer immunotherapy.

Unfortunately, the patient types addressed by the data being announced at ESMO are in some of the earlier stages, obviously with fully resectable tumors. But with screening, we could see that patient population grow. Full disclosure: I also run an mRNA therapeutics company, not a vaccine company. The general sentiment is that mRNA is back on the menu again. The general biotech community and investor sentiment in the market are incredibly excited about the ways mRNA can go from vaccines to therapeutic vaccines and, ideally, into real therapeutics in the future. That’s something we haven’t seen succeed over the past decade or so of its promise.

Jake Becraft

So everyone's keeping an eye on that data. The late-breaker will be released at ESMO, and we'll see the full picture. I would have loved to see a control with an mRNA vaccine that was not antigen-specific to the cancers. Maybe in the future we'll see that.

Graig Suvannavejh

All right. That was great. Jake, thanks for that. That’s all the time we have for today. Thanks to my esteemed co-hosts for making today’s hangout a great one. And thanks to many of you who dialed in live, and perhaps those of you who will dial in on the replay. Have a great rest of your day, and we hope you’ll join us for our next Biotech Hangout.

注：BidClub 仅提供原文全文文稿；中文版为标题、要点与摘要的译文。

来源：YouTube

item.title: EP55 Token 价格因模型迁移而下跌：Silicon Data & Compute Exchange CEO Carmen Li
item.description: Silicon Data 跟踪 300 个开源、开放权重及闭源模型，Li 观察到客户正将部分消耗从高端模型转向更便宜的选择。Token 指数衡量实际支出，而非模型质量；Doug 提出的工作流路由只是可能解释，Li 并不了解客户的具体使用场景。迁移是否代表对低价模型的持续需求仍未明朗，Li 也没有确认客户转用模型的具体原因。
item.content:encoded:
Pitch The PM · Doug、Carmen Li · 2026-10-16 · 57 min · 原语言 EN

Silicon Data 跟踪 300 个开源、开放权重及闭源模型，Li 观察到客户正将部分消耗从高端模型转向更便宜的选择。Token 指数衡量实际支出，而非模型质量；Doug 提出的工作流路由只是可能解释，Li 并不了解客户的具体使用场景。迁移是否代表对低价模型的持续需求仍未明朗，Li 也没有确认客户转用模型的具体原因。

要点 TL;DR

  • Li 将 Token 价格下跌归因于客户转向更便宜的模型。 Silicon Data 跟踪 300 个开源/开放权重模型及闭源模型的消耗情况，观察到“token-mixing 时代之后，人们正从高端模型转向更便宜的模型”。Doug 提出，工作流路由可能解释这一变化，但 Li 看不到客户的具体使用场景，也没有确认这一机制。
  • 全球新云市场的 B200 按需价格约为每 GPU 小时 5 美元，但其隐含远期曲线仍然向上。 去年向下倾斜的曲线已转为正价差结构；最近，A100 和 H100 曲线趋平。这些曲线来自预留合同，早于期货交易。Li 明确提醒：“市场有周期。”
  • 老一代 GPU 的盈利能力可能超过简单折旧年限所暗示的水平。 Li 仍看到为 A100 签订的 3 年期合同，尽管这一架构已有约 4 至 6 年历史；她还提到二手市场上每张 GPU 售价为 4,000 至 9,000 美元。Doug 质疑这反映的是持久的经济价值还是单纯的物理寿命；Li 提及散热限制、设备更换延迟和工作流适配性，同时提醒：“我不是说每张 A100 都能用 9 年。”
  • 算力对冲针对的是长期融资承诺与较短客户合同之间的期限错配。 GPU 融资期限可能长达 5 至 7 年，而预留合同只有 3 至 5 年，后续租赁收入因此面临风险。CME 期货可覆盖前 36 个月，更长期的对冲则需要场外交易；目标是让运营商锁定“生产成本”，使融资更容易通过承销评估。
  • Silicon Data 的商业机会，取决于可信基准能否嵌入算力融资。 Li 称 CME 将在“未来几周内”推出 H100 和 B200 期货，已有 4 只 ETF 提交申请，其中包括 1 倍反向产品。她所说的成熟期 30 万亿美元衍生品市场，指年度名义交易额，并非数据授权收入预测。
  • 芯片设计公司增多，并不意味着算力供给约束会自动消失。 Doug 强调晶圆制造产能正在扩张；Li 则指出，晶圆制造、封装、基础设施和审批都必须同步扩张。否则，产出仍会受增长最慢的环节限制；专用推理芯片可能补充 Nvidia，而不是取代其全部作用。
  • Li 对 AI 最终由哪一层获取价值仍持开放态度。 Doug 提到互联网平台凭借客户和分销渠道占据优势，而 Nvidia 目前获取了可观的经济租金。Li 称 AI 还是“一个巨大的婴儿”：基础设施、模型、工具链和应用仍在发展，她并未声称知道未来哪一层会诞生最大的赢家。

摘要 Digest

1. 固定价 AI 收入催生算力对冲需求

  • Li 从 DRW 的能源期权交易和 Bloomberg 数据集成业务转向创业，起因是 2024 年客户遇到的一项难题：AI SaaS 公司按月收取固定收入，按需 GPU 费用却从每 GPU 小时 3 美元波动到 9 美元甚至 16 美元。客户增加，未必能扭转负毛利率。她用航空公司打比方说明：“押注 GPU 周期不是他们的工作。”运营商应锁定生产成本，把精力放在产品上。
  • 她的两家公司承担不同职能。Silicon Data 提供指数、估值和风险管理信息，定位为“算力的裁判层”，不提供 GPU 或 Token 访问。Compute Exchange 则通过算力、GPU 和 Token 的长期及远期合约，以及服务器二级市场交易提供流动性。Li 将两家公司的关系分别比作 Bloomberg 和 Nasdaq。
  • Li 预计，最先需要对冲的自然是 GPU 敞口集中的参与者，包括新云厂商、超大规模云服务商，或在资产负债表上持有服务器的融资方。她举例说，GB300 采购可能以 7 年期融资，而对应的预留合同只有 3 年、4 年或 5 年；即使已经锁定首批客户，之后的租赁收入仍暴露在市场风险之下。
  • Doug 的融资逻辑是，锁定未来收入可能让债权人更愿意为尚未签约的采购提供资金。Li 表示认同，同时强调对冲工具不等于无限流动性：CME 期货仅覆盖 36 个月。第 4 至第 7 年通常需要大宗或场外交易，交易定价可参考期货曲线，但期货曲线本身不会自动提供这部分流动性。

2. 基准的可信度支撑数据授权机会

  • 录制时，Li 称 CME 将在“未来几周内”推出 H100 和 B200 算力期货；她预计之后会有期权，但当时没有宣布相关计划。基于这些期货的 4 只 ETF 已提交申请，其中包括 1 倍反向产品。她认为这一进展来得很早：按她的经验，发行方通常会先观察期货流动性，再围绕它推出 ETF。
  • B200 这个名称并不代表标准化服务器。Li 称，市场上约有 50 种配置，CPU、RAM、硬盘和地理位置都可能不同。Silicon Data 会将这些配置标准化到基础配置，并每日跟踪价格关系的变化；地区溢价可能反映对延迟敏感的需求。其数据每天约有 25 万行，授权安排可以包含独家权利或付费客户关系。
  • Doug 追问利益冲突，包括 DRW 的投资以及指数套利机会。Li 表示，按设计，DRW“并未参与”。她称自己不在指数计算委员会任职，因为研究主管和指数主管更适合承担这项工作；她也会与外部学术顾问合作。她还表示，指数提供商应建立经第三方审计的合规计划，并将指数计算职能分开，做到这些的参与者寥寥无几。她的核心原则是保持中立：“不能既参与交易，又同时当裁判。”无论竞争对手多少，一旦指数不再反映供需，它就失去了用途。
  • Doug 询问数据本身能带来多少收入。Li 没有给出收入数字，而是提出一个有条件的市场规模框架：NVIDIA 现货市场的名义交易额目前可能每年达到 1 万亿至 3 万亿美元；成熟后的算力衍生品交易额可能达到现货市场的 10 倍，上限为 30 万亿美元。她认为，交易越活跃，市场对细分基准、区域敞口和风险工具的需求就越大，但没有相应估算授权收入。

3. A100 合同挑战统一折旧逻辑

  • Doug 提出 Michael Burry 相关的看空论点：延长服务器的使用寿命可能导致盈利被高估。Li 给出的反例来自实际交易：A100 问世已有约 4 至 6 年，她仍看到市场签订 3 年期合同。她称，维护良好的设备若先后签下 6 年和 3 年合同，累计现金盈利期可能至少达到 9 年，但明确限制了这一推论：“我不是说每张 A100 都能用 9 年。”
  • Doug 的反驳值得保留：能否物理运行，与是否仍有经济价值并非一回事；新芯片可能凭借生产效率和能耗节省，足以证明更换设备是合理的。Li 认同新架构效率更高，也能支持更大的模型。但散热系统、楼板承重、可用资本和交付周期都会限制设备更换；买家可能要等 6 个月或更久才能拿到新设备，二手设备却“明天”就能到。
  • Li 提到，A100 二手价格为每张 GPU 4,000 至 9,000 美元。她另称，H800 残值一直在下降，但仍高于按 5 年直线折旧计算的水平。她要表达的是盈利尾部更长、且分布不均，并不是说老硬件不会折旧，也不是说所有服务器都应采用相同的会计使用年限。
  • 软件也会改变硬件的经济性。更大的模型可能超出老 GPU 的显存容量，但更好的优化或量化技术，或许能让这些模型重新部署到老芯片上。这会改变需求和定价：GPU 层的价值，部分取决于其上方的软件和模型层如何发展。

4. 远期曲线已经改变了对周期的判断

  • Li 表示，大部分 GPU 消耗仍发生在超大规模云服务商内部；但新云厂商已从两年前的寥寥数家扩展到全球 300 多家，而且每天都有新服务商出现。供应商增加，客户选择更多，基准也更难被操纵；交易数据还可以来自客户账单，从而在服务商自有账户数据之外进行核验。
  • 过去 30 天里，大多数芯片价格趋于稳定，全球新云市场的 B200 按需价格约为每 GPU 小时 5 美元。Silicon Data 的隐含远期曲线汇总预留合同，涵盖 36 个月和 5 年期等期限。去年曲线向下倾斜；今年转为正价差结构。最近，A100 和 H100 曲线趋平，B200 仍处于正价差结构。
  • Doug 的说法是：“关于远期曲线，我唯一知道的就是它总会出错。”Li 认同曲线反映的是当下共识，并不代表掌握了未来现货价格。被问到 B200 年底价格是否高于 5 美元时，她说：“我确实不知道。”作为指数提供商，她也不提供前瞻指引或持有交易敞口。

5. Token 价格反映消耗变化，而非模型质量

  • Silicon Data 的 Token 指数估算，如果全社会是一个人，会愿意为 Token 支付多少。Li 跟踪 300 个开源和开放权重模型，以及闭源模型的消耗情况，并计入不同的输入与输出价格及用量。该产品衡量的是实际观察到的支出选择，不评判模型质量，也不只是复述高端供应商公布的价格。
  • Li 强调的机制是模型迁移：“token-mixing 时代之后”，人们正把至少一部分工作流转向更便宜的开源和开放权重模型。Doug 提出，工具链可能会将较简单的任务路由到前沿模型之外。Li 对此保留条件：“我们实际上不了解客户的使用场景。”她举例说，摘要任务可能不需要最强的模型。
  • Li 将 Token 指数与山寨币收入图表作比较，称它“几乎是一个领先指标”。指数开始上升时，山寨币收入也随之上升；后来指数跌至约 1 美元左右，收入也开始停滞。她将指数解释为支付意愿；她没有证明两者存在因果关系，也没有说明每位客户转用其他模型的原因。
  • Token 服务仍主要采用按需计费，不像 GPU 有预留定价。Li 提醒，供应商可能在没有明确披露的情况下更改价格或精度。Doug 希望设置限制，避免智能体带来意外账单；Li 补充，用户还会考虑质量、截止时间、延迟、安全性和地理位置偏好。拥有或租用 GPU 则是另一种消耗方式：在硬件容量范围内运行模型。不过，正如 Doug 提醒她的：“折旧是真实存在的。”

6. 芯片竞争仍受制于物理瓶颈

  • Doug 询问超大规模云服务商自研芯片会带来溢价还是折价。Li 回忆 AWS 曾宣布下调 Trainium 等型号的价格，但没有给出数值化的价格差异。她从功能上区分两类产品：一些专用推理芯片旨在补充 Nvidia 的应用场景，另一些则试图在特定推理工作负载上取代 Nvidia。不同芯片并不能互换，也无法覆盖所有任务。
  • Li 举例说，原本为 Nvidia 生产 100 颗芯片的工厂，可能改为生产 80 颗 Nvidia 芯片，再为另外两家设计公司各生产 10 颗。设计公司增加本身并不会提高总产量。Doug 强调工厂正在扩张；Li 表示认同，但封装或其他扩张较慢的环节仍可能限制最终交付能力。设计公司增加的速度，可能快于实体产能扩张。
  • 监管暂停也是潜在约束之一。Li 提到暂停审批的风险时，Doug 表示没听说过她描述的广泛情形；她则举例称，纽约州表示未来几年不会建设数据中心，同时承认政策可能改变。她也不认同期货推出本身就是泡沫信号：期货让看空的参与者能够做空，也有助于价格发现，而现货市场原本主要由多头敞口主导。

7. AI 最终赢家尚未定局，市场基础设施仍在发展

  • Doug 询问投资者应如何在晶圆制造、硬件、Token、数据和应用之间布局。Li 回顾互联网基础设施的发展，以及最终获取价值的平台。Doug 提到 Google 和 Meta 拥有客户，并补充了 Amazon 的分销能力。这些历史经验并不能确定哪些 AI 企业会重现同样的路径。
  • Li 称 AI 是“一个巨大的婴儿”：规模已经很大，但仍处于早期发展阶段。Doug 指出，Nvidia 当前获取了可观的经济租金；Li 则认为，基础设施仍在建设之中，模型、工具链和应用都建立在其上。未来或许会出现另一层赢家，但她的回答仍是：“我不知道。”
  • 同时经营两家公司，也让经验迁移没有想象中容易。Li 形容数据业务和交易市场有着不同的文化、利润率和获客路径，就像性格各异的女儿。她给创业者的建议由此而来：选择一件足够有吸引力的事，才能支撑持续学习，并应对意料之外的障碍。
  • Li 对 Compute Exchange 的具体目标，是把采购周期从“2 个月”缩短到“3 小时”，既服务较小买家，也满足 20,000 个节点的采购需求。Silicon Data 的对应目标，是为各层算力建立可信的估值和基准，让参与者每日评估敞口、了解融资成本，并据此决定如何对冲。

全文文稿（原文）

Carmen Li We see a lot of people shifting from premium models to cheaper models post token-mixing era. That’s why you see token prices start dropping. Most people think they can predict the future. If everyone thinks there’s going to be no cycle, or one cycle and that’s it, I keep telling people there are cycles.

From energy options market maker at DRW to Bloomberg Data, and why AI startups' swinging GPU costs made compute an industry-wide hedging problem

Doug The only thing I know about the future curve is that it’s always wrong.

Carmen Li The curve is the market consensus view today. If you map our token indices on top of the bar chart, you’ll see something really interesting: they’re almost a leading indicator. When our token indices ramp up, that’s when you see revenue dropping and ramping up.

Just like American Airlines can’t run an airline without hedging its oil prices. It’s not American Airlines’ job to speculate on oil prices. It’s their job to run an airline company. Similarly, it’s not AI companies’ job to speculate on GPU cycles. You want to lock in your cost of production, which is compute, and focus on products.

Silicon Data is the referee layer for compute. The flip side of that is Compute Exchange. It’s the liquidity layer for compute resources.

Doug Hello and welcome to Pitch the PM. My name is Doug Garber. After a decade at Citadel and Millennium, I interview top PMs on their highest conviction ideas. Be sure to subscribe to our Substack for more research updates. Today, I’m here with Carmen Li, the CEO of Silicon Data and Compute Exchange. Welcome.

Carmen Li Thank you. It’s good to be here.

Doug I’m glad you’re here. I know you’re very busy on the media circuit. I’d love to hear more about both your companies and how you came to run them.

Where to invest in the AI stack, lessons from the internet era and why "AI is a gigantic baby"

Carmen Li You’re right about the media circuit. I never realized how much media engagement I’d need to do, though we were just talking about this. I should have expected it. We’re essentially establishing a brand-new asset class: compute. By definition, compute is gigantic in scale. Everything we do will be impactful in terms of transparency and getting people the right products and benchmarks. We need to do a lot of education for the industry.

How did I get into compute? I started my career as an energy options market maker in Chicago. I worked for DRW Trading. In a way, compute is another form of commodity, another form of resource, just like oil and gas. I started my career in traditional commodities, in energy. That was really fun, and the experience gave me strong intuition about market making, what the index volatility is, and how to manage risk.

After that, I moved to different banks. My last job was at Bloomberg Data, where I managed global data integrations for Bloomberg. Any data leaving the Bloomberg Terminal and going into a third-party ecosystem, including back offices, cloud, and AI applications, was governed by me and my team. That included technical integrations, go-to-market, compliance, and everything else.

In 2024, after the ChatGPT moment, there were already a lot of AI companies. They were SaaS companies creating solutions and services, some of them aimed at financial services firms. I was excited for them. They were integrating, or looking to integrate, with Bloomberg Data, and I thought, “Great, you’re a young company. You’re doing really well. You’ve got big-name clients. That’s amazing.”

How DRW founder Don Wilson pre-seeded Silicon Data, and building products with no product or sales team

They were complaining that even though they looked like they were doing well in terms of client numbers, their margins could actually be negative. Think about SaaS: the customer pays them monthly fixed revenue. But at the time, in 2024, there were two new clouds, and most of the time they had to rely on hyperscaler on-demand GPU rates. They were paying $3 per GPU hour, sometimes up to $9 or $16. It was a big swing every single day. The market contracts they brought on didn’t really help them control margins. There was no scale, and they couldn’t really sign long-term contracts because they didn’t know what the future would look like. They were startups.

In my mind, this was obviously an industry issue, not an individual company’s issue. It’s an industry issue. Just like American Airlines can’t run an airline without hedging its oil prices, it’s not American Airlines’ job to speculate on oil prices. It’s their job to run an airline company. Similarly, it’s not AI companies’ job to speculate on GPU cycles. You want to lock in your cost of production, which is compute, GPUs, and tokens, and focus on products.

At that moment in 2024, I realized that if the whole industry grew at the speed it was supposed to, it would absolutely need all the traditional risk management tools, benchmarks, and platforms that every other asset class enjoyed. To me, it was a no-brainer. I left Bloomberg right away and started thinking about data.

Two sides of the coin: Silicon Data as "the Bloomberg for compute" and Compute Exchange as "the Nasdaq for compute"

Doug What was the first thing you did to take Silicon Data from zero to one? You’re affiliated with your former employer. What’s the relationship there, and how did you get your first customer?

Why token prices are falling: workflows moving to open-source and open-weight models

Carmen Li It’s really fascinating. Don Wilson is the former CEO of DRW Trading. When I was at DRW, I was a junior trader. I was definitely not one of the top-tier traders by any means, but I worked on a few initiatives at DRW back then. He knew me from those initiatives. We engaged again, and he saw the world even bigger than I did. He saw it not only from an index-linked perspective, but also through spot market auction processes and compute marketplaces. We got connected, and for us it was a no-brainer. He said, “Great. Why don’t you do Bloomberg, and we will seed you, and then the rest is history.”

This is really interesting: we’re in the process of hiring our first product manager for Silicon Data. For the past 2.5 years, there was no product person. We’re hiring our first salesperson, too. There hasn’t been a salesperson to this day. All the clients and products we have at Silicon Data were created by engineers and me, I guess, because everything is very intuitive. We’ve seen every other asset class, and I know exactly what an asset class would need: great benchmarking, indices, alternative data, and things that help people have transparency and efficiency and trust in the system.

Licensing indices to CME for H100 and B200 compute futures, and four ETFs filed before the futures even trade

Again, we’re not reinventing the wheel. We’re looking at other asset classes, following best practices, and creating relevant products. But now we’re reaching a scale where I can’t possibly do all that myself, so we’re hiring new people. We have about 30 people at Silicon Data and about 10 at Compute Exchange.

I took over Compute Exchange, as you mentioned in the intro, late last year. Compute Exchange is fascinating. Think of them as two sides of a coin. Silicon Data is like Bloomberg for compute. We give you market intelligence and tools for risk management, but you can’t get anything real from Silicon Data. You can’t get GPUs or API access for tokens. It’s the referee layer for compute.

The flip side is Compute Exchange, which is the liquidity layer for compute resources. You can procure long-term contracts and forward contracts on compute, GPUs, and tokens through Compute Exchange. You can also do secondary transactions on servers and physically get servers through Compute Exchange. We’re like Nasdaq for compute. So you’re managing two sides of a coin.

Doug So one company sells the data and is the industry benchmark, and the other company sells the GPUs.

Carmen Li The physical asset.

Doug Exactly, the physical asset. The spot market; the other one is for hedging.

Carmen Li That’s right.

Doug What are the actual products you sell to customers at Silicon Data, and who do you sell to?

Carmen Li We like to say licensing. The data world is about licensing. Think about S&P or Bloomberg index models. We license our indices to CME, one of our most famous products. CME is going to launch compute futures in the next few weeks based on our indices: H100 and B200 to start. We think that’s an excellent choice. H100 is one of the most popular chips for inference and some training, and B200 is the later-generation chip. It’s getting extremely popular globally for inference and training. Those are the first two chips on which futures will launch. I’m sure they’ll eventually launch options on top of the futures.

What makes an index the source of truth: tracking supply-demand, resisting manipulation, staying neutral

Another exciting product is a licensing agreement. It’s very similar to any other index. Usually, it’s a combination of different things. It can be a revenue-share model, for example. That’s the indices layer. We can also license indices for OTC transactions. If someone wants to do a bilateral trade with you, a block trade, or create any sort of vehicle based on my indices, such as swaps, there’s usually a fee involved for that particular creation.

Carmen Li

We have to continuously improve our methodology and underlying data sets to make sure our indices continue to reflect the demand and supply curve. There are a few golden rules for index providers.
